Page XVII

### CRITICAL NOTE

The works of the Platonist philosopher Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234 – c. 305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and a student of Plotinus.</note>, which were once very abundant and marked by the gifts of varied learning, have met with an extremely unfair fate. For most of those which have reached us are now available in a badly corrupted state, while others—and these the most significant—have been destroyed and lost, either through the mockery of fortune or the unholy fury of "pious" men <note>original: "piorum hominum furore impio". This refers to the historical decree to burn Porphyry’s work *Against the Christians*, which was considered a threat to the early Church.</note>. Although in recent times we have seen more intensive care dedicated to his individual books, no one has yet been found who could provide all the monuments of Porphyry’s genius, collected and corrected, in a form usable by learned men, and rescue the writer himself from decay and oblivion. 

Whether you survey the surviving books, for the most part very rare and difficult to read, or weigh the plentiful remnants of that vast shipwreck <note>The editor uses the metaphor of a shipwreck to describe the fragmentary and scattered state of Porphyry's lost writings.</note> hidden away in remote corners, you will easily concede that this philosopher is most worthy of such care. That I should undertake the management of this task, my former advisor and benevolent helper was **GOTTFRIED BERNHARDY** of Halle <note>Gottfried Bernhardy (1800–1875) was a prominent German philologist and professor at the University of Halle.</note>, an excellent director of our studies, who arranged that in the autumn of 1846, through the munificence of the most august King of Prussia, I might be permitted to examine the Porphyrian books in the Munich library <note>Referring to the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek in Munich.</note>. 

When I had spent three months on this business, having returned to Halle, I gave myself strenuously to collecting the remains of Porphyry from every side. But soon there followed such changes in my circumstances that I was turned away from the course I had begun, and afterward, overwhelmed by other business, I procrastinated in my Porphyrian studies. At last, in the year 1858, I once again set my hand to completing the web I had once begun to weave. Since, however, I had realized that a full and complete edition of Porphyry was a difficult and Herculean task, I decided in the meantime to narrow my scope and publish those books which seemed most likely to be of public interest in the **Teubner Library** <term>Bibliotheca Teubneriana: A prestigious series of Greek and Latin classical texts founded by B.G. Teubner, known for its rigorous scholarly standards.</term>. Just as [the plan] of this library—

<summary>In this preface, the editor laments the poor condition and loss of Porphyry’s philosophical works and describes his long-delayed journey to compile a new edition, supported by Gottfried Bernhardy and the King of Prussia.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Gottfried Bernhardy, University of Halle, Munich Library, Bibliotheca Teubneriana, Neoplatonism, book burning, manuscript scholarship</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page concludes the editor’s prose introduction and begins the "Annotatio Critica" (Critical Note), which lists specific textual corrections for Porphyry’s "Life of Pythagoras." The editor explains his selection process for which works to include in this volume.</meta>

Page VIII

->CRITICAL NOTE<-

Because the constraints of the series <note>original: "thecae rationes"; likely referring to the publisher’s series or the physical volume limits.</note> demanded it, I have excluded from this collection the life of Plotinus which Adolf Kirchhoff <note>A 19th-century German classical scholar.</note> recently added to his edition of Plotinus’s works. Nor did I admit the *Homeric Questions* or the short book *On the Cave of the Nymphs*, as we eagerly await the edition of those small works being prepared by Eugen Mehler. Therefore, I have chosen three small works for myself: *The Life of Pythagoras*, *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, and the *Letter to Marcella*. I believed that applying effort to the revision of these would be quite useful. I believe I have healed quite a few defects in the traditional text; however, to untangle the more serious difficulties that remain, there will be a need for more fortunate talents and the passage of time <note>original: "longo die", literally "a long day"; implying that time and future scholarship eventually reveal answers.</note>, which sometimes offers up freely that which you have sought for a long time in vain. If I should happen to turn the interest of others toward this study, I will consider my effort to have been worthwhile. Now, I wish to present those matters which pertain to this edition.

## I. ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.

To this fragment of the *History of Philosophers* <note>original: "philosóphou historías"; Porphyry wrote a multi-volume history of philosophy, of which only fragments survive.</note>, I have prefixed the other fragments of the otherwise intact work.

— Page 3, lines 7 and 8: "they educate" [ekpaideuousi] is corrupted; I would have written "they set out/expose" [ektitheasi].
— Page 4, lines 9 and 10: "from... history" and line 12: "into the Peloponnese" are omitted from Angelo Mai’s edition. Line 14: "6 years" [etē 6]] "60 years" [etē 60] according to Mai. Line 26: "406"] "407" in the B, V, and E manuscripts of the Suda <note>The Suda is a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>. "160 years only" in manuscript A of the Suda.
— Page 5, line 17: "of them" [autōn]] I have written "of themselves" [hautōn]. "discovery" [heurēsin]] I have written "discovery" [heuresin] <note>A minor spelling correction following the scholar Lobeck.</note>.
— Page 6, line 10: "those of Xenetus"] was long ago corrected to "those of Exaenetus" according to Diogenes Laertius, Book 8, chapter 53. Line 12: "in the history of the philosopher" is omitted in the B, V, and E manuscripts of the Suda. Line 17: "the Eleatic" [eleatou] in Suda manuscripts A, V, and E; "the Elaitic" [elaitou] in B; "of Elaea" [Elaitou] as suggested by Ludolf Kuster following Isaac Casaubon's notes on Athenaeus, Book 12, chapter 7.
— Page 7, line 1: "Melitus"] I have written "Meletus." Line 5: I have added the word "would" [an]. Line 11: "of Pintharus"] "of Spintharus" according to Holstenius <note>Lucas Holstenius (1596–1661), a German humanist and geographer.</note>. Line 12: "around himself"? Line 15: "form"? Line 16: I would have written "of character" [ēthous] following manuscript D of Theodoret. Line 18: "would be burned" [phlechtheiē] according to Cyril; "would be taken" [lēphtheiē] according to Theodoret. Line 20: "to abstain" [aposchesthai]] "to be keeping away" [apechesthai] according to Theodoret. Line 25: "the" and "and" are omitted by Cyril. Lines 26–28: the phrase "on the one hand... the things told in myths" was omitted by Cyril; I have added it from Theodoret. Line 28: "judging by tribe" [philokrinountes]] "sorting through" [phylokrinountes] in manuscript C of Theodoret. Line 29: "he had worked" according to Cyril. Line 30: "the art of stone-cutting" according to Theodoret. "either his father himself" according to Cyril.

<header>ON THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS.</header>

**8, 1** *was interrupting* <note>original: "ἐνέκοπτεν"</note> is omitted by Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century bishop whose works often quoted Porphyry to argue against him.</note>. **2** *at least* <note>original: "γε"</note> is omitted by Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrrhus, a theologian who preserved many fragments of Greek philosophy.</note>.
**3** *cleanly* <note>original: "καθάριος"</note>] *purifying* <note>original: "καθάρσιος"</note> in Cyril; I have written *elegant* <note>original: "καθάρειος"</note> following Carel Gabriel Cobet in *Mnemosyne* volume 8, page 291. **8** *trustworthy* <note>original: "ἀξιόπιστος"</note>] *untrustworthy* <note>original: "ἀναξιόπιστος"</note> according to Cobet in the work cited above. **11, 12** *in the work of Philocrates* <note>original: "ἐν τῷ Φιλοκράτους"</note> are faulty words; perhaps we should read *in the work about Socrates* <note>original: "ἐν τῷ περὶ Σωκράτους"</note>.

**9, 5** *to hold* <note>original: "σχεῖν"</note>] *to have* <note>original: "ἔχειν"</note> in Theodoret, who soon after has *citizen* <note>original: "πολίτην"</note>. **8** *to escape notice* <note>original: "λαθεῖν"</note>] I have restored *to take* <note>original: "λαβεῖν"</note> from Theodoret. *for himself* <note>original: "ἑαυτῷ"</note>] I have written *for him* <note>original: "αὐτῷ"</note>; Theodoret omits this pronoun. **9** *by marriage* <note>original: "γάμῳ"</note> in Cyril; *having been married* <note>original: "γαμηθεῖσαν"</note> in Theodoret. **14** *whenever* <note>original: "ἐπειδὰν"</note>] I have written *since* <note>original: "ἐπειδὴ"</note>. **18** *sometimes quarrelsome in social interactions* <note>original: "ὁμιλίαις ἐνίοτε φιλαπεχθήμονα"</note> in Theodoret’s manuscript D. **27** *being [some number of] years old* <note>original: "ἔτη ὄντι"</note>?

**10, 4** *of the first* <note>original: "πρώτου"</note> in the Suda <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note> under V. **22** *to wrestle* <note>original: "παλαῖσαι"</note>] I have written *to win* <note>original: "νικῆσαι"</note>.

**11, 10** I have added *if so* <note>original: "εἰ οὕτω"</note>. **15** *of the divine* <note>original: "τοῦ θείου"</note> in Cyril, Book I. **16** *highest* <note>original: "ἀνώτατον"</note> in Book VIII. **17** *third* <note>original: "τρίτην"</note> in Book VIII. *and also the* <note>original: "δὲ καὶ τὴν"</note> in Book I. **18** *divinity* <note>original: "θειότητα"</note> in Book I.

**12, 12—26** *but he came forth* — *of substance* <note>original: "προῆλθε δὲ — ὑποστάσεως"; nauck is questioning whether this passage on "hypostasis" or essential nature belongs to Porphyry.</note> these words seem to be foreign to Porphyry.

After I arranged these remains of the *History of Philosophy* <note>original: "philosphou historias"</note> and sent them to Leipzig to be printed, Daniel Chwolson <note>A prominent Orientalist and professor in St. Petersburg.</note> shared with me Shahrastani’s book, which was translated into the common tongue by Haarbrücker: *Abu-'l-Fath Muhammad asch-Schahrastânî’s Religious Parties and Philosophical Schools. Translated from Arabic by Th. Haarbrücker. Second Part. Halle 1851.* There, Porphyry’s name is repeatedly mentioned; these are the parts that seem to pertain to the *History of Philosophy*. Page 145: *Porphyry cites that Thales appeared in the 123rd year since the reign of Bukhtunassar (Nebuchadnezzar)* *). Concerning Anaxagoras on page 86: *Porphyry reports of him that he said the basis of things was "One Body," the matter of the universe, infinite; but he did not explain what this body was, whether it belonged to the fundamental elements or fell outside of them. He says: from him proceed all bodies and physical things—*

---

Page X

<header>CRITICAL NOTE.</header>

...forces and the types and the classes. He was the first to have claimed the "being-hidden" and "coming-into-appearance," insofar as he established the rule that all things were hidden in the first body, and existence was merely their coming-into-appearance from this body, and what follows. <note>The editor is quoting a German philosophical summary regarding early theories of matter and manifestation.</note> For the rest, I have recently shown in another case that this Arabic guide <note>original: "Arabe isto duce"</note> must be used with the greatest caution (see *Bulletin of the historical sciences class of the Imperial Academy of Sciences of St. Petersburg* vol. XVI no. 28 = *Greco-Roman Miscellany* vol. II pp. 181—199).

Those who long ago performed great service in correcting and illustrating the *Life of Pythagoras* were Conrad Rittershusius, whose first edition of all appeared at Altdorf in the year 1610, and Lucas Holstenius, who, among other writings of Porphyry, revised this little work at Rome in 1630, translated it into Latin, and added observations concerning the earlier chapters (1–26). The Holstenian edition was printed again at Cambridge in 1655; L. Kuster (Amsterdam, 1707) and Theophilus Kiessling (Leipzig, 1816), the editors of Iamblichus's books on the *Life of Pythagoras*, reused the materials of Rittershusius and Holstenius. Finally, in recent memory, A. Westermann provided a few corrected words of the author in various places following the Didot edition of Diogenes Laertius. For my part, I am noting the reading of the first edition—derived from I know not which manuscript—and I am adding the readings of the Munich Codex 91 <term>Codex Monacensis 91: A 13th-century parchment manuscript held in Munich, a primary source for this text.</term> which I collated myself. In this manuscript, the final part of the work, *the friendship of generations etc.* <note>original: "γενεῶν τὸ φιλικὸν κτἑ."</note> (pages 38, 21—39, 25 of this edition), is now missing due to a leaf being torn out. Furthermore, I pass over the typesetting errors in the first edition, which are all too frequent, in silence; nor do I think it necessary to note every time the Munich manuscript provides *not even* <note>original: "μὴ δέ"</note> as two words instead of one <note>original: "μηδέ"</note>, or confuses the rough and smooth breathing marks <note>Breathing marks in Greek indicate whether an initial vowel is aspirated (pronounced with an 'h' sound).</note>.

Page 14, 1 **THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS BY MALCHUS OR THE KING** <note>Porphyry's birth name was Malchus, which means "king" in his native Phoenician; "Porphyry" was a nickname meaning "clothed in purple," the color of royalty.</note>] **The Life of Pythagoras** in M (the Munich manuscript 91). **5** *Neanthes* <note>An ancient Greek historian.</note> is likely the correct reading according to C. Müller in *Fragments of the Greek Historians* vol. 3 p. 9: see however Athenaeus book XIII p. 572 E. *but in* <note>original: "δὲ ἐν"</note>] *but in* <note>original: "δ' ἐν"</note> in M. **6** *Pyrrhus* <note>original: "πύρρου"</note>] *Tyre* <note>original: "Τύρου"</note> according to Holstenius; or should we read *Cyrrhus*? *of Syria* <note>original: "τῆς συρρίας"</note> in M. **8** *on the island and having sold* <note>original: "νήσῳ καὶ ἀποδόμενον"</note>] *and* <note>original: "καὶ"</note> is omitted in M. **11** *Pyrrha* <note>original: "πύρραν"</note>] *Tyre* <note>original: "Τύρον"</note> according to Holstenius; perhaps *Gerrha* should be written.

*not even one* <note>original: "μὴ δὲ ἕν"</note> in Manuscript M. **Line 31:** *a certain one* <note>original: "ἕν τι"</note> in M. **Line 32:** *especially* <note>original: "ἄλλως τε καὶ"</note> according to Westermann <note>Anton Westermann, a 19th-century classical scholar</note>.

*of the Centuripinians* <note>original: "Κεντοριπίνων"</note> according to Holstenius. *of her* <note>original: "αὐτῆς"</note>] *of him* <note>original: "αὐτοῦ"</note> in M. **Line 19:** *Messapians* <note>original: "μεσάπιοι"</note>] *Messapians (with a final sigma)* <note>original: "μεσαπιοὶσ"</note> in M. **Line 20:** *Peucetians* <note>original: "πευκετιοὶ"</note> in M. **Lines 21–22:** The phrase *from the acquaintances — and generally* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶν γνωρίμων — καὶ καθόλου"</note> is omitted in the first edition. **Line 21:** *of the acquaintances* <note>original: "γνορίμων"</note> in M. **Line 24:** *both toward themselves* <note>original: "τε πρὸς ἑαυτὰς"</note> in M.

---

## II. ON ABSTINENCE.

We possess quite a few manuscripts of this excellent work, but all, as far as we know, are derived from the same highly corrupted source book: for my part, I have compared the Munich manuscripts 91 (Ma) and 39 (Mb); where these agree with one another, any disagreement in the other manuscripts, if there be any, may be neglected without loss. For in all cases, the primary goal is to determine what the common source (A) of our books contained, and this is usually easily perceived. There is no purpose in reporting the peculiar flaws of each individual book or the errors of previous editors. In the modern era, following the first editor Petrus Victorius <note>Pietro Vettori, a 16th-century Italian humanist</note>, those who have served well in correcting the faults of the manuscripts include Fogerolles, Valentin, Reiske, and Rudolph.

# XVIII
## CRITICAL ANNOTATION.

**Hercher.** Regarding the corrections of Felicianus (for I am certain I recognize the editor, and I do not believe he used better manuscripts than those available to us), I have made a conjecture based on his Latin translation, which was repeated by Rhoerius <note>Philippus Rhoerius, an 18th-century editor</note>. Furthermore, I thought certain <term>scholia</term> <note>ancient marginal explanations or comments</note> should be added in the margins of this edition that are common to our manuscripts; these are few in number and mostly trivial, but they are not entirely to be neglected because of the mention of Sopater <note>likely a 4th-century rhetorician or commentator</note> on page 92.

**Page 43, 10:** *having lamented* <note>original: "ἀποδυραμένῳ"</note>] *having stripped* <note>original: "ἀποδυσαμένῳ"</note> suggested by Sturzius in his work on Empedocles, page 504. **16:** *of them* <note>original: "αὐτῶν"</note> in Manuscript A. **19:** *indeed and of strength* <note>original: "μὲν καὶ ῥώμης"</note>] I would prefer *for the sake of or strength* <note>original: "ἕνεκα ἢ ῥώμης"</note>. **20:** *to transform* <note>original: "μεταβάλεσθαι"</note> in Manuscript A. I added *you* <note>original: "σε"</note>. **22:** *toward* <note>original: "πρὸς"</note>] I wrote *concerning* <note>original: "περὶ"</note>.

**44, 2:** *or to the* <note>original: "ἢ τῷ"</note> suggested by Hercher. **4:** *the fear* <note>original: "τὸν φόβον"</note>] *fear* <note>original: "φόβον"</note> suggested by Hercher. **7:** *fear* <note>original: "φόβον"</note>] *longing* <note>original: "πόθον"</note> suggested by Fogerolles. **14:** *of words* <note>original: "λόγων"</note>] I wrote *words* <note>original: "λόγους"</note>. **26:** *they have spoken against* <note>original: "ἀντειρήκασιν"</note> was previously read after *showing* <note>original: "δεικνύντα"</note> (line 25); it was transposed by R (that is, Reiske). # CRITICAL NOTES. XXII

*becoming* <note>original: "εὐπρεπῆ"</note> in Manuscript Mm. **26:** *him/it* <note>original: "αὐτὸν"</note> in the common reading. **30:** *meat-eating* <note>original: "κρεηφαγία"</note> in Manuscript A.
**32:** *of those needing* <note>original: "δεομένων"</note>] *of the one [feminine] needing* <note>original: "δεομένης"</note> I have written.

**73, 3:** *of the [feminine] into the body thicker* <note>original: "τῆς εἰς τὸ σῶμα παχυτέρα"</note> in Manuscript Mm. **4:** *of distribution* <note>original: "ἀναδόσεως"</note> <note>This term often refers to the distribution of nutrients in the body during digestion.</note> seems it should be deleted. **5:** *suffering* <note>original: "πάθος"</note>] *thickness* <note>original: "πάχος"</note> I have written. **9:** *them* <note>original: "αὐτοὺς"</note> in Manuscript Mm. **11:** *him/it* <note>original: "αὐτὸν"</note> in Manuscript Mm. **22:** *of meat-eaters* <note>original: "κρεωφάγων"</note> in some manuscripts.
**25. 26:** *having been removed — having been lightened* [plural] <note>original: "περιαιρεθέντων — κουφισθέντων"</note>] *having been removed — having been lightened* [singular] <note>original: "περιαιρεθέντος — κουφισθέντος"</note> suggested by Fogerolles. <note>François de Fogerolles was a 17th-century physician and editor.</note>

**74, 2:** *the [masculine] in* or *the [neuter] in* <note>original: "τὸν ἐν vel τὸ ἐν"</note> in the manuscripts; *the [masculine]* <note>original: "τὸν"</note> I have written. **4:** *would/perhaps* <note>original: "ἂν"</note> I have added.
**5:** the words *I mean* <note>original: "λέγω δὲ"</note> I have noted as spurious. <note>In textual criticism, "spurious" means the editor believes these words were added later and were not part of the original author's text.</note> **6:** *on account of pleasure* <note>original: "δι’ ἡδονὴν"</note>] *and pleasure* <note>original: "δ’ ἡδονὴν"</note> in Manuscript Ma; *pleasure* <note>original: "ἡδονὴν"</note> I have written. **13:** *but the [one] from the* <note>original: "ὁ δ’ ἐκ τῶν"</note>] *but the [one] of the* <note>original: "ὁ δὲ τῶν"</note> I have written, following Diogenes Laertius (Book 10, section 144) and Porphyry's *Letter to Marcella* (section 27). **14:** *both at once and* <note>original: "τε ἅμα καὶ"</note> by Rhoer. <note>Jacob de Rhoer, an 18th-century Dutch philologist.</note> **18:** *has fallen away* <note>original: "ἐκπέπτωκεν"</note> suggested by Rhoer; *to have by nature the* <note>original: "ἔχειν φύσει τὴν"</note> by Rhoer. **21. 22:** *the [one] entirely from the [one] rejoicing, the [one] from the empty [things]* <note>original: "τὴν δὲ ὅλως ἀπὸ τοῦ χαίροντος, τὴν δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν κενῶν"</note> in Manuscript A; *entirely* <note>original: "ὅλως"</note> was moved by Rhoer. **28:** *meat-eating* <note>original: "κρεηφαγίας"</note> in Manuscript A.

**75, 8:** *of complete [feminine]* <note>original: "τελέας"</note>] *complete* <note>original: "τελείας"</note> by Valentinus. <note>Benedictus Felicianus, or "Valentinus," a 16th-century translator.</note> **19:** *an exchange* <note>original: "ἀντάλλαγος"</note> I would prefer. **30:** *and/both* <note>original: "τε"</note>] *but* <note>original: "δὲ"</note> I have written. *so many* <note>original: "τοσαῦτα"</note>] *such things* <note>original: "τοιαῦτα"</note> I have written.
**31:** *and painful?* <note>original: "καὶ ἀλγεινόν;"</note>

**76, 3. 4:** *increases together with* <note>original: "συνεπαυξεῖ"</note> in Manuscript A. **18:** *of the thinnest* <note>original: "λεπτοτάτης"</note>] *of the simplest* <note>original: "λιτοτάτης"</note> I have written. **20:** *not even* <note>original: "οὐδὲ"</note>] *nor* <note>original: "μηδὲ"</note> I have written. **22:** *is about to* <note>original: "μέλλει"</note> by Victorius. <note>Piero Vettori, a famous Italian scholar.</note> **24:** *health* <note>original: "ὑγίειαν"</note> in Manuscript Ma; *health* <note>original: "ὑγείαν"</note> in Manuscript Mb. **24. 25:** *meat-eating* <note>original: "κρεηφαγίαν"</note> in Manuscript A. **26:** *of which* <note>original: "ὧν"</note>] *which things* <note>original: "ἃ"</note> I have written. **27. 28:** *if however* <note>original: "εἰ δὲ"</note>] *if however the* <note>original: "εἰ δ’ οἱ"</note> I have written. **31:** *neither of the* <note>original: "οὔτε τοῦ"</note>] *nor of the* <note>original: "οὐδὲ τοῦ"</note> silently by Hercher. <note>Rudolf Hercher, a 19th-century German philologist.</note> **32:** *not even of the common* <note>original: "οὐδὲ τοῦ κοινοῦ"</note>] *neither of the common* <note>original: "οὔτε τοῦ κοινοῦ"</note> I have written.

# DE ABSTINENTIA.
## XXIII

**Mm. 22:** *of them* <note>original: "αὐτῶν"</note> in the common reading <note>original: "vulgo"</note>. **24:** *not* <note>original: "μὴ"</note>] *or* <note>original: "ἢ"</note> suggested by Reiske <note>Johann Jakob Reiske was an 18th-century German physician and philologist.</note>. **25:** *but from* <note>original: "δὲ ἐκ"</note>] *but also* <note>original: "δὲ καὶ"</note> I have written; *but of the* <note>original: "δὲ τοῦ"</note> suggested by Reiske. **26:** *of these* <note>original: "τούτων"</note>] *of this* <note>original: "τούτου"</note> suggested by Valentinus. **28:** *gods* <note>original: "θεῶν"</note> in Manuscript Mm; *to God* <note>original: "θεῷ"</note> following the editors led by Victorius.

**81, 1:** *for the one born* <note>original: "φύντι"</note> in Manuscript Mm. *but* <note>original: "δὲ"</note>] *and* <note>original: "τε"</note> I have written. **2:** *simpler* <note>original: "ἁπλούστερος"</note>] *more dispassionate* <note>original: "ἀπαθέστερος"</note> I have written. **3:** *more self-sufficient* <note>original: "αὐταρκέστερος"</note> suggested by Hercher. Perhaps it is better to restore the superlative forms everywhere. **13:** *of those needing* <note>original: "δεομένων"</note> is a corrupted reading. **22:** *having surpassed* <note>original: "ὑπερβαλόμενοι"</note> I would prefer. **24:** *towards the* <note>original: "πρὸς τὴν"</note>?

**82, 5:** *it was fitting* <note>original: "προσῆκεν"</note>] *it is fitting* <note>original: "προσήκει"</note> I have written. **7:** *it needs* <note>original: "δεῖται"</note>] *it is necessary* <note>original: "δεῖ"</note> suggested by Valentinus. **12:** *animals, the same transgression is altogether overlooked* <note>original: "ζῶα τὸ αὐτὸ παρορᾶται πλημμέλημα πάντως"</note> in Manuscript Mm. **18:** *in the social life* <note>original: "τῷ πολιτικῷ βίῳ"</note>? **23:** *for* <note>original: "γὰρ"</note>] *consequently* <note>original: "ἄρα"</note> I have written. **29:** *for humans* <note>original: "ἀνθρώποις"</note> seems incorrect; perhaps read *otherwise* <note>original: "ἄλλως"</note>.

**83, 5:** *wickednesses* <note>original: "μοχθηρίαι"</note>] *wicked things* <note>original: "μοχθηραὶ"</note> in the Bodleian Manuscript. **6:** *it falls forward* <note>original: "προπίπτει"</note>] *it strikes* <note>original: "προσπίπτει"</note> suggested by Fogerolles. **10:** *and* <note>original: "τε"</note> added from the Leipzig Manuscript. **12:** *which [feminine plural] through* <note>original: "αἳ διὰ"</note> in Manuscript Mm. **23:** *and these things* <note>original: "καὶ ταῦτα"</note>] *these things and* <note>original: "ταῦτα καὶ"</note> in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: "PE."</note>, page 28, section D. *The step of error when* <note>original: "πλάνης κλιμακτὴρ ὅτε"</note>] *the seeker of error* <note>original: "πλάνης μαστὴρ ὁ"</note> in Eusebius; *and the seeker of error* <note>original: "πλάνης καὶ μαστὴρ ὁ"</note> in Toupius, *Short Works* <note>original: "opusc."</note> volume II, page 403. **26:** *divine things* <note>original: "θείοις"</note>] *gods* <note>original: "θεοῖς"</note> in Eusebius. *of these* <note>original: "τούτων"</note>] *of these things then* <note>original: "τούτων οὖν"</note> by the same [Eusebius]. **28:** *reaping with hands* <note>original: "χερσὶν ἀμώμενοι"</note> I would have written.

**84, 1:** *through* <note>original: "διὰ"</note> omitted by Eusebius. **3:** *we guard* <note>original: "φυλάττομεν"</note>] *they were guarding* <note>original: "ἐφύλαττον"</note> by the same [Eusebius]. *as* <note>original: "ὡς"</note> added from the same. **4:** *most similar* <note>original: "ὁμοιώτατον"</note> in Manuscript Mm. **6:** *turning out* <note>original: "ἐκβαίνοντα"</note>] *signifying* <note>original: "σημαίνοντα"</note> in Eusebius. **9:** *was about to* <note>original: "ἔμελλεν"</note> in Manuscript Mm. **10:** *of those having introduced further* <note>original: "ἐπεισαγαγόντων"</note>] *of those introducing further* <note>original: "ἐπεισαγόντων"</note> in Eusebius. **11:** *those about to pray* <note>original: "ἀρασομένους"</note>] *those having prayed* <note>original: "ἀρασαμένους"</note> by the same [Eusebius]. *now being burned as incense* <note>original: "θυμιώμενα νῦν"</note>] *now* is omitted by Eusebius. **15:** *of the — grass* <note>original: "τῆς — πόας"</note>] *the — grass* <note>original: "την — πόαν"</note> suggested by Reiske. I would prefer *of the [earth] producing trees* <note>original: "δένδρα φυούσης"</note>. **16:** *and first* <note>original: "καὶ πρώτης"</note>] *first* <note>original: "πρώτης"</note> suggested by Hercher. **20:** *the* <note>original: "τὰ"</note> I have added. *of nuts* <note>original: "καρύων"</note>] *of fruits* <note>original: "καρπῶν"</note> suggested by Reiske. **20, 21:** *of Demetreius* <note>original: "Δημητρείου"</note>] *of Demetrius* <note>original: "Δημητρίου"</note> I have written. **21, 22:** *the barley first appearing* <note>original: "πρώτου φανέντος τοῦ τῶν κριθῶν"</note> or *the barleys first having appeared* <note>original: "πρώτων φανεισῶν τῶν κριθῶν"</note> conjectured by Reiske. *having appeared* <note>original: "φανέντος"</note> is omitted in Manuscript Ma. **24:** *having bruised* <note>original: "ἐρειξαμένων"</note> suggested by Hercher, perhaps correctly; however, see Arcadius <note>A 4th-century Greek grammarian.</note>, page 152, line 13. **27:** *the* [neuter] <note>original: "τὸ"</note>] *the* [masculine] <note>original: "τὸν"</note> suggested by Reiske. **28:** *and they offered first fruits of* <note>original: "ἀπήρξαντό τε τῆς"</note>] *and* <note>original: "τε"</note> I have deleted. **30:** *of sacrificial offerings* <note>original: "θυηλῶν"</note>] *of sacrifices* <note>original: "θυσιῶν"</note> suggested by Reiske. *by those having touched late* <note>original: "ὀψαισθεῖσι"</note>] *by barley-groats* <note>original: "ψαισθεῖσι"</note> suggested by Fogerolles. **31, 32:** *of the sacrifices from the beginning* <note>original: "τῶν ἐξ ἀρχῆς θυμάτων"</note>?

**85, 2–10:** This passage is heavily laboring <note>This indicates the text is extremely difficult to decipher or reconstruct in this section.</note>. **12:** *being led* <note>original: "ἀγομένη"</note> or *being seen* <note>original: "ὁρωμένη"</note> I would prefer. *and seeing* <note>original: "καὶ ὁρῶν"</note> in Manuscript Mm. **13:** One might expect *mud-grass* <note>original: "ἰλυσπόα"</note>, but even this does not seem probable. In the phrase *upon berry-stones* <note>original: "ἐπὶ πυρηνίων"</note>, I suspected *olive stones* <note>original: "ἐλᾶαι πυρῆνες"</note> were hidden. **14, 15:** *offerings of first-fruits* <note>original: "ἡγητήρια"</note> in Manuscript Ma. **15:** *cake* <note>original: "φθόις"</note>] *cakes* <note>original: "φθοῖς"</note> suggested by Rhoer. **15, 16:** *to upright-stands* or *upright-stands* <note>original: "ὀρθοστάταις" or "ὀρθοστάτας"</note> in the books [manuscripts]; *upright-stand* <note>original: "ὀρθοστάτης"</note> suggested by Valentinus; *upright-stands* <note>original: "ὀρθοστάται"</note> suggested by Rhoer. **17:** *of those excelling* <note>original: "προεχουσῶν"</note>] *of those going forward* <note>original: "προϊουσῶν"</note> in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, page 29 B [151 A], and Theodoret, *Cure of Greek Maladies* <note>original: "affect." refers to his 'Graecarum affectionum curatio'.</note>, section VII, page 108, line 29. **29:** *or to the gods* <note>original: "ἢ θεοῖς"</note> in Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> under the entry for *sacrificial cakes* <note>original: "πέλανοι"</note>.

<header>CRITICAL NOTES</header>

<term>apparatus criticus</term> <note>This is a technical list where the editor compares different versions of the manuscript to decide on the most accurate wording. Numbers like "86, 9" refer to the page and line number of the Greek edition.</note>

**86, 9:** *suddenly* <note>original: "ἐξαίφνης"</note> should either be deleted or placed before *snatched away* <note>original: "ἀνάρπαστοι"</note> (line 6), as conjectured by Hercher <note>Rudolf Hercher (1821–1878) was a German classical scholar.</note>. **11:** *of one another* <note>original: "ἀλλήλων"</note> omitted by Manuscript A. **12:** *not even to see* <note>original: "οὐδὲ ἰδεῖν"</note>] *not even to do* <note>original: "οὐδ’ ἔρδειν"</note> according to Hesiod. **16:** *blessed ones* <note>original: "μακάρεσι"</note> in Manuscripts M and m. **19:** *the* <note>original: "τὴν"</note>] *the* <note>feminine dative case</note> according to Valentinus. **20:** *to these* <note>original: "τούτοις"</note>] *of these* <note>original: "τούτων"</note> by the same scholar. **26:** *last* <note>original: "ὑστάτη"</note> in Manuscript R.

**87, 3:** *to use* <note>original: "χρῆσθαι"</note>] *to use* <note>aorist tense change</note> I have written. **6:** *descendant* <note>original: "ἔγγονος"</note> in Manuscript R. **9:** *violently* <note>original: "βιαίως"</note> by Valentinus. **11:** *to wash the hands and to sacrifice you, O overseer* <note>original: "χερνίπτειν θύειν τέ σ’, ἐπίσκοπε"</note>—I was attempting this reconstruction. It is written otherwise by G. Wolff in *On Porphyry's Philosophy from Oracles*, page 39. **12:** *to Icarus* <note>original: "Ἰκάρῳ"</note>] *to Icarius* <note>original: "Ἰκαρίῳ"</note> by Meursius. **13:** *reaped* <note>original: "ἀπέθρεισεν"</note>] *reaped* <note>variant spelling</note> by Fogerolles. *Siomos* in Manuscripts M and m. **14:** *of the Citizen* <note>a title for Zeus</note>] *of the City-dweller* I have written. **14, 15:** *of the Diipolia* <note>an ancient Athenian festival</note>] *of the Diipoleia* <note>variant spelling</note> I have written. **21:** *of payments* <note>original: "ἀποδόσεων"</note>] *of defenses* <note>original: "ἀπολογιῶν"</note> I have written. **29:** *not from* <note>original: "οὐκ ἐξ"</note>] *from* <note>original: "ἐξ"</note> by Rhoer. **31:** *them* <note>original: "αὐτοὺς"</note>] *them* <note>accentuation change</note> silently changed by Hercher.

**88, 5:** *to touch* <note>original: "ἅψεσθαι"</note> in Manuscripts M, m, and the Bodleian. **5, 6:** *and from the need?* **6:** *of the oxen* <note>original: "τῶν βοῶν"</note>—I would delete this. **11:** *we say* <note>original: "φαμὲν"</note>] *we said* <note>original: "ἔφαμεν"</note> by Valentinus. **16:** *otherwise* <note>original: "ἄλλως"</note>] *others* <note>original: "ἄλλας"</note> in Manuscript R. **18:** *of the more valuable* <note>original: "τιμιωτέρων"</note>] *of the most valuable* <note>original: "τιμιωτάτων"</note> by Hercher. **26:** *the god [gave] for use*—Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, page 151 C. *but because* <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ὅτι"</note>] *but then* <note>original: "ἀλλ’ οὖν"</note> according to Eusebius. **28:** *therefore* <note>original: "οὖν"</note> added from Eusebius. **31:** *out of wishing* <note>original: "ἐκ θέλοντος"</note>] *wishing* <note>original: "ἐθέλοντος"</note>—Eusebius. **32:** *neither does he who touches the fruits of others [touch] holily*—Eusebius.

<header>### CRITICAL ANNOTATION.</header>

*...horses indeed* <note>original: πων μὲν</note>] *indeed* <note>original: μὲν</note> is omitted in Manuscript Ma. *land-based* <note>original: χερσαίων</note> is absurd: Plutarch correctly has *river horses compared with storks* <note>original: παραβαλλομένων πελαργοῖς ἵππων ποταμίων</note>. I am inclined to believe that Porphyry was deceived by a faulty reading. **26. 27** I would prefer *purity* <note>original: καθαρειότητος</note>. **27** *he knows how* <note>original: οἶδεν ὅπως</note>] *I know how* <note>original: οἶδα πῶς</note> Plutarch page 962 F, I have written *I know how* <note>original: οἶδ' ὅπως</note>. *lynxes* <note>original: λύγγας</note>] *lynxes* <note>original: λύγκας</note> silently corrected by Hercher. **29** *the lynx-stone* <note>original: τὸ λυγνούριον; a mythical gemstone believed to be formed from the solidified urine of lynxes</note> added from Plutarch, where the manuscripts have *the lynx-stone* <note>original: τὸ λυγνούριον</note>.

**149, 19** *we say* <note>original: λέγομεν</note> in Manuscript Mm, *we should say* <note>original: λέγωμεν</note> Plutarch page 963 B.

**150, 7** *I have not encountered* <note>original: μὴ ἐντετύχηκα</note>] *surely you have encountered* <note>original: μὴν ἐντετύχηκάς</note> the same author [Plutarch] page 963 D.
**9** *those of the* <note>original: τὰ τῶν</note> in Ma, *of the* <note>original: τῶν</note> in Mb, *the [thing] of the* <note>original: τὸ τῶν</note> Plutarch. **18** *to them* <note>original: αὐτοῖς</note> in the common reading.
**23. 24** *companions* <note>original: συντρόφους</note> added from Plutarch page 963 F. **25** *to be contentious* <note>original: φιλονικεῖν</note> in Ma.

**151, 2** I would set aside *we consider them kin* <note>original: οἰκείους — νομίζομεν</note>. *and indeed* <note>original: καὶ μέντοι</note>] I have written *and indeed also* <note>original: καὶ μέντοι καὶ</note>. **3** *and toward* <note>original: καὶ πρὸς</note>] I have written *and of the [thing] toward* <note>original: καὶ τῆς πρὸς</note>. **5** *then* <note>original: τότε</note>] I have written *the* <note>original: τοὺς</note>. **6** *to them* <note>original: αὐτοῖς</note> in Manuscript Mm. **8** *but also* <note>original: δὲ καὶ</note>] I have written *but* <note>original: δέ</note>. **13** I would prefer *of the same race* <note>original: γένους ταὐτοῦ</note>. **14** *men related to one another* <note>original: ἀνθρώπους οἰκείους ἀλλήλοις</note> according to Fogerolles. **15** *if both* <note>original: αἴτε</note>] *those which* <note>original: αἵ γε</note> silently corrected by Hercher. **17** *of this* <note>original: τούτου</note>] *of these* <note>original: τούτων</note> according to Valentinus, or rather Felicianus. **23** *and the souls thus* <note>original: καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς οὕτω</note>] *thus also the souls* <note>original: οὕτω καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς</note> according to Reiske. **31** *all nourishments* <note>original: τροφαὶ πᾶσαι</note>] *nourishments* <note>original: τροφαὶ</note> according to Reiske.

**152, 3** *and the* <note>original: καὶ τὴν</note>] I have written *and* <note>original: καὶ</note>. **5** I judge the phrase *of injustice* <note>original: τῆς ἀδικίας</note> to be a spurious addition. **15** *not* <note>original: οὐκ</note> was added by Fogerolles. **18** *that* <note>original: ὅτι</note> and **19** *and the unjust things* <note>original: καὶ τὰ ἄδικα</note> seem like they should be deleted. **20** I would delete *for* <note>original: γὰρ</note>. **24** *stretching out?* <note>original: παρατείνων?</note> **26** *he increases* <note>original: ἐπαυξεῖ</note> in Manuscript A.

**153, 1. 2** *by how much greater the kinship toward the race of animals, by so much* <note>original: ὅσῳ μείζων ἡ οἰκείωσις πρὸς τὸ γένος τὸ τῶν ζῴων, τοσούτῳ</note> conjectured by Reiske. I suspect the words *that of the animals* <note>original: τὸ τῶν ζῴων</note> and **2. 3** *and the kinship* <note>original: καὶ τὸ οἰκεῖον</note> are spurious additions. **4** Reiske: *this one and man* (or *the fellow-tribesman*) *because he is an animal* <note>original: οὗτος καὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον (aut τὸ ὁμόφυλον) ὅτι ζῷον</note>. Abresch: *this one and that which is an animal* <note>original: οὗτος καὶ τὸ ὅ τι ζῷον</note>. I would prefer *this one and everything that is an animal* <note>original: οὗτος καὶ πᾶν ὅ τι ζῷον</note>. **6** *to cast away* <note>original: ἀπορίψαι</note> in Manuscript Mm. **17** *in this way* <note>original: ταύτῃ</note> in Manuscript Mm and the Meerman manuscript. **25** *to be* <note>original: εἶναι</note> is omitted in Manuscript Ma.

**154, 8** *it falls forward* <note>original: προπίπτει</note>] *it strikes against* <note>original: προσπίπτει</note> according to Fogerolles. **10** *it increases [something else]* <note>original: αὔξει</note>] I have written *it increases [itself]* <note>original: αὔξεται</note>. **13** *of the first things* <note>original: τῶν πρώτων</note>] I have written *of the things which* <note>original: τῶν ἃ</note>. **14** *or of those set forth* <note>original: ἢ ἐκκειμένων</note> is a corrupted reading. **16** *and the need?* <note>original: καὶ ἡ χρεία?</note>

**155, 4** *divine and* <note>original: θεῖον καὶ</note>] I have written *divine* <note>original: θεῖον</note>. **15** I would prefer *and everything* <note>original: καὶ πάντα</note>. **16** *existing in scarcity?* <note>original: σπάνει ὑπάρχων?</note> **21** *satiety* <note>original: κόρον</note>] *resource* <note>original: πόρον</note> according to Reiske. I would prefer *and it yields* <note>original: εἴκει δὲ</note>. **22** *of him* <note>original: αὐτοῦ</note> in Manuscript A. **23** *to judge* <note>original: δικάζειν</note>] *to bribe* <note>original: δεκάζειν</note> according to Fogerolles. **24** *to her/it* <note>original: αὐτῇ</note>] I have written *of her/it* <note>original: αὐτῆς</note>. **30** *the things lying above* <note>original: τὰ ὑπερκείμενα</note> conjectured by Valentinus. **32** *desirable* <note>original: αἱρετὸν</note>] *must be chosen* <note>original: αἱρετέον</note> according to Reiske.

<page-num>XXXVI</page-num>

### III. LETTER TO MARCELLA

This small book, rarely mentioned by ancient writers, was first brought to light by Angelo Mai in Milan in the year 1816. A few years later, Johann Konrad Orelli reprinted it in his *Collection of Sentences and Morals*, volume 1 (Leipzig, 1819), pages 282–314. For a third time, Mai himself oversaw its printing in *Classical Authors*, volume 4 (Rome, 1831), pages 356–401. We possess only one manuscript, the Ambrosian Codex, the readings of which I have included below as excerpted from Mai’s editions; however, I generally pass over in silence the errors in accents and similar defects with which both of Mai’s editions abound.

**Page 193, 3** *to be in one's prime* <note>original: ἡβᾶν</note>: I suspect this should be deleted. **7** *the* <note>original: τοὺς</note> added by Creuzer in *Minor Works* III, 2, page 157. **13** *deviating* <note>original: ἀποκλίνοντα</note>] *deviating* [dative case] <note>original: ἀποκλίνοντι</note> Mai; *having deviated* <note>original: ἀποκλίναντι</note> I have written. **15** *to protect* <note>original: προστάτειν</note>] *to stand by* <note>original: παραστατεῖν</note> I have written. **18** *to do good* <note>original: εὐποιεῖν</note> in the common reading. **23** *no one* <note>original: οὐδένα</note>] *of no one* <note>original: οὐδενὸς</note> I have written. **25** *did I judge?* <note>original: ἔκρινα?</note>
**194, 13** *otherwise* <note>original: ἄλλως</note>] *others* <note>original: ἄλλους</note> I have written. **25** *and* <note>original: τε</note> I have added. **27** *more accurate* <note>original: ἀκριβέστερος</note>] *more accurate* Mai. Should we perhaps read *clearer* <note>original: εὐκρινέστερος</note>? **30** *for one preferring* <note>original: προτιμώσῃ</note>:] in the margin of the manuscript it is written as *for one loving* <note>original: ἀγαπώσῃ</note>. **32** *reminding* [masculine] <note>original: ὑπομιμνήσκων</note>] *reminding* [neuter] <note>original: ὑπομιμνῆσκον</note> I have written.
**195, 1** *further* <note>original: ἐπιπλέον</note> in the common reading (just as 199, 12 *during the day* <note>original: μεθημέραν</note> and similar things elsewhere, which I shall omit). **2** *it was in* <note>original: ἐνῆν</note>] *it would be* <note>original: ἂν ἦν</note> I have written. **3** *to flow away* <note>original: ἀπαρρύεσθαι</note> in the common reading. **4** *of her* <note>original: αὐτῆς</note>] *would... of the* <note>original: ἂν τῆς</note> I have written. **6** *to provide* <note>original: παρέχεσθαι</note>] *to procure* <note>original: πορίζεσθαι</note> I would have written (see page 197, 13). Nor does *through authority* <note>original: δι’ ἐξουσίας</note> seem healthy <note>In textual criticism, a "healthy" reading is one that makes sense and is grammatically correct; "not healthy" implies the text is likely corrupted.</note>. **17** *I am able* <note>original: δύναμαι</note>] *I might be able* <note>original: δύνωμαι</note> I have written. **20** *to inspect* <note>original: ἐπισκέπτειν</note>] *to enjoin upon* <note>original: ἐπισκήπτειν</note> Jacobs in *Philostratus*, page 675. **20—22** *more personal—to yourself* <note>original: οἰκειότερον — σεαυτῇ</note>] I would have written *of your own self, but more personally, I might say, of that which is in yourself* <note>original: τοῦ σαυτῆς, οἰκειότερον δ’ εἴποιμ’ ἂν τοῦ ἐν σεαυτῇ</note>. **23** *being left behind* <note>original: καταλειπομένη</note> conjectured by Mai.
**196, 1** *neither* <note>original: μήτε</note> in the common reading. **2** *from us?* <note>original: παρ’ ἡμῶν?</note> **2. 3** *having knocked out* <note>original: ἐκκροῦσα</note>] *to knock out* <note>original: ἐκκροῦαι</note> Mai. **6** *of the things that are* <note>original: ὄντων</note>] *truly* <note>original: ὄντως</note> I have written. **7. 8** *to those who have happened upon* <note>original: συγκυρήσασιν</note>] *to occurrences* <note>original: συγκυρήμασιν</note> I have written. **21** *where* <note>original: οὗ</note>] *not* <note>original: οὐ</note> Kaspar Orelli, which Mai silently adopted in his second edition. **23—25** The words are displaced.
**197, 2** *the* [singular] <note>original: τὸ</note> Mai; the manuscript seems to have *the* [plural] <note>original: τὰ</note>. **8** *to contribute* <note>original: συντελεῖν</note>]

After the word *burden* <note>original: φορτίον</note>, I believe some words have been lost. **23** *being corrected?* <note>original: ἐπανορθουμένη</note>

In the anthology <term>florilegium: a collection of literary excerpts</term> of Johannes Stobaeus, quite a few passages from this letter are, by a consistent error, attributed not to their true author but to Pythagoras; I have provided examples in the journal *Philologus*, volume 9, page 368. From this, a suspicion arises that the letter, which is now incomplete, could be enriched by several fragments sought from that same source. For the sake of a sample, it will suffice to have cited several maxims and exhortations <term>paraeneses: moral instructions or advice</term> which Stobaeus records as Pythagorean, but which I believe are owed to Porphyry:

> One must seek a husband, children, and friends who will remain by one's side at the departure from life (1, 21).

> Choose to be strong in the soul rather than in the body (1, 22. *Monacensis Anthology*, page 268, line 22, edited by Meineke).

> Be persuaded that nothing is your own possession which you do not hold within your mind (1, 23).

Learn to give birth to children <note>Porphyry is likely referring here to spiritual or intellectual "offspring"—virtues or ideas—rather than biological children</note>—not those that will nourish the body in old age, but those that will nourish the soul with eternal food (1, 25).

(Florilegium Monacense), a collection of excerpts used by scholars</note> page 270, line 13, edited by Meineke).

I was writing this at St. Petersburg <note>Latin: Petropoli</note>.

## BOOK I.

I. Eusebius, *Chronicon* p. 139, or *Anecdota Parisiensia* vol. 2 <margin>5</margin>
p. 140: The events from the fall of Troy <note>original: "Iliou halosis." The fall of Troy was used as a foundational "year zero" by ancient Greek chronologists.</note> until the first Olympiad <note>776 BCE, the date of the first recorded Olympic Games and a primary marker for Greek historical dating.</note> were not even themselves considered worthy of a complete record; nevertheless, Porphyry, in the first book of his *Philosophical History*, summarizes them roughly word-for-word as follows:

From the first book of Porphyry’s *Philosophical History*: <margin>10</margin>
From the fall of Troy to the return of the Heracleidae <note>original: "kathodon." Literally "the descent," referring to the legendary return of the descendants of Hercules, often associated by historians with the Dorian invasion of the Peloponnese.</note> into the Peloponnese, Apollodorus says there are 80 years; from that return to the founding of Ionia, 60 years; from then until Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note>, 159 <margin>15</margin> years; and from Lycurgus until the first Olympiad, 108 years. The total from the fall of Troy until the first Olympiad is 407 years. *Anecdota Parisiensia* vol. 2 p. 188, 28: From the fall of Troy until the first Olympiad, 407 <margin>20</margin> years; for this is also Porphyry's opinion. Cf. C. Müller in *Fragments of the Greek Historians* <note>original: "fragmenta historicorum Graecorum"</note> vol. 3 p. 689.

II. The Suda, under the entry "Homer": And he lived 460 years before the establishment of the first Olympiad; <margin>25</margin> but Porphyry in his *Philosophical History* says 132 years before; and this [the Olympiad] was established 407 years after the fall of Troy. Some record that Homer was born 160 years after the fall of Troy; but the aforementioned Porphyry says 275 years after. <margin>30</margin>

III. Suidas, under "Hesiod of Cyme": <note>The *Suidas* (or *Suda*) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> He was, according to some, older than Homer, but according to others, a contemporary. Porphyry and many others define him as younger by a hundred <margin>5</margin> years, so that he precedes the first Olympiad <note>776 BCE.</note> by only 32 years.

IV. Cyril, *Against Julian*, Book I, p. 28 A: <note>Cyril of Alexandria was a 5th-century Church Father who wrote a famous polemic against the Emperor Julian the Apostate. He quotes Porphyry despite Porphyry's anti-Christian reputation.</note> Porphyry, then—the one who poured out bitter words against us and all but danced in mockery of the Christian religion—says that those named the "Seven Sages" <note>A group of 7th–6th century BCE Greek philosophers and statesmen famous for their short, pithy wisdom.</note> claimed such a title for the following reason. <margin>10</margin> He writes as follows in the first book of the *Philosophical History*:
> “Though there were nine individuals, seven were called ‘wise’ for this reason. A fisherman sold a single cast of his net to some young men, and it happened that a golden tripod was found in the <margin>15</margin> catch. The fisherman said he had sold fish but not a tripod, while the young men claimed the find based on their own luck. It seemed best to entrust the judgment to the god <note>Typically referring to the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi.</note>. When the oracle declared that the tripod should be given to the ‘wise one,’ the <margin>20</margin> tripod was first brought to Thales. He, however, sent it to Bias, declaring that he was the truly wise one. Bias then sent it to another, and that one to another, until the tripod had been passed around all seven. When it returned <margin>25</margin> again to the first, it was decided to dedicate it to the god; for he alone was the wisest of all.”

V. Suidas: Pherecydes of Athens, older than the Syrian <note>Pherecydes of Syros, another early philosopher often associated with the first prose writings.</note>, of whom account says he collected the works of Orpheus. He wrote *Autochthones* <note>original: "Autochthonas." Referring to those "sprung from the earth," or the original inhabitants of a land.</note>, which is about the ancient history of Attica, in ten books; he also wrote exhortations in verse. Porphyry <margin>30</margin> accepts no one as older than the former... <note>The text here breaks off, but implies that Porphyry considered the Athenian Pherecydes to be of great antiquity.</note>

...how to predicate anything of him. But if it is necessary to dare to say something about him using our own words, the title of "the One" and "the Good" should rather be applied to him. XV. **Cyril**, *Against Julian* VIII, page 271 A: Porphyry writes in the fourth book of his *History of Philosophy*: "Plato said that <margin>15</margin> the essence of God proceeds as far as three fundamental realities <term>hypostases: the distinct levels or "persons" of divine existence in Neoplatonic thought</term>. For it is set apart from all fellowship because it is entirely simple and <margin>25</margin> does not admit of any combination; instead, the Triad <note>original: *triada*—the group of three divine principles</note> is preserved as a unity starting from the Intellect <term>Nous: the Divine Mind or pure intelligence</term>, for this is the principle."

<margin>5</margin> XVII. **Cyril**, *Against Julian* I, page 32 C: For **Porphyry** says in the fourth book of his *History of Philosophy* that **Plato** spoke about **the Good** in this way: "From this <note>the First Principle or the One</note>, in a manner that is somehow inconceivable to human thought, the **Mind** <term>Nous: the Divine Intellect, the second level of reality in Neoplatonism</term> came into being, both as a whole and existing by itself. Within this Mind are the things that truly exist <note>the eternal Forms or Ideas</note> <margin>10</margin> and the entire essence of all beings. This is also what is primarily 'the Beautiful' and 'Beauty-itself,' possessing the form of beauty from within its own nature. It came forth pre-eternally, having its impulse from God the Cause, being self-generated and its own father. For its procession <note>the act of flowing out from the source</note> <margin>15</margin> did not occur because the First Principle moved toward creating it; rather, the Mind came forth by its own generative power from God. Furthermore, it did not come forth from any beginning in time, for time did not yet exist. Even after time came to be, time is nothing in relation to the Mind; for the Mind is always timeless and alone <margin>20</margin> eternal. Just as the first and only God exists always—even if all things are born from him—he cannot be numbered among them, nor can his dignity be ranked alongside their existence. In the same way, the Mind alone is eternal, having its existence <term>hypostasis: a distinct, foundational reality</term> <margin>25</margin> outside of time. While things in time are themselves subject to time, the Mind remains in the identity of its own eternal existence." Compare **Cyril**, *Against Julian* I, page 28 D: "Both **Plutarch** and others among their most distinguished men, as well as the bold **Porphyry** who speaks against us <note>original: *kath’ hēmōn*—referring to Porphyry’s famously critical work, "Against the Christians"</note>, have written about these matters <note>concerning the philosophers who define the nature of God</note>." <margin>30</margin>

<header>PORPHYRY’S LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS</header>

# LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS

1 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ... it is agreed by most that he was the son of Mnesarchus; however, there is disagreement regarding the lineage of Mnesarchus. Some say he was a Samian, but Cleanthes, in the fifth book of his *Myths*, says he was a Syrian from Tyre in Syria. 
<margin>5</margin> When a grain shortage struck the Samians, Mnesarchus sailed there for trade with a cargo of grain and sold it; in return, he was honored with citizenship. From childhood, Pythagoras was naturally gifted for every kind of learning, so Mnesarchus 
<margin>10</margin> brought him to Tyre. There, he was introduced to the Chaldaeans <term>Chaldaeans: Babylonian priests and scholars renowned in antiquity for their expertise in astronomy, mathematics, and the occult</term> and shared in their studies for some time. Returning to Ionia, Pythagoras first studied with Pherecydes of Syros <note>an early thinker often credited with the first prose work on philosophy and the doctrine of the transmigration of souls</note>, and second with 
<margin>15</margin> Hermodamas the Creophylian <note>a descendant of Creophylus, who was legendarily the host or rival of Homer</note> in Samos, who was by then an old man. 

2 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Cleanthes says there are others who declare his father was a Tyrrhenian <term>Tyrrhenian: a term often applied to the Etruscans or the pre-Greek inhabitants of the Aegean islands</term> among those who settled in Lemnos, and that from there he went to Samos for business, 
<margin>20</margin> stayed, and became a citizen. When Mnesarchus sailed to Italy, Pythagoras—who was still quite young—sailed with him to that land, which was then exceptionally prosperous; Pythagoras later sailed back to it again. He lists his two brothers as well, Eunostus and <unclear>Tyrrhenus</unclear> <note>The text cuts off here, but historical parallels suggest the third brother's name</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the origins of Pythagoras, debating whether his father Mnesarchus was Samian, Syrian, or Tyrrhenian, and describes Pythagoras’s early education under the Chaldaeans and Pherecydes.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Mnesarchus, Tyre, Samos, Chaldaeans, Pherecydes of Syros, Cleanthes, Italy, biography</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Pythagoras' parentage and early life. <header>VITA PYTHAGORAE.</header>

...Tyrrhenian <term>Tyrrhenian: a term for the non-Greek peoples of the Mediterranean, often associated with the Etruscans or early inhabitants of Lemnos</term>, among the elders. Apollonius, in his works *On Pythagoras*, also records that his mother was Pythais, a descendant of Ancaeus, the founding colonizer of Samos. Apollonius says that some report Pythagoras was the biological son of Apollo and Pythais, 
<margin>5</margin> but was called the son of Mnesarchus only in name. Indeed, one of the Samian poets said:

> Pythais, who possessed the greatest beauty of the Samians,
> bore Pythagoras, dear to Zeus, to the god Apollo.
<note>original: Πυθαγόραν θ’ ὃν ἔτικτε Διὶ φίλον Ἀπόλλωνι Πυθαΐς, ἣ κάλλος πλεῖστον ἔχεν Σαμίων.</note>

This author [Apollonius] says that Pythagoras was a pupil not only of Pherecydes and Hermodamas, 
<margin>10</margin> but also of Anaximander <note>a major Pre-Socratic philosopher known for being the first to write a book on nature</note>. 3 Duris of Samos, in the second book of his *Annals* <term>Annals: "Horoi" in Greek, these were local histories arranged chronologically</term>, records that Pythagoras had a son named Arimnestus, and says he was the teacher of Democritus <note>the "Laughing Philosopher" who proposed the atomic theory of the universe</note>. It is said that Arimnestus, upon returning from exile, dedicated a bronze offering in the temple of Hera 
<margin>15</margin> that was nearly two cubits <term>cubit: an ancient measurement of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm</term> in diameter, upon which this epigram was inscribed:

> Arimnestus, the dear son of Pythagoras, dedicated me here,
> having discovered many points of wisdom in his teachings.

However, it is said that Simus the harmonicist <term>harmonicist: a specialist in the mathematical theory of music and intervals</term> removed this inscription and, 
<margin>20</margin> having usurped the "canon" <note>original: kanona; here referring to the mathematical rule of the monochord or a fundamental musical principle</note>, published it as his own. Thus, while there were seven "wisdoms" recorded there, because of the one that Simus stole, the others inscribed on the offering also disappeared. 4 Others 
<margin>25</margin> record that Pythagoras had a son named Telauges by Theano (the daughter of Pythonax and a Cretan by birth) and a daughter named Myia; some also mention a daughter named Arignote. It is said that Pythagorean writings by these children are still preserved. Timaeus reports that Pythagoras’ daughter, while a maiden, led the companies of maidens in Croton, and as a wife, she led the married women.

As a ship was sailing into harbor and his friends were praying that the cargo brought in would be profitable for them, Pythagoras said, "Then there will be a corpse for you," and the ship sailed into port carrying a corpse. Ten thousand other things even more wonderful and divine <margin>5</margin> have been told about the man, consistently and with one voice. To put it simply, more extraordinary or numerous things have been attributed to no one else. For instance, infallible predictions of earthquakes are remembered of him, as well as the swift turning away of plagues, the calming of violent winds and hailstorms, <margin>10</margin> and the soothing of waves on both rivers and seas to allow for the easy passage of his companions. Having shared in these powers, **Empedocles**, **Epimenides**, and **Abaris** <note>Three famous wonder-workers and philosophers of the ancient world often associated with the Pythagorean tradition</note> performed such feats in many places, as is clear from their own poems. <margin>15</margin> Furthermore, "Wind-stayer" was the epithet given to **Empedocles**, "Purifier" to **Epimenides**, and "Air-walker" to **Abaris**, because he had been gifted an arrow by the **Hyperborean Apollo** <note>Apollo was the god of light and music; the Hyperboreans were a mythical people living in the far north who were said to be specially blessed by him</note> and, riding upon it, he crossed rivers, seas, and inaccessible places, walking through the air <margin>20</margin> after a fashion. Some suspected that Pythagoras also experienced this at the time when he conversed with his companions in both **Metapontum** and **Tauromenium** <note>Two cities separated by a great distance and the sea; Metapontum is in Italy and Tauromenium is in Sicily</note> on the same day. <margin>30</margin> He would also soothe the passions of the soul and the ailments of the body with rhythms, melodies, and incantations. And while <margin>25</margin> he arranged these for his companions, he himself listened to the **Harmony of the Universe**, understanding the universal harmony of the spheres and the stars that move within them—a harmony which we...

# THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS
### VITA PYTHAGORAE.

...he thought [this routine] should prepare for the body. He did not go on walks with large crowds to avoid drawing envy, but rather with just two or three companions in temples or groves, choosing the quietest and most beautiful locations. 

<margin>5</margin><margin>33</margin> He loved his friends exceedingly, being the first to declare that **"friends' possessions are common"** <note>original: *koina ta tōn philōn*; a famous Pythagorean maxim suggesting communal living</note> and that **"a friend is another self."** He would spend all his time with them when they were in good health, but if they fell ill, he would treat their bodies and comfort their souls when they were distressed. As we mentioned, <margin>10</margin> he did this for some through incantations and charms, and for others through music. For he possessed melodies that served as healing remedies <term>paionia; songs of Apollo the healer</term> for bodily diseases, which he would sing to restore the sick. There were also songs that brought about a forgetfulness of grief, calmed anger, and uprooted improper desires. 

<margin>34</margin> Regarding his diet, his breakfast <term>ariston; the morning meal</term> <margin>15</margin> consisted of honeycomb or honey, while his dinner was bread made of millet or barley cake, and vegetables both boiled and raw. He rarely ate the meat of sacrificial animals, and even then, not from every part. 

Most of the time, whenever he intended to enter the inner sanctuaries <term>adyta; the most sacred "off-limits" parts of a temple</term> of the gods and remain there for some time, <margin>20</margin> he used foods that warded off hunger and thirst. The hunger-warding food <note>original: *alimos*</note> he prepared from poppy seed, sesame, and the skin of a squill <note>a bulbous plant of the lily family, often used in ancient medicine</note>—carefully washed until the bitter sap was removed—along with asphodel stalks, mallow leaves, groats, barley, <margin>25</margin> and chickpeas. These were all pounded in equal weight and mixed with honey from **Mount Hymettus** <note>a mountain range near Athens famous for its high-quality honey</note>. 

The thirst-warding food <note>original: *adipsos*</note> he made from cucumber seeds and plump raisins (with the seeds removed), coriander flowers, mallow seeds, purslane, <margin>30</margin> grated cheese, fine flour, and cream. All these he mixed with honey from the islands.

However, he did not accept that pleasure which is common and deceptive, but rather that which is stable, most dignified, and free from slander. For he taught that there is a twofold difference between pleasures: <margin>15</margin> one type, which gratifies the belly and the sexual appetites through luxury, he compared to the murderous songs of the **Sirens** <note>In Greek mythology, the Sirens were creatures who lured sailors to their deaths with enchanting music</note>. The other type, which is found in noble and just things and those necessary for life—being equally pleasant in the moment and leaving no regrets for the future—he <margin>20</margin> said was like the harmony of a **Muse** <note>The Muses were the goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences</note>.

<margin>40</margin> He recommended two particular times for self-reflection: the first when one is turning toward sleep, and the second when one is rising from sleep. It is proper in each of these moments to examine both one's past actions and one's future plans—taking an account from oneself <margin>25</margin> regarding what has happened, and making provision for what is to come. Therefore, before sleep, each person should chant these verses to themselves:

> Do not admit sleep to your soft eyes 
> before you have gone over each of the day's deeds three times: 
<margin>30</margin> > Where did I go wrong? What did I do? What duty did I leave unfulfilled?

<margin>46</margin> The philosophy he practiced had as its goal to rescue and set free from such prisons and <margin>15</margin> bonds that Mind <term>Mind; the "nous," the highest part of the soul capable of direct intellectual intuition</term> which is partitioned within us. Without this liberation, no one could ever learn anything healthy or true at all, nor could they perceive anything through the activity of any sense whatsoever. For, according to him, "it is the Mind that sees all and the Mind that hears all; all other things are blind and deaf." <note>original: "νοῦς γὰρ... πάνθ' ὁρᾷ"; a famous maxim attributed to Epicharmus, suggesting that the senses are useless without the intellect to interpret them</note> <margin>20</margin> He said that once a person has been purified, they must then be introduced to things that bring benefit. He introduced these by devising certain methods: first, he gently trained himself <margin>23</margin> toward the contemplation of the eternal, incorporeal things which are of the same nature as the soul—those which always exist in the same state and in the same way. He led himself forward little by little, <margin>25</margin> so that he would not be thrown into confusion by a sudden and total change, nor turn away and give up because of the poor quality of the "nourishment" <note>Referring to the base, material concerns and false opinions of common life</note> he had received for so long. <margin>47</margin> Therefore, he used mathematics and the study of things that exist in the borderland between bodies and incorporeal things <margin>30</margin> to prepare himself gradually for the things that truly exist.

Being unable to convey the incorporeal forms and the first principles in speech, they resorted to demonstrating them through numbers. And thus, the principle of unity, <margin>30</margin> and that of identity, and that of equality, and the cause of the harmony <note>original: "συμπνοίας"; literally "breathing together" or concord</note> and the "sympathy" <term>Sympathy; "sympatheia," the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and affect one another</term> of the whole...

## VITA PYTHAGORAE.

...and for the preservation of that which is always the same and in the same state, they called it the **One** <note>original: "ἓν"; the Monad, representing unity and stability</note>. For even in particular things, the "one" exists as such, being unified in its parts and concordant <note>original: "σύμπνουν"; literally "breathing together," implying a deep internal harmony</note> through its participation in the First Cause. <margin>50</margin> But for the principle of "otherness" and inequality, and for everything that is divisible and in a state of change—existing now in one way and now in another—they called this the "two-fold" <term>logos; principle, ratio, or definition</term> and named it the **Dyad** <note>original: "δυάδα"; the principle of duality, division, and change</note>. For such is the nature of "two" even in particular things. And these definitions <meta>10</meta> are not exclusive to them [the Pythagoreans], while being absent in others; rather, one can see that other philosophers also left behind certain powers that are "unifying" and "sustaining" of the whole. There are also among those philosophers certain principles of equality, dissimilarity, and otherness. Therefore, for the sake of clear instruction, they designate these principles by the name of the "One" <meta>15</meta> and the name of the "Dyad." It makes no difference to these men whether they use the terms "two-fold," "unequal-natured," or "other-natured." <margin>51</margin> Similarly, the same logic applies to the other numbers, for each has been assigned according to certain powers. For again, there is something in the <meta>20</meta> nature of things that possesses a beginning, a middle, and an end. To this kind of form and to this kind of nature, they applied the number **Three**. Therefore, they say that everything which makes use of a middle point is "three-fold." In this way, they also designated everything that is "complete" <note>original: "πᾶν τὸ τέλειον"; referring to the Triad as the first number with a beginning, middle, and end, making it "perfect" or "complete"</note>. <meta>25</meta> And if anything is complete, they say it makes use of that principle and has been ordered according to it. Being unable to name it otherwise, they used the name of the **Triad** for it; and wishing to lead us to a conceptual understanding of this principle, they introduced it through this form. <meta>30</meta> And the same logic applies to the other numbers. <margin>52</margin> These, then, are the principles according to which the aforementioned numbers were arranged. And those that follow are contained under one...

<summary>Porphyry explains the symbolic logic of Pythagorean numerology, where the One represents eternal stability, the Dyad represents change and division, and the Triad represents completeness (having a beginning, middle, and end).</summary>

# THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS
## VITA PYTHAGORAE.
### 3*

...of a certain form and power; this they named the **Decad** <note>original: "δεκάδα"; the number ten</note>, as if it were a "container" <note>original: "δεχάδα"; a pun on the verb *dechomai*, meaning "to receive" or "to contain"</note>. For this reason, they say that the number ten is a "perfect number," or rather the most perfect of all, <margin>5</margin> as it encompasses within itself every difference of number, every kind of ratio <term>logos; here meaning mathematical ratio or definition</term>, and every proportion. For if the nature of the universe is defined according to the ratios and proportions of numbers, and everything that is born, grows, and reaches completion follows the ratios of numbers, <margin>10</margin> and if the **Decad** contains every ratio, every proportion, and every kind of number, how could it not be called a "perfect number"?

<margin>53</margin> Such, then, was the study of numbers among the Pythagoreans. And it happened that this philosophy—the very first of its kind—was extinguished. This occurred first because of its enigmatic <margin>15</margin> nature, and second because the writings were composed in the **Doric dialect** <note>an archaic and regional dialect of Greek which later scholars found difficult to read</note>. This dialect possesses a certain obscurity, which led to the misunderstanding of its teachings. Consequently, the doctrines recounted from these works were even considered illegitimate and misinterpreted, because those who brought them forward were not <margin>20</margin> true Pythagoreans.

In addition to this, the Pythagoreans claim that **Plato**, **Aristotle**, **Speusippus**, **Aristoxenus**, and **Xenocrates** <note>major figures of the Academy and Peripatetic schools who were influenced by Pythagorean thought</note> appropriated the "fruitful" parts of their teachings after only a brief revision. However, they say these men collected the superficial and trivial elements—as well as those things <margin>25</margin> put forward by spiteful slanderers later on to distort and mock the school—and recorded them as being the specific doctrines of the sect <note>original: "αἱρέσεως"; here meaning a chosen school of thought</note>.

<margin>54</margin> But these things happened later. For a long time, Pythagoras himself and his companions were so admired in Italy that the <margin>30</margin> cities entrusted their governments to his followers. Much later, however, they were envied, and a conspiracy of the following sort was formed against them. **Cylon**, a man of Croton...

# THE LIFE OF PYTHAGORAS
## VITA PYTHAGORAE.

...[this man, Cylon], surpassing all citizens in lineage, ancestral reputation, and the abundance of his life’s wealth, was otherwise a difficult, violent, and tyrannical man. He used his circle of friends and the power of his wealth to provide the <margin>5</margin> strength to commit injustices. He considered himself worthy of every distinction that was held in high regard, and he also believed himself most worthy to participate in Pythagoras’s philosophy. He approached Pythagoras, praising himself as one wishing to associate with him. But Pythagoras, having immediately judged the man's character by his features <term>physiognomy; the practice of assessing a person's character from their outward appearance</term>, <margin>10</margin> and seeing what sort of person he was from the signs he sought in the bodies of those who approached him, commanded him to go away and mind his own business. This distressed Cylon immensely, as if he had been insulted; he was, in other respects, a <margin>55</margin> difficult man and one who could not control his anger. He gathered his <margin>15</margin> friends together and began to slander Pythagoras, preparing to plot against both the master himself and his followers.

From there, some say that while Pythagoras’s companions were gathered in the house of Milo the athlete—during the time when Pythagoras was traveling abroad (for he had gone to <margin>20</margin> Delos to nurse his teacher, Pherecydes of Syros, who had fallen victim to the famous "lice disease" <term>phthiriasis; a gruesome historical malady where parasites were said to consume the flesh</term>, and to bury him)—the attackers set fire to the house from all sides and stoned them. Only two escaped the blaze: Archippus <margin>25</margin> and Lysis, as Neanthes relates. Of these, Lysis went to live in Greece and settled in Thebes, where he associated with Epaminondas <note>A famous Theban general and statesman known for his virtue and military tactics</note> and became his teacher. <margin>56</margin> But Dicaearchus and the more precise historians say that Pythagoras himself was present during the plot; for they say that <margin>30</margin> Pherecydes died before Pythagoras departed from Samos. They report that forty of the companions were caught together while holding a meeting in a house, while many others were taken one by one throughout the city as they happened to be found.

Having escaped from the fire, Pythagoras became so discouraged by the loss of his close associates that he took his own life. When disaster thus overcame these men, their unspoken knowledge also <margin>30</margin> <margin>82</margin> perished, remaining guarded secretly within their breasts.

They strictly charged their sons, daughters, or <margin>15</margin> wives to give them to no one outside the household. These women, in turn, maintained this tradition for a long time, passing down the same command in succession to their descendants. 

We may take as evidence, says Nicomachus <note>Nicomachus of Gerasa (c. 60–120 CE), a mathematician and Pythagorean biographer.</note>, the fact that they did <margin>59</margin> not casually avoid the friendships of outsiders, <margin>20</margin> but very earnestly turned away from them and guarded themselves against them. This is also clear from what Aristoxenus <note>Aristoxenus of Tarentum, a student of Aristotle who wrote extensively on music and the life of Pythagoras.</note> says in his *On the Life of Pythagoras*; he claims to have personally heard it from Dionysius, <margin>25</margin> the tyrant of Sicily, at the time when he had fallen from his monarchy and was teaching letters in Corinth <note>Dionysius II of Syracuse was deposed and famously lived out his life as a humble schoolteacher in Corinth.</note>. "Those men kept themselves away from lamentations and tears and all such things as much as possible. The same rule applied to flattery, petitioning, <margin>60</margin> <margin>30</margin> supplication, and all such behaviors."
