# DISCOURSE OF GREGORY
<note>original: ΓΡΗΓΟΡΙΟΥ ΛΟΓΟΣ. This refers to Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Church Father.</note>

<warning>This page suffers from significant ink bleed-through from the verso and severe fading of the original text. The transcription identifies visible characters and follows the established text of Gregory of Nazianzus' Oratio VII (Funeral Oration for his brother Caesarius) which matches the legible fragments.</warning>

— These people, then, because of the virtue of those men <note>Gregory likely refers to the virtuous reputation of Caesarius’ parents</note>, and the blamelessness of their fortune, and the prime of his age, and the glory of his ancestors, and the consolation of his relatives—who honored him while he lived and cared for him <note>original: περιέστελλον, literally "wrapped around," referring to the ritual preparation of a body for burial</note> at his death—and after their death, it is likely that those who were not present, or rather more likely, those pointing out the uncertainty of fortune, or those taking the common calamity as their own, or even those overcome by the man's virtue, would break out into this cry, which we hear most in such circumstances: "Alas, Caesarius! What is this? How were you torn from us? What is life? And what is this mystery concerning us? How great was the wealth? And how did such a life have such an end?" These things are said by the many and the humble, who look only at the present. 

But what do I say to them? And what consolation do I offer to the lament? Or rather, what healing do I bring through this discourse? It is to not remain in present things, nor to look only at the body, nor to mourn what is visible, as if it were nothing compared to the brilliance of the soul—which he adorned in every way, and through which he was united with greater things. I speak of him not as one who has died, but as one departing <note>original: μεθισταμένου (methistamenou), a word implying a move from one place to another, common in Christian funeral rhetoric to describe death as a journey</note>, being loosed from bonds, freed from the things that trouble him, and setting off for the blessed lot <term>blessed lot: λῆξις (lēxis), referring to the divine inheritance or the portion of heaven assigned to the righteous</term>.

<summary>In this opening section of the funeral oration for his brother Caesarius, Gregory of Nazianzus contrasts the superficial mourning of the crowds with a deeper spiritual perspective on death. He argues that death is not a tragic end to a successful life, but a liberation of the soul into its divine inheritance.</summary>

->ON ABSTINENCE<-

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>1</margin>When I heard from those who have come to visit us, Firmus, that you have condemned a fleshless <note>original: ἀσάρκου (asarkou). Porphyry uses this to describe a vegetarian diet.</note> diet and have run back again to the eating of meat, at first I did not believe it. I considered your self-control <margin>5</margin> and the reverence which we have both shown toward those ancient and god-fearing men who first pointed out these truths. But when others confirmed the news by reporting the message, it seemed to me that to simply rebuke you would be uncouth and far from the persuasive power of reason. This is true whether you were, according to <margin>10</margin> the proverb, "finding the better by fleeing the evil," or whether, according to Empedocles <note>Empedocles (c. 494–434 BCE) was a philosopher who taught that eating animals was a form of murder because souls transmigrate between humans and animals.</note>, you were stripping off your former life and returning to a better one. However, I deemed it worthy of our mutual friendship, and fitting for those who have organized their lives according to truth, to reveal through <margin>15</margin> reason the refutation of your errors—showing from what heights to what depths you have descended.

<margin>2</margin>For as I consider within myself the cause of this change, I could not say that you have changed your ways for the sake of health and strength—as the common and unlearned crowd might suggest. <margin>20</margin> On the contrary, while you were living with us, you yourself used to admit that a fleshless diet <note>original: ἄσαρκον δίαιταν (asarkon diaitan)</note> contributed both to health and to a measured endurance of those labors required by philosophy. Experience proved this to be true.

->DE ABSTINENTIA I.<-

...one can know that you were speaking the truth when you said these things. Either through deception, then, or through thinking that it makes no difference to wisdom whether one diets in this way or that, or perhaps for some other 
<margin>5</margin> reason of which I am ignorant—hanging a greater fear of impiety <note>original: ἀσεβείας (asebeias). <margin>4</margin> Immediately, then, those who argue against us claim that <term>justice</term> <note>original: δικαιοσύνη (dikaiosyne). In Greek thought, justice was often defined as a contract or relationship between beings who can reason and make agreements.</note>

<margin>15</margin> bear; he destroys its power and ruins what is proper to it by mixing it with what is foreign. # DE ABSTINENTIA I.

...accomplishing [this]. For, hanging over them, it <note>the threat of punishment</note> compels control over those impulses that lead toward disadvantageous actions, and by force it necessitates doing what is required. Indeed, the legislators did not leave even involuntary homicide free from all penalty, so that they might grant no excuse to those who might choose to intentionally mimic the deeds of those acting unintentionally. They did this so that such an act would not be left unguarded or neglected, which would otherwise result in many truly involuntary occurrences. For even this [accidental killing] was not beneficial, for the same reasons that it is not beneficial to destroy one another in a voluntary manner. 

<margin>8</margin>
Thus, regarding involuntary acts—some occurring because of unpredictable causes that human nature cannot guard against, and others because of our own negligence and lack of attention to the difference—wishing to prevent the carelessness that harms one's neighbors, they <note>the early lawgivers</note> did not establish even the involuntary act as free from penalty. Instead, through the fear of punishments, they removed the greater part of such error. 

And I believe that even those homicides permitted by the law receive the customary ritual expiations through <term>purifications</term> <note>original: καθαρμῶν (katharmōn). In ancient Greek religion, killing—even if legal or accidental—resulted in a "miasma" or spiritual pollution that had to be cleansed through ritual.</note> for no other reason than the desire of those who first wisely introduced these things to distance people as much as possible from the voluntary act of killing. For common people required every possible means of prevention to stop them from readily doing what is not beneficial. Therefore, those who first perceived this did not only establish legal penalties, but they also hung another **irrational fear** <note>original: ἄλογον φόβον (alogon phobon). This refers to the use of "supernatural" or religious dread as a tool for social control.</note> over them, proclaiming that those who had killed a human being in any way whatsoever were not "pure" unless they had made use of purifications. 

For the irrational part of the soul, being guided in various ways, reached its established state of gentleness, as those who originally [governed] the masses <note>The Greek text cuts off at πλή-, likely referring to τὰ πλήθη (ta plēthē), the masses or the multitudes.</note> devised ways to tame the irrational impulse of desire...

# DE ABSTINENTIA I.

...of those who administered affairs; among which is the prohibition against killing one another indiscriminately. Regarding the rest of the animals, however, it is reasonable that those who first defined what we must and must not do did not prevent us from destroying them. For in their case <note>referring to non-human animals</note>, <term>utility</term> <note>original: συμφέρον (sympheron); a central Epicurean concept meaning "the collective advantage" or "what is beneficial."</note> was achieved through the opposite course of action. 

<margin>5</margin> 

Indeed, it was not possible to survive without attempting to ward off the threats of animals while being raised together with one another. However, some of the most refined individuals of that era, remembering how they abstained from killing [their own kind] because it was useful for survival, also instilled in the rest of the people a memory of the benefits that result from social association. They did this so that, by abstaining from their <term>kin</term> <note>original: συγγενοῦς (syngenous); here meaning fellow humans, emphasizing the natural bond within the species.</note>, they might preserve the <term>social community</term> <note>original: κοινωνίαν (koinonian)</note> which cooperated toward the individual safety of each person. 

<margin>10</margin> 

It was not only useful to separate from and avoid harming those gathered in the same place for the purpose of driving out animals of other species, but also for protection against humans who arrived with the intent to harm. 

<margin>15</margin> 

For a certain time, therefore, they abstained from their own kind for this reason—as long as a person participated in the same community of necessities and provided certain services toward both of the objectives mentioned <note>safety from wild animals and safety from hostile humans</note>. 

<margin>20</margin> 

But as time went on and the human lineage advanced significantly through mutual procreation, and as the animals of other species were driven out and the threat of being torn apart diminished, some individuals attained a rational calculation of <term>utility</term> in their mutual support, rather than relying only on an unreasoning memory. 

<margin>25</margin> 

Whence they attempted to more firmly restrain those who would readily destroy one another and who, through forgetfulness of the past, were making the common defense weaker. 

<margin>11</margin> 

In attempting to achieve this, they introduced the <term>legislations</term> <note>original: νομοθεσίας (nomothesias)</note> that still remain today among cities and nations. The multitude followed them voluntarily because they now better perceived the utility found in the gathering of men with one another.

...to perceive [this utility]. For in a similar way, the unsparing killing of everything harmful and the preservation of what was useful for the destruction of these threats contributed to our freedom from fear. Therefore, it was logical that while the former [killing humans] was forbidden, the latter [killing animals] was not prohibited. 

<margin>5</margin>

It cannot be argued that the law permitted us to kill certain animals that are not destructive to human nature or harmful to our lives in any other way. For there is, so to speak, nothing among the animals permitted by the law which, if allowed to reach an excessive abundance, would not become harmful to us. 

<margin>10</margin>

<margin>15</margin>

<margin>20</margin>

For this very reason, it was not forbidden to destroy even these sorts of animals, so that a population beneficial to our needs might be left behind, and one that could be easily managed. For the situation is not the same as it is with lions and wolves and wild animals in general, whether small or large. 

<margin>25</margin>

In their case, there is no population size which, if left alone, would ease the burdens of our necessary life; but it is different for cattle, horses, sheep, and all those called "tame" animals. Therefore, we destroy some species entirely, but of others, we remove only the portion that exceeds the <term>proper balance</term> <note>original: συμμετρίας (symmetrias); meaning a state of due proportion or moderation.</note>.

### ON ABSTINENCE I. 51

...by those who from the start established these things by law; but regarding animals that are not eaten, the reason is what is advantageous or disadvantageous. Consequently, those who claim that everything noble and just regarding established laws is merely a matter of private opinion are full of an immense foolishness. 

<margin>5</margin>

For the matter is not like that, but functions in the same way as other forms of utility—such as health and countless other categories—where people often make mistakes regarding both common and personal interests. 

Indeed, some people fail to recognize legislative acts that apply similarly to everyone; some, believing these matters to be indifferent, neglect them, while others hold the opposite view. Furthermore, some believe that things which are not universally advantageous are beneficial everywhere. 

<margin>15</margin>

For this reason, they cling to customs that do not fit their situation, even if in certain instances they discover what is profitable to themselves and what provides a common benefit. Among these are the regulations concerning the eating and killing of <term>living beings</term> <note>original: ἐμψύχων (empsychōn); literally "those with souls," a standard term for animals.</note> established among most nations because of the specific nature of their territory—regulations which we are not required to follow, as we do not inhabit the same region. 

<margin>20</margin>

Now, if it were possible to make a <term>covenant</term> <note>original: συνθήκην (synthēkēn); a contract or agreement, central to Epicurean social contract theory.</note> with the other animals just as we do with humans, so that they would not kill us and we would not indiscriminately kill them, it would be well to extend the scope of justice to that point, for it would increase our security. 

<margin>25</margin>

However, since it is impossible for animals that lack <term>reason</term> <note>original: λόγον (logon); meaning speech, reason, or rational thought.</note> to share in law, it is not possible to establish our security through such a contract with other living beings any more than we could with inanimate objects. # DE ABSTINENCE I. 52

### 13
Next, we must set forth what the common and ordinary person is accustomed to say. They claim that the ancients abstained from <term>living beings</term> <note>original: ἐμψύχων (empsychōn); literally "things with souls," referring to animals.</note> not out of piety, but because they did not yet know the use of fire. But once they learned of it, they considered it most precious and sacred, calling it **Hestia** <note>The Greek goddess of the hearth and home; her name literally means "hearth."</note>; from this, they became "sharers of the hearth" with one another and subsequently began to make use of animals. For they argue that while eating flesh is natural for a human, eating it raw is contrary to nature. Therefore, when fire was discovered, they reclaimed their natural state through boiling and roasting, and thus accepted the eating of meat. 

Because of this, "jackals" are called "raw-eaters," and it is used as a reproach: <margin>Kalu</margin> "You would eat Priam raw," <note>original: ὠμὸν βεβρώθοις Πρίαμον (ōmon bebrōthois Priamon); a quote from Homer's *Iliad* 4.35, where Zeus speaks to Hera.</note> and "to cut off and eat raw meat," <note>original: ὠμ’ ἀποτεμνόμενον κρέα ἔδμεναι (ōm’ apotemnomenon krea edmenai); from *Iliad* 22.347, Achilles' threat to Hector.</note> as if the eating of raw meat were a trait reserved for the godless. <unclear>.....</unclear> "Lifting up platters of meat of all kinds, he set them before them." <note>A quote from Homer's *Odyssey* 1.141, describing a hospitable feast.</note> In the beginning, then, they did not consume living beings because man was not a raw-meat eating animal; but once the use of fire was discovered, they began to use "fire-wrought" methods not only for meat but for nearly all other foods. 

That man is not naturally a raw-meat eater is demonstrated by certain "Fish-eating" tribes; for they roast their fish—some on rocks that have been made red-hot by the sun, and others in the sand. But that man *is* a flesh-eater is shown by the very fact that no nation abstains from living beings. This was not a practice the Greeks adopted through some corruption of character, since the same custom exists among the barbarians.

### 14
Furthermore, the person who commands us not to eat meat and considers it unjust would also have to say that it is not right to kill animals or take away their lives. Yet, we have a war against wild beasts that is both innate to us and just. For some attack humans of their own accord, such as wolves and lions; while others...

# DE ABSTINENCE I. 53

...not willingly, just like vipers; for when stepped on, they sometimes bite. Some animals attack humans, while others destroy crops. For all these reasons we pursue them, and we kill both the beasts that strike first and those that do <margin>5</margin> not strike first, so that we may not suffer anything from them. For there is no one who, seeing a snake and being able to kill it, does not do so, so that neither he nor any other human might be bitten. For this is not only a matter of hatred toward those animals being killed, but also a matter of the affection <margin>10</margin> of one human for another. Since war against wild beasts is just, we nevertheless abstain from eating many of the animals that live alongside humans. 

Hence the Greeks eat neither dogs, nor horses, nor donkeys. They do, however, eat pigs, as the domestic variety is considered of the same genus as the wild ones; likewise, they eat birds. For a pig is useful <margin>15</margin> for nothing else than for food <note>This was a common ancient Greek proverb: that the pig's soul was given to it only as salt to keep its meat from rotting.</note>. The Phoenicians and Jews abstained from them because they did not exist in their regions at all; for they say even now this animal is not seen in *Ethiopia*. 

Just as no one among the Greeks sacrifices a camel or an elephant to the gods, since Greece did not produce these <margin>20</margin> animals, so too in *Cyprus* or *Phoenicia* this animal was not offered to the gods, since it was not native. Neither do the Egyptians sacrifice pigs to the gods for the same reason. The total abstinence from this animal by some people is therefore similar to our own refusal to eat camel meat <note>The author is arguing that religious taboos are often based on local environmental factors rather than moral laws.</note>. 

But why <margin>25</margin> should anyone abstain from <term>living beings</term>? <note>original: ἐμψύχων (empsychōn); literally "things with souls," the standard Greek term for animals.</note> Does it make the soul worse, or the body? It is evident that it does neither. For meat-eating animals are more intelligent than others. They are certainly hunters and possess this craft from which they make their living; they have acquired strength and courage, <margin>30</margin> just like lions and wolves. Thus, meat-eating harms neither the soul nor the body. This is also clear from the fact that athletes make their bodies stronger through meat-eating...

# DE ABSTINENTIA I.

<margin>27</margin> First of all, then, it must be understood that my discourse will not offer its advice to every way of human life. For it is not for those pursuing **manual trades** <note>original: "βαναύσους τέχνας" — mechanical or "low" crafts that were thought to distract the mind from higher contemplation.</note>, nor for athletes of the body, nor for soldiers, nor for sailors, nor for <margin>5</margin> orators, nor for those who have chosen the **practical life** <note>The "active life" of politics and business, as opposed to the "contemplative life" of the philosopher.</note>. Therefore, we would not mutter a word to those <margin>10</margin> others. For surely in this common life, the same advice is not given to the one who is sleeping—and who, if it should happen, is eager to do so through his whole life, surrounding himself with sleep-inducing things from every side—and to the one who is eager to drive sleep away, arranging everything <margin>15</margin> about himself toward **wakefulness**.

To the sleeper, it is necessary to suggest drunkenness, hangovers, and surfeit, and to recommend choosing a dark house and a "soft, wide, and rich" couch, as the poets say, and everything that causes drowsiness and produces <margin><unclear>nearly</unclear></margin> sloth and **forgetfulness** <note>original: "λήθης" — referring to Lethe, the state of mental oblivion or the mythical river of the underworld.</note>, whether <margin>20</margin> it be a scent, an ointment, or a medicinal drink or food. # DE ABSTINENTIA I.

For they say that, while there are various goals for various aims, for us the goal is to achieve the **contemplation of Being** <note>original: "θεωρίας τοῦ ὄντος" (theōrias tou ontos) — a central Neoplatonic concept of perceiving ultimate reality through the mind rather than the senses.</note>. This achievement brings about, according to our own power, a union between the contemplator and that which is contemplated. For our return is not <margin>5</margin> toward something else, but toward our truly **inner self** <note>original: "τὸν ὄντως αὐτὸν" — literally "the truly him[self]," referring to the soul's essential identity.</note>; nor is our union with another, but with our truly inner self. This true self is the **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — the highest part of the soul, capable of direct spiritual perception.</note>, so that the ultimate goal is to live according to the Intellect. Toward this end, both rational discourses and external studies are directed; they serve as a means of **purification** <note>original: "καθαρτικόν" (kathartikon)</note> for us, <margin>10</margin> but they do not themselves complete our happiness. Therefore, if happiness were defined merely by the gathering of words, it would be possible to reach the goal while neglecting both food and conduct. But since we must exchange one life for another—having been purified from our current life through both words and <margin>15</margin> deeds—come, let us consider what kind of words and what kind of deeds establish us in this state. 

Would these not be the things that separate us from **perceivable objects** <note>original: "αἰσθητῶν" (aisthētōn) — things perceived through the five senses.</note> <margin>30</margin> and the passions associated with them, while leading us upward toward an intellectual, imageless, and passionless life as much as possible? And are not their opposites foreign to us <margin>20</margin> and worthy of rejection? I believe it follows that we must concede this: a thing is to be rejected in proportion to how much it leads us away from our goal or drags us down. 

For we resemble people who have gone away to a **foreign nation** <note>A classic Platonic metaphor for the soul’s descent from the divine realm into the physical body.</note>, whether voluntarily or as exiles from their own kin. Not only have we been banished from our own people, but <margin>25</margin> while in this foreign land, we have become filled with alien passions, customs, and strange laws, and have developed a leaning toward them. In the same way, then, a person who intends to return home from abroad not only desires to make the journey, but also—in order to be accepted back—practices stripping <margin>30</margin> away every foreign thing they have acquired. They remind themselves of those things they once possessed but have forgotten, for without these things, they cannot be received by their kin. In the same way, we too must travel from here, if indeed we wish to return to the things that truly **exist** <note>Refers to the realm of "the Beings," or permanent spiritual realities.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument regarding the soul's journey. # DE ABSTINENTIA I.

We are about to return to our own true nature. We must, therefore, strip away everything we have taken on from our mortal nature, along with the attachment to these things through which our **descent** <note>original: "κατάβασις" (katabasis) — in Neoplatonism, the soul's "fall" or "descent" from the divine realm into a physical body.</note> occurred. We must remember that blessed and eternal essence and <margin>5</margin> hasten our return toward that which is **colorless and without qualities** <note>original: "ἀχρώματον καὶ ἄποιον" — referring to the Pure Being or Intellect, which exists beyond the physical attributes of the material world.</note>. To do this, we must engage in two practices: one by which we strip off everything material and mortal, and another by which we return and prevail, ascending back to those higher realms in a manner opposite to how we descended here. For <margin>10</margin> we were, and still are, **intellectual essences** <note>original: "νοεραὶ οὐσίαι" (noerai ousiai) — beings whose fundamental nature is mind or spirit rather than matter.</note>, pure of all sensation and irrationality. However, we became entwined with the world of the senses because of our weakness in maintaining an eternal union with the **intellectual realm** <note>original: "τὸ νοητὸν" (to noēton) — the world of pure thought and divine reality.</note>, and because of a power directed toward things here below. For all the powers that act <margin>15</margin> through sensation and the body sprouted forth when the soul did not remain in the intellectual realm. <insert>They are like a blight on the soil, or as the earth, having often received the seed of wheat, produces **weeds** instead</insert> <note>original: "αἴρας" (airas) — darnel or cockle, a common weed that looks like wheat but is poisonous.</note>. This happened through a certain wretchedness of the soul; it does not destroy its own essence by generating irrationality, but through this irrationality, it is joined to the <margin>20</margin> mortal and dragged down from its own home toward something foreign. Therefore, if we are eager to return to our original state, we must practice, as far as we are <margin>31</margin> able, a withdrawal from sensation, from imagination, and from the **irrationality** <note>original: "ἀλογία" (alogia)</note> that follows them, as well as the passions associated with it, except insofar as the <margin>25</margin> necessity of our birth requires. We must articulate the things of the **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note>, preparing peace and silence for it by ending the war against irrationality. We do this so that we might not only hear about the Intellect and the intellectual realities, but also, with all our power, enjoy the **contemplation** <note>original: "θεωρίας" (theōrias)</note> of it, being established in <margin>30</margin> **incorporeality** <note>original: "ἀσωματίαν" — the state of existing without a physical body.</note> and living in truth through the Intellect, rather than living falsely with things of the same tribe as our bodies. We must strip off...

<summary>Porphyry describes the soul's need to "ascend" back to its original intellectual state by stripping away material attachments and the "weeds" of irrationality. He emphasizes that the philosopher must move beyond mere talk of the Intellect to a direct, silent contemplation of incorporeal reality.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE I.

Therefore, let us strip off our many **tunics** <note>original: "χιτῶνας" (chitōnas) — a metaphor for the layers of physical and emotional attachment that clothe the soul, a common image in Neoplatonism.</note>, both this visible and fleshy one and those we have put on underneath, which are closely attached to the **garments of skin** <note>original: "δερματίνοις" — a reference to the "coats of skin" from Genesis 3:21, interpreted by philosophers as the gross physical body acquired after the soul's fall.</note>. Naked and without tunics, let us go up into the stadium to <margin>5</margin> compete in the **Olympic games of the soul** <note>Porphyry compares spiritual discipline to the rigorous training and naked competition of Greek athletes.</note>. The beginning of this struggle is the "stripping off," without which no competition can take place. Since some of our garments are on the outside and others are within, the stripping also occurs in two ways: one through manifest things and the other through things more hidden. For instance, not eating or not accepting <margin>10</margin> offered money belongs to the manifest and obvious things, but to not even feel a desire for them belongs to the more hidden things. Therefore, we must withdraw not only from the deeds themselves but also from our **internal attachment** <note>original: "προσπαθείας" (prospatheias) — a technical term for the emotional "glue" that binds the soul to material objects.</note> and passion toward them. For what is the use of abstaining from deeds while remaining nailed to the causes from which those <margin>15</margin> deeds arise? <margin>32</margin> This withdrawal might happen by force, but it might also happen by persuasion and reason through a "withering away" and—as one might say—a forgetting and death of these attachments. This is indeed the best kind of withdrawal, for the soul then no longer touches that from which it has been pulled away. When something is torn away by force, it often carries <margin>20</margin> some part or trace of the tearing with it into the world of the senses; but the soul enters a state of purity through constant **lack of practice** <note>original: "ἀμελετησίαν" (ameletēsian) — the intentional ignoring or "un-training" of the senses to focus on the divine.</note>. This lack of practice is provided by abstaining from the sensations that stir the passions, while maintaining a constant concern for the **intellectual realm** <note>original: "νοητὰ" (noēta) — the world of pure thought and divine reality.</note>. Among these sensations are those that come from food. <margin>24</margin> <margin>33</margin> Therefore, we must abstain from certain foods no less than from other things—specifically those foods that are naturally suited to stir the **passionate part** <note>original: "παθητικὸν" (pathētikon) — the part of the soul responsible for emotions and physical drives.</note> of our soul. We must consider the matter in this way:

Two springs are let loose to bind the soul here in this world. From these, as if from **deadly drinks** <note>A reference to the "cup of forgetfulness" (Lethe) which souls drink before incarnation.</note>, the soul is filled and <margin>30</margin> becomes forgetful of its own divine visions. ...and pain <note>original: "λύπη" (lypē). The senses operate through things seen, heard, <margin>10</margin> tasted, smelled, or touched. Sensation is, as it were, the **metropolis** <note>original: "μητρόπολις" — Porphyry uses a political metaphor: sensation is the "mother-city" that sends out "colonies" of passions to occupy the soul.</note> of the alien colony of passions within us.

For look and see how much fuel for the passions flows into us from each sense! <margin>33</margin> On one hand, it flows from the sight of horse races and athletic contests or **effeminate dances** <note>original: "ἐκλελυγισμένων ὀρχήσεων" — literally "limber" or "twisted" dances, which Porphyry viewed as morally degrading and overstimulating.</note>; <margin>15</margin> and on the other hand, from the gazing upon women, which acts as a bait for the irrational part and overpowers it with all sorts of added snares. <margin>34</margin> For in all such matters, the soul, driven to frenzy by irrationality, is made to leap and cry out and scream, the internal agitation being <margin>20</margin> ignited by the external disturbance which sensation kindled.

Furthermore, movements of passion through the ears arise from certain noises and sounds, from foul language and insults, which make most people—having completely stripped off their reason—be carried away as if goaded by a sting, <margin>25</margin> while others, becoming effeminate, twist themselves into all sorts of physical turnings. And as for the use of incense or fragrant scents, which smuggle their own desires into lovers—who is unaware how much they fatten the irrationality of the soul?

And regarding the passions that come through taste, what could one even say? <margin>30</margin> For here especially the bond is doubly intertwined: the passions arising from the taste itself fatten the irrational part, while the ingestion of **foreign bodies** <note>original: "ἀλλοτρίων σωμάτων" — a reference to eating animal flesh, which Porphyry considers "foreign" to the human soul's nature.</note>...

...performances <note>This completes the thought from the previous page regarding visual spectacles.</note> we make the soul heavy and powerful in its attachment to the body. For **drugs** <note>original: "φάρμακα" (pharmaka) — in Greek, this term refers to both medicine and poison.</note>, as some physician once said, are not only those substances prepared by the medical art, but also the food and drink we take in for our daily nourishment. And <margin>5</margin> a lethal effect is transmitted to the soul from these foods far more than any death is produced by the medical drugs intended to dissolve the body. As for the sense of touch, it almost turns the soul into matter, and it often provokes it to fall into inarticulate noises, just as if it were a mere body. From these things, memories, imaginations, and <margin>10</margin> opinions are gathered, stirring up a swarm of **passions** <note>original: "πάθη" (pathē) — here meaning passive reactions or suffering caused by external stimuli.</note>. Therefore, there is a great <margin>35</margin> struggle to become pure of these, and great labor is required to be rid of the practice of them, since the inevitable entanglement with <margin>15</margin> sensation is present with us both by night and by day. Hence, as much as possible, we must withdraw from such places where, even against one's will, one is liable to fall into passion. We must be wary of the battle that comes from experience—and even of victory, if you like—and [instead] choose the "lack of training" <note>Porphyry suggests it is better to never be "trained" in sensory pleasure than to try to master it through experience.</note> <margin>20</margin> that comes from inexperience. Others even went so far as to sacrifice their eyesight out of a longing for the undistracted **contemplation** <note>original: "θεωρία" (theōria) — the highest state of intellectual or divine vision.</note> within. But if anyone thinks that while living among men and filling his <margin>30</margin> senses with the passions belonging to them, he can remain **dispassionate** <note>original: "ἀπαθής" (apathēs) — the philosophical ideal of being unaffected by external emotions or physical needs.</note>, he is unaware that he is deceiving himself and those who believe him; he does not realize how much he has been enslaved to the passions...

Whether something has happened well or ill in the city, or what misfortune has befallen someone from their ancestors, whether men or women, escapes the philosopher’s notice more than the proverbial 'measures of the sea' <note>original: "χόες" (choes) — a unit of liquid measure. For he does not keep away <margin>14</margin> from them for the sake of a good reputation, but in reality, his body alone lies in the <margin>15</margin> city and dwells there, while his mind, having considered all these things small and of no value, and having held them in contempt, 'flies everywhere' according to Pindar, never lowering itself to anything nearby." <margin>37</margin> <note>This marker likely refers to Chapter 37 of Porphyry's first book.</note> Through these words, Plato <margin>20</margin> says that the philosopher remains **impassive** <note>original: "ἀπαθῆ" (apathē) — free from the disturbances of the passions.</note> by not descending into the aforementioned affairs, but by refusing to involve himself with any of them.

For this reason, he knows neither the way nor where the law-court or council-chamber is, nor any other particular matter. It is not that he happens upon them and, while happening upon them, fills <margin>24</margin> his senses with them and then claims to know nothing; on the contrary, <margin>25</margin> Plato says the philosopher **abstains** from them and, because he does not know them, he is unaware even that he does not know. As for joining in dinners, it does not even occur to him in a dream, he says. It is unlikely, then, that he would be annoyed at being deprived of broths and bits of meat. <margin>30</margin> Or would he accept these things at all? Would he not rather consider them all to be small and nothing-at-all through **abstinence** <note>original: "ἀποχή" (apochē) — the title of this work, translated as "abstinence."</note>, but great and harmful through their introduction?

...realities established in truth. Since there are two patterns—the divine being most blessed and the godless being most wretched—the philosopher will become like the one and unlike the other by living a life that reflects what he resembles. This is a life that is simple, self-sufficient, and as little as possible filled with mortal concerns. <margin>5</margin> For as long as someone disputes about food <margin>38</margin> and argues that "this too must be eaten," rather than realizing that he should abstain from all food if it were possible, he is merely advocating for the passions. He hunts for reputation, behaving as if he is not at all concerned about the very things he is disputing. <margin>10</margin> Now, the philosopher will not lead himself out of life by force <note>Porphyry is arguing against suicide as a means of spiritual escape. Neoplatonists believed that a violent exit from the body leaves the soul still "sticky" with passions, whereas a natural or purified exit allows for true liberation.</note>; for by using force, he remains no less in that place from which he is struggling to depart. Yet, he will not believe that "thickening the bond" <note>The "bond" is the soul's attachment to the physical body. To "thicken" it means to strengthen that attachment through gluttony or physical pleasure.</note> is a matter of indifference. Therefore, granting to nature only what is necessary—and even then, only light food—he will reject <margin>15</margin> everything beyond this as something that contributes to pleasure. For he is persuaded by the one who said <note>original: "κατὰ τὸν εἰπόντα" (kata ton eiponta). Footnote 16 clarifies this refers to "the marvelous Plato." This specific image of the "nail" is found in Plato’s *Phaedo* 83d.</note> that sensation is like a "nail" of the soul to the body. Through the sheer force of passion, sensation glues and, as it were, nails the soul to the enjoyment found through the body. <margin>20</margin> Indeed, if sensations did not obstruct the soul's pure activity, what harm would there be in existing within a body while remaining unaffected by the impulses that arise through it? <margin>39</margin> But how could you judge or speak of what you have experienced, if you were not actually suffering <note>original: "πάσχων" (paschōn) — In this philosophical context, "suffering" refers to the soul being "acted upon" by external stimuli or sensations.</note> and were not present with the things you felt? <margin>25</margin> For the Intellect <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — the higher, contemplative mind.</note> is present to itself, even if we are not present to it. But that part of the intellect which has strayed is exactly where it has wandered; by running to and fro, up and down, through the attention of its perception, it is present wherever that perception <note>original: "ἀντίληψις" (antilēpsis) — the conscious grasp or apprehension of a sensation.</note> is. <margin>30</margin> It is one thing not to attend to sensory things because one is focused elsewhere, but it is another for someone to imagine he is not present when he has not truly withdrawn. Someone might point out that <term>Plato</term> <note>The famous Athenian philosopher (c. 427–347 BCE) whose works form the foundation of Neoplatonism.</note> allows this, unless one could show that he is deceiving himself. For the man who lets himself sink into the consumption of food and into the spectacles of the eyes—the social gatherings and the laughter—is, by that very sinking, <margin>5</margin> exactly where his <term>passion</term> <note>original: "πάθος" (pathos). In this context, it refers to an internal state of being moved or affected by external, physical desires.</note> is. But the man who is focused on other things and has stood apart from these is the one who, through "inexperience," provides a source of laughter not only to <term>Thracian servant girls</term> <note>A reference to a famous anecdote in Plato's "Theaetetus" where a Thracian girl laughs at the philosopher Thales for falling into a well while looking at the stars; he knew the heavens but not what was at his feet.</note> but to the rest of the crowd as well. Whenever he does sink down, he falls into every kind of difficulty, though not because he is senseless; rather, he does not focus on the <margin>10</margin> <term>irrational part</term> <note>The part of the soul responsible for basic instincts and physical desires, as opposed to the "nous" or intellect.</note> alone (for Plato did not dare to say that). Instead, just as in the case of insults, he has no private knowledge of anyone’s flaws and thus cannot insult anyone, because he has not made a habit of such things, as Plato says. Thus, <margin>15</margin> he appears ridiculous when he is at a loss, and in the face of praises and the boasting of others, he is seen to laugh—not mockingly, but truly—and so he appears to be a fool. <margin>40</margin> Thus, because of his "inexperience" and his abstinence, he does not know these things; it is not that he sinks into the experience and acts through the irrational part while still being <margin>20</margin> able to contemplate the things of the <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous). The highest part of the soul, capable of direct intuitive knowledge of divine reality.</note> in their purity. 

Nor should we listen to those who say we have "two souls" and who have granted us "two attentions." For they would thus be creating a union of two living beings, such that while <margin>25</margin> one was focused on one thing, it would be possible for the other not to notice the actions of the first. <margin>41</margin> But why was it necessary to "wither the passions" and to "die away" from them and to practice this daily, if it were possible for us to act according to the Mind while being joined to mortal things without the Mind's supervision, as some have claimed? For as the saying goes:
> "The Mind sees and the Mind hears." <note>A famous line attributed to the poet and philosopher Epicharmus (5th century BCE), suggesting that the physical senses are useless without the active participation of the intellect.</note>
<margin>30</margin> If, while eating rich food and drinking the sweetest wine, you are able to remain focused on immaterial things, why can you not do so while also being with concubines and doing things that are not even honorable to mention? For these passions belong everywhere to the "child" within us, and...

For it is not possible for one who is carried here and there, being in this physical place, to be simultaneously in that higher place. For we do not give our attention with only a part of ourselves, but with our whole being.

consistent with their own deception; and instead of achieving freedom,

This is what made some of the Cynics into "all-eaters" <note>original: "παντορέκτας" (pantorektas). Literally "all-reaching" or "all-stretching," used here to describe those who would eat anything or indulge every appetite without restraint.</note>, 
<margin>10</margin> clinging to the very thing that was the cause of their sins, 
<margin>43</margin> which they are accustomed to call <term>indifferent</term> <note>original: "ἀδιάφορον" (adiaphoron). In Stoic and Cynic philosophy, this refers to things that are neither morally good nor evil, such as wealth, health, or food.</note>. 
But a man who is cautious and suspicious toward the enchantments of 
nature, having examined the nature of the body and knowing how it 
is fitted like an instrument to the powers of the soul, 
<margin>15</margin> knows that the <term>passion</term> <note>original: "τὸ πάθος" (to pathos). Here, the physical sensation or reaction of the body.</note> is ready to sound out—whether 
we wish it or not—whenever the body is struck by external things 
and the strike reaches the point of perception. For perception 
happens to be the "sounding" <note>original: "φθέγξις" (phthegxis). Porphyry uses a musical metaphor: the body is the instrument, and physical sensation is the sound it makes.</note>. 
It is not possible for the soul to "sound" without the whole soul 
<margin>20</margin> turning toward the sound and shifting its supervising eye 
toward it. In general, since the <term>irrational part</term> <note>original: "τῆς ἀλογίας" (tēs alogias). The part of the soul driven by instinct and appetite rather than reason.</note> 
lacks the ability to judge the "to what extent," the "how," the 
"from where," and "toward whom"—and being by its very 
nature unreflective—it is like horses without a charioteer <note>A famous reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul is compared to a charioteer driving two horses (reason and appetite).</note>. 
<margin>25</margin> In such a state, it is impossible either to manage one’s duties 
toward external things or to know the proper timing and measure 
of food, unless the eye of the charioteer is standing over it, who 
regulates the movements and drives the irrationality which is, 
by itself, blind. 
<margin>30</margin> But he who removes the supervision of reason from the irrational part, 
permitting it to be carried away according to its own nature, would 
be like one who allows desire to proceed as far as its own movement 
wishes, and to...

<summary>Porphyry refutes the idea that a person can remain spiritually pure while indulging in physical excess, using the metaphor of a charioteer (reason) who must control the blind, irrational instincts of the body.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE I.

The same applies to anger. At any rate, it is reason that will make the <term>virtuous person</term> <note>original: "σπουδαῖον" (spoudaion). Literally "earnest" or "excellent," this refers to the person who has achieved philosophical maturity.</note> beautiful to us, making his actions well-considered and ensuring that the activities of the <term>irrational part</term> <note>original: "τοῦ ἀλόγου" (tou alogou). In Platonic and Neoplatonic thought, this is the part of the soul responsible for instincts and emotions, which lacks its own logic.</note> are not left unrestrained by the presiding reason. And yet, in this very respect, the <margin>44</margin>
<margin>5</margin> virtuous person seems to differ from the base person: the former has his <term>reason</term> <note>original: "λογισμὸν" (logismon). The faculty of calculation and rational judgment.</note> present everywhere, ruling and acting as a <term>charioteer</term> <note>original: "ἡνιοχοῦντα" (hēniochounta). A reference to Plato’s famous image in the *Phaedrus* where the soul is a chariot and reason is the driver.</note> over the irrational part; whereas the base person does many things by dismissing reason, even when he claims to act with it. This is why the one is called "irrational" and is carried away by his lack of reason, 
<margin>10</margin> while the other is called "rational" and is the master of everything irrational. Therefore, committing errors—which happens to the masses in speech, in action, in their desires, and in their fits of anger—stands in contrast to the "right actions" of the virtuous. This is because the former allow the <term>child</term> <note>original: "παιδὶ" (paidi). Porphyry uses "child" as a metaphor for the undisciplined, irrational impulses.</note> to do whatever he wishes on his own, 
<margin>15</margin> while the latter leave things to the <term>tutor</term> <note>original: "παιδαγωγῷ" (paidagōgō). So, both in the matter of food and in other bodily activities or pleasures, when the charioteer is present, he defines what is proportionate and what is timely. But when he is absent—or as some say, 
<margin>20</margin> when he is "minding his own business"—if he keeps our attention focused on himself, he does not allow the irrational part to be moved by passion or to act at all. But if he permits the soul to be with the "child" without his supervision, he destroys the man, who is then dragged along by the folly of the irrational. 
<margin>25</margin> For this reason, <term>abstinence</term> <note>original: "ἀποχὴ" (apochē). The core subject of the book: refraining from eating meat and other physical indulgences.</note> is more appropriate for <margin>45</margin> virtuous people—both abstinence from certain foods and from the pursuit of bodily pleasures and actions. For by engaging with physical things, one is forced to descend from one's own character to the "school-mastering" of the irrational part within us. 
<margin>30</margin> This is especially true regarding types of food; for not even for the sake of future...

<page-num>72</page-num>

# ON ABSTINENCE I.

...the <term>irrational part</term> <note>original: "τὸ ἄλογον" (to alogon). Referring to the part of the soul driven by instinct and appetite rather than logic.</note> is incapable of reflection. For by its very nature, the irrational is unable to recognize what is absent. Regarding our food, if it were possible to be rid of the need for it as easily as we can turn away from visible objects—for we can simply put to rest the <term>mental impressions</term> <note>original: "φαντασίας" (phantasias). In this context, the lingering mental images or "appearances" of things we have seen.</note> of such things by focusing on others—it would be a small matter; we could yield briefly to the necessity of our <margin>5</margin> mortal nature and then immediately be free of it. However, because food requires a delay of time for <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "πέψεως" (pepseōs). Literally "cooking" or "ripening," the standard term for the stomach's processing of food.</note> and distribution throughout the body, as well as the cooperation of sleep, rest, and general inactivity, followed by the specific state of the body during assimilation <margin>10</margin> and the excretion of waste, it is necessary for a <term>guardian</term> <note>original: "παιδαγωγὸν" (paidagōgon). A "pedagogue" or tutor; here, reason is envisioned as a chaperone who monitors the body's needs.</note> to be present. This guardian, selecting those things that are light and do not hinder him, will permit them to nature, looking forward to what is to come and seeing how great an obstacle is created when we allow our desires <margin>15</margin> to introduce a "burden" that is difficult to carry for the sake of a brief pleasure—a pleasure which is only perceived at the moment the food is accepted for swallowing.

<margin>46</margin> It is not without reason, then, that <term>rationality</term> <note>original: "ὁ λόγος" (ho logos).</note> rejects what is excessive and superfluous, and restricts the "necessary" to a small amount. This is done so that reason will not <margin>20</margin> struggle to provide for many things, nor require a multitude of servants to prepare them, nor be overwhelmed by sensory pleasures while eating, nor be filled with sluggishness from being "too full," nor become sleepy from being stuffed with a heavy load. Furthermore, reason seeks to avoid filling the body with things that fatten it, which would make the <term>bond</term> <note>original: "δεσμόν" (desmon). A common Platonic metaphor where the physical body is described as a "chain" or "bond" that ties the soul to the material world.</note> <margin>25</margin> stronger while making reason itself more sluggish and weaker for its own proper tasks.

Therefore, let someone show us—some man who is striving as much as possible to live according to the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun). The highest faculty of the soul, capable of direct spiritual perception.</note> and to remain undisturbed by the passions of the body—how <margin>30</margin> <term>meat-eating</term> <note>original: "κρεοφαγία" (kreophagia).</note> is more easily provided than a diet of fruits and vegetables, or how the preparation of meat is cheaper than a meatless diet (which requires no cooks at all), or how it is less pleasurable...

<summary>Porphyry argues that reason must act as a guardian over the body's digestive needs to prevent heavy foods from weighing down the soul. He begins to challenge the idea that meat is more practical or beneficial than a simple plant-based diet.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE I.

...when compared in itself to the inanimate <note>original: "ἄψυχον" (apsychon). Literally "soulless," referring to a diet of plants and minerals rather than animals.</note> diet, [the flesh diet] is heavier in digestion, whereas the other is lighter. The inanimate diet is also quicker in its <term>distribution</term> <note>original: "ἀναδόσεσιν" (anadosesin). The physiological process of nutrients spreading from the stomach to the rest of the body.</note> through the body—faster even than the distribution from vegetables—and it provokes the desires to a lesser degree. <margin>5</margin> Furthermore, it contributes less to the thickness and physical strength of the body than a meat-heavy diet. If neither a doctor, <margin>47</margin> nor a philosopher, nor a physical trainer, nor even a common person has dared to claim otherwise, why do we not willingly set aside this bodily burden? Why do we not liberate ourselves, by this very <margin>10</margin> act of withdrawal, from a multitude of troubles? For it is not just one thing, but ten thousand things that a person escapes by training themselves to be satisfied with the smallest amount: they are freed from the pursuit of excessive wealth, from the service of many attendants, from a vast collection of household goods, from a state of constant lethargy, from the severity and frequency of diseases, <margin>15</margin> from the need for doctors, from sexual provocations, from thick <term>exhalations</term> <note>original: "ἀναθυμιάσεων" (anathymiaseōn). Ancient medical theory held that digesting food produced "vapors" that could cloud the mind or affect the soul.</note>, from a mass of waste products, from the thickening of the <term>bond</term> <note>original: "δεσμοῦ" (desmou). A common Platonic metaphor for the physical body which "binds" the soul.</note>, and from that physical strength which rouses one to worldly actions—in short, from an <term>Iliad of woes</term> <note>original: "Ἰλιάδος κακῶν". A classical Greek idiom meaning a vast or endless series of troubles, referencing the length and tragedy of the Trojan War.</note>. The inanimate and simple diet, which is easily <margin>20</margin> provided for everyone, removes us from these things, preparing peace for the reason that provides us with salvation. For, as <term>Diogenes</term> <note>Diogenes the Cynic (c. 412–323 BCE), a philosopher famous for his extreme simplicity and rejection of social norms.</note> says, "Thieves and warmongers do not come from the <term>barley-eaters</term> <note>original: "μαζοφάγων" (mazophagōn). Those who eat "maza," a basic barley cake; used here to mean those on a simple, vegetarian diet.</note>, but sycophants and tyrants come from the meat-eaters." When the cause of needing many things is removed, <margin>25</margin> and the mass of substances brought into the body is cleared away, and the weight of what is being distributed is lightened, the "eye" of the soul becomes free from the smoke and the waves of the body, and it finds itself safely anchored in a harbor. This truth requires neither <margin>48</margin> reminder nor proof, because the clarity is self-evident. <margin>30</margin> Hence, not only those who are eager to live according to the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun). The highest part of the soul, capable of direct spiritual perception.</note> and who have established a life consistent with it see this abstinence as necessary for their goal, but also...

<summary>Porphyry argues that a plant-based (inanimate) diet is medically and philosophically superior to eating meat, as it reduces physical bulk and frees the mind from the "Iliad of woes" caused by bodily excess. He quotes Diogenes to link meat-eating with social vices like tyranny and theft.</summary>

<page-num>74</page-num>

# ON ABSTINENCE I.

Almost every philosopher, I believe, who prefers <term>simplicity</term> <note>original: "εὐτέλειαν" (euteleian). This refers to a lifestyle of frugality and low cost, often contrasted with the "luxury" of the wealthy.</note> over extravagance, would sooner approve of the person who is satisfied with little than the one who requires many things. And—though it might seem paradoxical to the masses—we find those who consider **pleasure** to be the ultimate goal of the philosophical life <margin>5</margin> saying and valuing this very thing. For most of the **Epicureans**, beginning with the <term>leader</term> <note>original: "κορυφαίου" (koryphaiou). Here referring to Epicurus himself.</note> himself, appear to be satisfied with a simple barley-cake and fruits; they have filled their writings with accounts of how little nature actually requires, <margin>10</margin> and they demonstrate that her necessary needs are sufficiently satisfied by simple and easily obtained things. 

"The wealth of nature," he says, "is limited and easy to obtain, but the wealth of empty opinions is both unlimited and difficult to procure." <margin>49</margin> For that which troubles the flesh through <margin>15</margin> deficiency is well and sufficiently removed by easily obtained things that have a simple nature, whether liquid or solid. But as for the rest, which falls into the category of luxury, they say that the desire for it is not necessary, nor does it arise from a necessary pain. Instead, one type of desire arises from <margin>20</margin> something that causes pain or a "sting" only when it is absent; another arises from mere delight; and another arises entirely from empty and false opinions. These latter desires do not lead back to any natural deficiency, nor to anything that would dissolve the body’s <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "σύστασιν" (systasin). The functional balance of the body's elements.</note> if they were missing. <margin>25</margin> 

Indeed, even ordinary things are enough to sustain what nature necessarily requires. These things are easily obtained because of their simplicity and their scarcity. To the person who takes up **meat-eating**, there is a need for inanimate food <note>meaning plant-based food</note> as well; but for the person satisfied with inanimate food, the <margin>30</margin> burden of preparation is halved, easily obtained, and requires very little expense. <margin>50</margin> They say one must not first prepare the necessities and then use **philosophy** as a mere accessory; rather...

<summary>Porphyry cites the Epicureans to argue that a simple, meatless diet is the most "natural" and easiest to maintain, distinguishing between necessary physical needs and unnecessary "empty" desires.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK I
## Page 78

54 ...falling into satiety <note>original: "πλησμονῇ" (plēsmone) — a state of being over-filled or glutted.</note> or distractions. For this reason, even with simple foods, one must guard against over-fullness. In every instance, we must consider what results from enjoyment or possession: how great it is, and what physical or mental nuisance it might dissolve. <margin>5</margin> We should ensure that the intensity we direct toward each thing is not for the sake of <unclear>....</unclear> just as for one whose life is <unclear>....</unclear> conceived. For one must never be without limits; instead, one must hold to a boundary and a measure in such matters. 

We should reason that the person who fears abstaining from living beings—if indeed he <margin>10</margin> clings to meat-eating <term>meat-eating: "κρεοφαγίας" (kreophagias), the practice of consuming animal flesh</term> for the sake of pleasure—actually fears death <note>original: "θάνατον" (thanaton)</note>. For he immediately connects the deprivation of these foods with the presence of some undefined terror, out of which death arises. 

It is from such causes, and others of the same kind, that the insatiable <margin>15</margin> appetite for living arises, as well as the desire for riches, money, and glory. This stems from the belief that the "total good" will increase alongside these things over a longer span of time, and from fearing the terrors associated with death as if they were endless. 

But the pleasure found through luxury does not even come close <margin>20</margin> to the pleasure that comes through self-sufficiency <note>original: "αὐταρκείας" (autarkeias) — a key philosophical concept of being content with what is necessary.</note> to one who has experienced it. For there is great delight in contemplating how little one truly needs. If luxury were removed, and if the excitement surrounding sexual matters were taken away, what ambition would remain? What <margin>25</margin> further need would there be for idle wealth, which serves us for nothing but only weighs us down? 

Just as a state of being full is achieved, so the pleasure arising from such satiety <note>original: "κόρου" (korou) — a sense of being "fed up" or fully satisfied.</note> is pure and unmixed. One must also unaccustom the body, as much as possible, to the pleasure of gluttony—not the fullness that comes from simple hunger—and <margin>30</margin> taste only enough so that <unclear>....</unclear> it passes through all things. One must set a limit at what is necessary rather than what is undefined. For in this way, it will be possible to have attained the "attainable good" through self-sufficiency and the likeness to God <note>original: "ὁμοιώσεως τοῦ θεοῦ" (homoiōseōs tou theou) — the Platonic ideal of becoming as much like the divine as possible</note>. In this state, one will not desire anything further, nor will they desire [more] time...

<summary>Porphyry argues that the craving for meat and luxury is rooted in a subconscious fear of death and a lack of self-sufficiency. He suggests that true pleasure and a "god-like" state are achieved by limiting one's desires to the bare necessities.</summary>

For it was for these gods that they kept the fire immortal in their temples, as it was the element most similar to the gods themselves. From the burning <note>original: "thumiasis"</note> of these products of the earth, they derived the names for "censers," <margin>5</margin> the act of "sacrificing," and "sacrifices." These are terms which we today understand incorrectly, as if they signified our later error; for we now apply the word **sacrifice** <note>original: "thusia"</note> to the supposed worship performed by killing animals. 

The ancients were so concerned not to transgress this custom that they pronounced curses against those who abandoned the ancient way and <margin>10</margin> introduced something new. They called the substances to be burned "aromatics" <note>original: "aromata"</note>. One might recognize the antiquity of the aforementioned incense-offerings by observing that even now many people still sacrifice certain pieces of fragrant wood cut into small pieces. 

Hence, after the era of the original grasses, once the earth began to grow trees, <margin>15</margin> humans first ate the fruit of the **oak**. Because this food was scarce, they offered only a little of it to the gods, but they burned more of the oak’s leaves in their sacrifices. After this, when human life transitioned to cultivated food and sacrifices made from crops, they said, **"Enough of the oak."** <note>This was a famous Greek proverb (halis druos) used when moving from a primitive or crude way of life to a more civilized one.</note> 

<margin>20</margin> When the fruit of **Demeter** <note>the goddess of the harvest</note>—barley—first appeared after the legumes, the human race initially used whole barley-corns in their first sacrifices. Later, after they had ground these grains and made the food into meal, they hid the tools of labor <margin>25</margin>—which had provided divine assistance to their lives—away as something secret, treating them as if they were sacred. 

Because the life sustained by ground grain was considered more blessed than the former way of life, they began by offering the first of this ground food into the fire for the gods. For this reason, even to this day, <margin>30</margin> at the conclusion of our sacrifices we use ground meal-cakes <note>original: "thulemata"</note>. By doing this, we bear witness to how sacrifices have grown from their original beginnings, even if we do not fully perceive the reason why.

...as if someone tasted human flesh or that of a female cow. The reason for this was that this animal, being extremely useful, was scarce among them. For this reason, while they did taste and offer the first-fruits of bulls, they spared the females for the sake of breeding, and they decreed it an **abomination** <note>original: "mysos," a religious pollution or defilement</note> even to touch them. And yet, <margin>5</margin> based solely on utility, they distinguished between the **pious** and the **impious** act within one and the same genus of cattle.

Since these matters are so, **Theophrastus** <note>Aristotle’s successor, known for his work on ethics and nature</note> rightly forbids those who truly wish to be pious from sacrificing **animate beings** <note>original: "empsycha," literally "beings with souls"</note>, <margin>12</margin> employing these and other similar reasons. First, because <margin>10</margin> we only began to sacrifice them—as we said—out of a dire necessity that overtook us; for famines and wars were the causes that forced us even to taste them. Since fruits are now available, what need is there to continue using a sacrifice born of desperation?

Furthermore, when returning favors and thanks, <margin>15</margin> different rewards should be given to different beings according to the value of their kindness. To those who have granted us the greatest benefits, we must return the greatest thanks from our most precious possessions—especially if they were the ones who provided those things in the first place. Now, the most beautiful and precious things the gods bestow upon us are the **fruits of the earth**; <margin>20</margin> for through these they preserve us and allow us to live in an orderly, civilized manner. Therefore, we should honor the gods with these.

Moreover, one ought to sacrifice only those things which, in the offering, cause no harm to anyone; for nothing should be as harmless to all as a sacrifice. But if <margin>25</margin> someone should argue that God gave us animals for our use no less than fruits, it remains true that when animals are sacrificed, it brings a certain harm to them, as they are robbed of their life <note>original: "psyche," the soul or vital principle</note>. <margin>11</margin> Therefore, these should not be sacrificed; for the very word "sacrifice" implies a **holy** <note>original: "hosia," suggesting something sanctioned by divine law</note> act. No one is holy who gives thanks using what belongs to another, whether it be fruits or plants taken against the owner's will. For how can it be holy when those who are deprived are wronged? If not even fruits taken [by force]...

<summary>Porphyry quotes Theophrastus to argue that animal sacrifice originated from desperate necessity (war and famine) rather than piety. He asserts that true sacrifice must be harmless and should consist of the fruits of the earth, which are the gods' most precious gifts to humanity.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE II.

...while one may sacrifice other things piously, it is entirely **impious** <note>original: "ouch hosion"</note> to sacrifice by taking away things that are far more precious; for in doing so, the injustice becomes even greater. A **soul** <note>original: "psyche," the life-force that distinguishes living creatures from plants</note> is far more precious than the things that grow from the earth, and it is not right to take it away by sacrificing animals. <margin>5</margin> <margin>13</margin> But perhaps someone might say that we also take something away from plants? Is this not so? Indeed, but the taking is not of the same kind. For it is not taken from an unwilling source. If we leave them alone, they drop their fruits naturally; furthermore, the taking of fruit does not involve the **destruction** of the plant, unlike when animals must surrender their life-force. <margin>10</margin> Even the taking of the "fruit" produced by bees—honey—which results from our own hard work, should be a shared benefit. For while the bees collect the honey from plants, we are the ones who tend to them. Therefore, it should be divided <margin>15</margin> in such a way that no harm comes to them. What is useless to them, but useful to us, serves as our "wage" from them.

One must, therefore, abstain from animals in sacrifices. For in another sense, while all things belong to the gods, the fruits of the earth seem to be specifically ours; <margin>20</margin> it is we who sow them, plant them, and nourish them through our own labor and care. We should, therefore, sacrifice from what is truly our own, not from what belongs to others. After all, that which is inexpensive and easy to procure is more **holy** and pleasing to the gods than that which is difficult to obtain; that which is easiest for the worshiper is always ready for the practice of <margin>25</margin> continuous **piety** <note>original: "eusebeia"</note>. Therefore, that which is neither holy nor inexpensive should not be sacrificed at all, even if it were available. <margin>14</margin> One can see that animals are not among these easy or inexpensive things by looking at the majority of the human race. <margin>30</margin> We should not just look at those few men who are "rich in lambs" or "rich in oxen" <note>These are traditional Homeric epithets (polyrrhenes, polyboutai) used to describe wealthy kings</note>. We must consider, first, that many nations possess none of these sacrificial animals at all (unless one counts "worthless" creatures); and second, that even for those living in the cities...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animals should not be sacrificed because they possess souls, unlike plants, and because true piety should rely on inexpensive offerings resulting from one's own labor rather than the destruction of life.</summary>

# DE ABSTINENTIA II.

...most people lack these things. Even if someone were to say they lack cultivated crops, they certainly do not lack the other things that grow from the earth; and even so, it is not as difficult to provide fruits as it is animals. For the provision of fruits and things from the earth is **easier** <margin>5</margin> than that of animals.

<margin>15</margin> That which is **inexpensive** <note>original: "eudapanon," literally "well-spent" or low-cost</note> and **easy to obtain** contributes toward continuous piety for all people. Experience itself bears witness that the gods rejoice in this more than in that which is highly expensive. For once, when a certain Thessalian brought <margin>10</margin> gold-horned oxen and whole **hecatombs** <term>a massive public sacrifice, historically involving one hundred oxen</term> to the Pythian shrine, the **Pythia** <note>the high priestess of Apollo at Delphi</note> declared that the man from Hermione was more pleasing to the god, though he had offered only some **sacrificial meal** <note>original: "psaista," simple barley cakes or groats used in humble offerings</note> from his small pouch using just three fingers. But when that man, having heard what was said, cast everything remaining in his pouch onto the altar as an extra offering, the priestess spoke again, saying that by doing this, he had become twice as hateful as he had previously been pleasing. Thus, the inexpensive is dear to the gods, and the **Divine** <note>original: "daimonion"</note> looks more toward the **moral character** <note>original: "ethos"</note> of those who sacrifice than toward the **quantity** of the things sacrificed.

<margin>16</margin> The historian **Theopompus** <note>a Greek historian of the 4th century BCE</note> recorded similar things. He says that a man from Magnesia in Asia arrived <margin>20</margin> at Delphi—an extremely wealthy man who owned numerous herds. This man was accustomed to performing many magnificent sacrifices to the gods every single year; he did this partly because of his great wealth, and partly out of **piety** and a desire to please the gods. Being so disposed toward the Divine, he went to Delphi, and after <margin>25</margin> leading a procession of a hecatomb for the god and honoring **Apollo** magnificently, he entered the oracle to consult the shrine. Thinking that he served the gods better than any other human, he asked the Pythia to reveal who it was that honored the Divine <margin>30</margin> best and most zealously, and whose sacrifices were most pleasing to the gods.

<summary>Porphyry argues that simple, inexpensive plant offerings are superior to lavish animal sacrifices, illustrating this with stories from Delphi where the Pythia prefers humble gifts over "gold-horned oxen."</summary>

# DE ABSTINENTIA II.

<margin>71</margin> ...expecting that the first prize for piety would be awarded to him. The priestess, however, replied that Clearchus, who lived in Methydrium in Arcadia, served the gods better than anyone else. <margin>5</margin> Astounded by this, the man felt an intense desire to see this person and, upon meeting him, to learn exactly how he performed his sacrifices. So, he hurried to Methydrium. At first, he looked down on the place because it was such a small and humble village; he believed that not only could no individual there, but not even the <margin>10</margin> city itself, honor the gods with more splendor or beauty than he did. 

<margin>79</margin> Nonetheless, when he met the man, he asked him to describe the manner in which he honors the gods. Clearchus replied that he performs his duties and <margin>15</margin> sacrifices with great care at the appropriate times. Every month, on the **new moons**, he garlands and polishes the statues of **Hermes** and **Hecate** <note>Hermes was the messenger god and protector of travelers; Hecate was a goddess associated with boundaries and protection from evil</note> and the other sacred relics left by his ancestors, honoring them with **frankincense** <note>original: "libanōtos," an aromatic resin from the Levant</note>, **sacrificial meal** <note>original: "psaista"; barley meal mixed with oil and wine, often gathered from the scrapings of the mill</note>, and **sacred cakes** <note>original: "popana"; thin, broad, circular cakes</note>. <margin>81</margin> Every year, he conducts public sacrifices and never misses a single festival. In these celebrations, he <margin>20</margin> serves the gods not by **slaughtering oxen** or butchering sacrificial animals, but by offering whatever happens to be available. He makes a point of dedicating the **first-fruits** <term>the first results of a harvest, offered as a gift of thanks to the divine</term> to the gods from all the surplus produce and seasonal fruits gathered from the earth. <margin>25</margin> <margin>81</margin> Some of these he sets out as an offering, while others he burns for them. Having dedicated himself to a life of **self-sufficiency** <note>original: "autarkeia," a core Greek virtue of needing very little</note>, he gives no thought to the sacrifice of oxen.

# ON ABSTINENCE II.

<margin>17</margin> It is related by some historians that when the **Tyrrhenians** <note>The Greeks' name for the Etruscans of Italy</note> defeated the **Carthaginians** in battle, they engaged in a great rivalry with one another to present the most magnificent **hecatombs** <note>original: "hekatombas"; literally a sacrifice of one hundred oxen, but often used for any large, costly public sacrifice</note> to **Apollo**. When they inquired of the god which offerings pleased him most, he replied, contrary to all their expectations, that he preferred the **sacrificial meal** <note>original: "psaistois"; coarse barley meal mixed with oil and wine</note> of Docimus. This Docimus was a man from **Delphi** <note>The site of the most famous oracle of Apollo in Greece</note> who farmed a harsh, stony patch of land. On that very day, coming down from his field, he had offered a few handfuls of barley meal from the pouch he carried around him, delighting the god more than those who performed such grandiose sacrifices. For this reason, it seemed to some of the poets—because it was a well-known truth—that they should declare such things, as is said by **Antiphanes** <note>An important writer of Greek Middle Comedy</note> in his play *The Woman Initiate*:

> For the gods delight in inexpensive things;
> and here is the proof: when people
> sacrifice hecatombs, upon all of these, last of
> all, the **frankincense** <note>original: "libanōtos"; an aromatic resin burned as an offering</note> is placed.
> This shows that while the rest of the great expense
> is a vain waste for their sake,
> this small thing alone is what is pleasing to the gods.

And **Menander** <note>The most famous writer of Greek New Comedy</note> says in *The Grouch*:

> The frankincense is a pious thing,
> as is the **sacred cake** <note>original: "popanon"; a round, thin sacrificial cake</note>; for the god receives
> this when it is placed entirely upon the fire.

<margin>18</margin> For this reason, people also used vessels made of clay, wood, and wicker, especially for public religious rites, being convinced that the divine world delights in such things. Thus, even the oldest statues, being made of clay or wood, are considered more divine because of their material.

# ON ABSTINENCE II.

...the material and the simplicity of the craft.
