# ON ABSTINENCE II.

...natural kinship. In **Epidaurus** <note>The site of the most famous healing sanctuary of Asclepius</note>, at least, there was an inscription:

> One must be pure when entering the fragrant temple;
> and purity is to think holy thoughts.

<margin>20</margin> <margin>5</margin> That the god does not rejoice in the massive scale of sacrifices, but in whatever is at hand, is clear from our daily food. No matter what kind of food is served, everyone offers a small **first-fruit** <note>original: "aparchesthai"; a ritual portion set aside for the gods before eating</note> before enjoying it. Although this portion is small, by this very smallness, it is a very great <margin>10</margin> honor. **Theophrastus** <note>Successor to Aristotle and author of a lost work "On Piety"</note> has demonstrated through many examples of ancestral customs that in ancient times, sacrifices consisted of the yearly fruits—first the grasses being taken—and he explains the history of **libations** <note>original: "spondōn"; the ritual pouring of liquids as an offering</note> in this same way. Among many peoples, the ancient rites were **sober** <note>original: "nephalia"; meaning "without wine"</note> (and sober rites are those where water is poured as a libation); <margin>15</margin> after these came the **honey-libations** <note>original: "melisponda"</note>, for we first received this liquid fruit ready-made from bees; then came **oil-libations** <note>original: "elaiosponda"</note>; and finally, the last to appear were **wine-libations** <note>original: "oinosponda"</note>. 

<margin>21</margin> These facts are attested not only by the **ritual tablets** <note>original: "kyrbeōn"; ancient wooden or stone pillars inscribed with laws and sacred rites</note>, which are effectively copies <margin>20</margin> of the **Corybantic** <note>Relating to the Corybantes, the armored dancers who guarded the infant Zeus in Crete</note> rites from **Crete**, but also by **Empedocles** <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who advocated for the "Golden Age" of peace and non-violence</note>. When discussing sacrifices and the origin of the gods, he indicates the same thing by saying:

<margin>25</margin> > Among them, there was no god **Ares** <note>God of war</note> nor **Uproar** <note>original: "Kydoimos"; the personification of the din of battle</note>,
> nor was there King **Zeus**, nor **Cronus**, nor **Poseidon**,
> but **Cypris** <note>Aphrodite, the goddess of Love</note> was Queen.
> She is **Friendship** <note>original: "Philia"; in Empedocles’ philosophy, the force that binds the universe together</note>;
> and her they appeased with pious images,
<margin>30</margin> > with painted animals and perfumes of varied scents,
> with sacrifices of pure myrrh and fragrant frankincense,
> throwing libations of yellow honey upon the ground.

<summary>Porphyry argues that true purity is a state of mind and that the history of religion shows a shift from simple plant and liquid offerings to modern, bloody sacrifices. He quotes Empedocles to describe an ancient "Golden Age" where Love (Cypris) ruled and no animals were killed for the gods.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE II.

...nor those that do evil, how is it not clearer than anything else that one must especially abstain from and not sacrifice any of the remaining **living beings** <note>original: "zōiōn"; while often translated as 'animals,' the term implies all things possessing life</note>, even if it is indeed fitting to do away with some of the others?

<margin>24</margin>
Furthermore, there are three reasons to sacrifice to the **gods** <note>original: "theois"</note>: either for the sake of **honor** <note>original: "timē"</note>, or out of **gratitude** <note>original: "charin"</note>, or because of a **need** <note>original: "chreian"</note> for good things.

<margin>5</margin>
For just as we do for good men, so too we believe we must offer the **first-fruits** <note>original: "aparchas"; the first portion of a crop or harvest dedicated to a deity</note> to them. We honor the gods either seeking the turning away of evils and the provision of good things for ourselves, or because we have already been treated well, or so that we might obtain some benefit,

<margin>10</margin>
or simply out of a pure appreciation of their own excellent state. Thus, if animals are to be offered as first-fruits to the gods, they must be sacrificed for one of these reasons. For whatever we sacrifice, we sacrifice for one of these purposes. Would the god then consider himself to be receiving

<margin>15</margin>
honor from us when we appear to be acting unjustly through the very act of offering the first-fruits? Or would he instead think such an action is a dishonor? By killing animals that do no wrong in the act of sacrificing, we admit that we are acting unjustly. Therefore, for the sake of honor, none

<margin>20</margin>
of the other animals should be sacrificed. Nor, indeed, should they be sacrificed to return gratitude for benefits received. For he who returns a just exchange for a benefit and a worthy return for a good deed ought not to provide these by doing evil to anyone. One would no more

<margin>25</margin>
be seen as making a return than if someone were to snatch the property of a neighbor and then crown certain people as if returning gratitude and honor. But neither should it be done for the sake of any need for good things. For he who hunts for good treatment through an unjust act is suspected of not being grateful even after he has been treated well.

<margin>30</margin>
Therefore, not even in the hope of an expected benefit should animals be sacrificed to the gods. For one might perhaps escape the notice of men while doing this, but it is impossible to escape the notice of God. If, therefore, sacrifice must be made for these reasons...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animal sacrifice fails to meet the three traditional criteria for religious offerings—honor, gratitude, and petition—because killing an innocent creature is inherently unjust and cannot please a divine being.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE II.

...for some reason, but if it must be done for none of these, it is clear that one should not sacrifice **living beings** <note>original: "zōia"; the Greek term for animals or any animated beings</note> to the gods at all.

<margin>25</margin>
For through the pleasures derived from these sacrifices, we try to blot out the truth regarding them, and in doing so we deceive ourselves—for we certainly do not deceive **God**.

<margin>5</margin>
Now, of the "worthless" animals, those that provide no use for our lives and offer no enjoyment, we sacrifice none to the gods. For who has ever sacrificed **snakes and scorpions** or **apes**, or any such creatures?

<margin>10</margin>
But regarding those that provide some use to our lives, or contain within themselves something for our enjoyment, we abstain from none of them. We truly slaughter and skin them under the pretense of protecting the divine realm.

<margin>14</margin>
For we sacrifice **oxen and sheep**, and in addition to these, **deer and birds** to the gods; we even sacrifice **fat hogs** <note>original: "sialous"; specifically refers to well-fed or fatted pigs destined for slaughter</note>, who share nothing in the way of cleanliness but provide us with great enjoyment.

<margin>18</margin>
Some of these assist our lives by working alongside us, while others provide help for our nourishment or other needs. But even those that do none of these things are destroyed by men in sacrifices because of the **enjoyment** <note>original: "apolausin"; here referring to the sensory pleasure of eating meat</note> they provide, just like those that are useful.

<margin>22</margin>
Yet we do not sacrifice **donkeys or elephants** or any others among those who work alongside us but offer no pleasure as food. And yet, even apart from the act of sacrifice, we do not abstain from such edible creatures, slaughtering them for our enjoyment.

<margin>26</margin>
We do not sacrifice to the gods those parts of the victims that truly belong to them, but rather those things which are pleasing to the **desires of men** <note>original: "anthrōpōn epithymiais"</note>. In this, we bear witness against ourselves: it is for the sake of our own enjoyment that we persist in these types of sacrifices.

<margin>30</margin>
And yet, among the **Syrians** <note>Porphyry is following a Greek tradition that classified Jews as a sub-group of Syrians</note>, the **Jews**—on account of their original sacrifice—still now, as **Theophrastus** <note>a student of Aristotle; his work "On Piety" is a major source for Porphyry</note> says, perform animal sacrifices; if they were to command us to do so in the same way...

->PORPHYRIUS. 7<-

# ON ABSTINENCE II.

...[if they were commanded] to sacrifice, we would desist from the action. For we do not feast upon the victims; instead, by making **whole-burnt offerings** <note>original: "holokaustountes"; sacrifices where the entire animal was consumed by fire for the gods rather than shared as a meal by the worshippers</note> of them at night and pouring much honey and wine over them, they consumed the sacrifice quickly, so that the <margin>5</margin> **All-Seeing One** <note>original: "panoptēs"; a title usually referring to the Sun or Zeus as the witness of all human deeds</note> might not behold the dread deed. And they perform this while fasting during the days between these rites. Throughout this entire time, being **philosophers by nature** <note>original: "philosophoi to genos"; Porphyry often refers to ancient priestly castes, like the Magi or Egyptian priests, as philosophers by birth or race</note>, they converse with one another about the divine, and at night they engage in the **study of the stars** <note>original: "theōrian"; a contemplative looking or theoretical study</note>, <margin>10</margin> gazing at them and calling upon the gods through their prayers. For these people were the first to make offerings of other animals and of themselves, doing so out of necessity and not out of desire.

One might learn this by looking at the **Egyptians**, the most learned of all, who were so <margin>15</margin> far from killing any of the other animals that they made images of them as likenesses of the gods. So much did they consider these creatures to be kindred and related to the gods and to men. 

<margin>27</margin> For from the beginning, the sacrifices made to the gods consisted of **fruits**; but in time, when we became neglectful of our holiness and <margin>20</margin> fruits became scarce—and because of the lack of lawful food, men were driven to eat one another’s flesh—then, with many prayers entreating the divine, they first **offered themselves** <note>original: "sphōn autōn apērxanto"; the beginning of human sacrifice as a desperate substitute for cannibalism</note> to the gods. They did this not only by dedicating the most beautiful among them to the gods, but <margin>25</margin> even taking those beyond the most beautiful of their race. From that time until now, it is not only in **Arcadia** at the festival of Lycaean Zeus, nor in **Carthage** to Kronos, that everyone commonly performs human sacrifice, but according to a cycle, for the sake of preserving the memory of the ancient law, <margin>30</margin> they sprinkle **kindred blood** <note>original: "emphulion haima"; blood from one's own people or family</note> upon the altars, even though their own sense of holiness now excludes the unholy from the temples...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animal and human sacrifices originated from ancient periods of starvation and "dread deeds" rather than true piety. He cites the Egyptians as a counter-example, noting their historical reverence for animals as kindred to the divine.</summary>

This is exactly what happens now among all people regarding the food derived from fruits. For once they have relieved their necessary hunger with such offerings, <margin>10</margin> they seek the excess of satiety and labor to produce many foods for eating that lie outside the bounds of **temperance** <note>original: "sōphrosynē"; self-control or moderation</note>. Consequently, as if they were not treating the victims offered to the gods as things without honor, they were led to taste them. Because of the origin of this practice, <margin>15</margin> **meat-eating** <note>original: "zōophagia"; the eating of living things</note> became an addition to the fruit-based diet of mankind. 

Just as in ancient times they offered the first-fruits to the gods and then gladly tasted the consecrated offerings after the holy rite, they thought they should do the same with animals after the initial sacrifice— <margin>20</margin> even though in ancient times **holy law** <note>original: "hosia"; divine law as opposed to human law</note> did not ordain it this way, but rather honored each of the divine beings with fruits. ### ON ABSTINENCE II.

...similarly, they also shared this sense of **piety** <note>original: "eusebeia"; the proper fulfillment of religious duties</note> with those who practiced it. Whenever they set aside a portion of an animal for the gods as a **first-fruit offering** <note>original: "aparchēn"; the first portion of a harvest or sacrifice dedicated to a deity</note> in place of themselves, they would taste only that portion; in truth, they lived their lives without touching anything else. 

But we do not act this way. We fill ourselves to excess and have arrived at a manifold state of lawlessness regarding these matters throughout our lives. For one should neither stain the altars of the gods with slaughter, nor should humans touch such food—just as they would not touch their own bodies. Instead, we should observe throughout our whole lives the instruction that is still preserved in Athens.

<margin>29</margin> For in ancient times, as we mentioned before, when men sacrificed fruits to the gods and not animals—nor even using animals for their own food—it is said that during a public sacrifice in Athens, a certain **Diomos** or **Sopatros** (who was not a native Athenian but a farmer in Attica), saw one of his oxen come in from work and devour some of the **sacrificial cakes** <note>original: "pelanos"; a thick, liquid offering of meal, honey, and oil</note> and **offerings** <note>original: "thylēmata"; specifically, grain or meal offerings</note> that were lying clearly on the table intended for sacrifice to the gods. The ox even trampled some of them. In a fit of extreme rage at what had happened, he grabbed an axe that was being sharpened nearby and struck the ox down. 

When the ox died and his anger had subsided, he realized what a terrible deed he had done. He buried the ox and, taking upon himself a voluntary exile as one who had committed an **impious act** <note>original: "ēsebēkōs"; having acted without proper respect for the divine</note>, he fled to Crete. However, when droughts took hold and a terrible crop failure occurred, the people collectively consulted the god. The **Pythia** <note>the high priestess of Apollo at Delphi who delivered oracles</note> responded that the exile in Crete would resolve these troubles; she declared that they must punish the killer and "raise up" the dead animal in the very sacrifice in which it died, and that it would be better for those who tasted of the dead and not...

### ON ABSTINENCE II.

...participated. When an investigation took place and Sopatros was caught in the act, he believed he would be freed from the burden of being "under a curse" if everyone shared in the deed together. He told those who had pursued him that the city itself must slaughter an ox. When they were at a loss as to who would be the one to strike the blow, he offered to perform the task for them, provided they made him a citizen and shared in the guilt of the **murder** <note>original: "phonou"; the text treats the killing of a laboring animal as a legal homicide</note>.

<margin>10</margin> Once these terms were agreed upon and they returned to the city, they organized the ritual action which continues among them to this day. <margin>30</margin> They selected young women as "water-bearers"; these women bring water to sharpen the axe and the knife. After they are sharpened, one person hands over the axe, another strikes the ox, and another slaughters it. After those who came next had skinned the animal, everyone tasted the meat.

<margin>15</margin> When these things were finished, they sewed up the hide of the ox and, stuffing it with hay, they stood it back up so that it had the same appearance as it did when it was alive, and they hitched it to a plow as if it were working.

<margin>20</margin> They then held a formal trial for the murder, calling all those who participated in the act to offer a defense. The water-bearers blamed those who had sharpened the tools more than themselves; those who sharpened the tools blamed the one who handed over the axe; he blamed the one who struck the blow; and <margin>25</margin> he in turn blamed the one who cut the throat. The one who performed this last act blamed the knife. Since the knife was voiceless, they convicted it of the murder.

From that time until now, during the **Dipolieia** <note>a festival held in early summer in honor of Zeus Polieus, "Zeus of the City"</note> in Athens on the Acropolis, the designated participants perform the sacrifice of the ox in this same manner. After placing **sacrificial cakes** <note>original: "pelanos" and "psaista"; offerings made of meal, oil, and honey</note> on a bronze table, <margin>30</margin> they drive the selected oxen around it, and the one that tastes the offerings is the one to be struck down. There are specific families who perform these tasks today: those descended from...

### ON ABSTINENCE II.

...the descendants of Sopatros, who struck the blow, are all called "ox-strikers" (**boutupoi**); those descended from the one who drove the animal around are called "goaders" (**kentriadai**); and those from the one who cut the throat are named "carvers" (**daitroi**) because of the "feast" (**dais**) <note>original: "dais"; Porphyry is highlighting the linguistic connection between the word for carver and the word for a banquet</note> that results from the distribution of meat. 

<margin>5</margin> After filling the hide <note>referring to the previous page's description of stuffing the ox hide with hay to "resurrect" it</note>, when they are brought to trial, they "sink" <note>or "drown"</note> the knife into the sea. Thus, <margin>31</margin> in the ancient days, it was not considered holy to kill the animals that work alongside us in our lives, and we must still be careful about doing this now. 

And just as it was once not holy for men <margin>10</margin> to touch these animals, so now we must consider it unholy to touch animals for the sake of food. This is not even something to be done merely for the sake of ritual purity toward the divine; rather, it is because all such "passion" <note>original: "pathos"; here referring to the violent impulse or the emotional stain of killing</note> must be expelled from our bodies entirely. We do this so that we do not carry "pollution" <note>original: "miasma"; a ritual or spiritual stain caused by bloodshed</note> as a housemate <margin>15</margin> in our own lives by procuring food from sources where it is not proper. 

For even if there were no other benefit, we would all benefit greatly in terms of "mutual peace" <note>original: "ekecheiria"; a term often used for a sacred truce, literally a "holding of hands"</note> toward one another. For those whose sensitivity has turned them away from touching animals of other species, it is perfectly obvious that their mind will also keep them from harming those of their own species <note>meaning other human beings</note>. <margin>20</margin> 

Perhaps it would have been best to abstain from everything from the start; but since no one is without sin, it remains for us to heal our previous sins regarding food through purifications. This could happen if, placing the horror before our eyes, we spoke with reverence <margin>25</margin> according to the words of Empedocles <note>a 5th-century BCE philosopher who taught that animals had souls and that eating them was a crime</note>, saying:

> "Alas, that the pitiless day did not destroy me,
> before I devised the wretched deed of bringing food to my lips!"

For those who feel pain in their own hearts for their sins, and who seek a "remedy" <note>original: "akos"; a healing or compensation</note> <margin>30</margin> for the evils that exist, they seek a way of life so that each person might happen to offer themselves like holy sacrifices to the divine as a "first-fruit"...

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Porphyry moves from discussing the history of sacrifice according to Theophrastus to presenting his own Neoplatonic hierarchy of worship. ### ON ABSTINENCE II.

We say that there was a time when humans did not touch the food 
of living souls <note>original: "empsychou boras"; meat or food derived from creatures with a soul</note> nor did they offer first-fruits from 
animals, but from the time they first tasted meat, they also began 
offering first-fruits of animals to the gods. Consequently, even now 
it is surely proper that he who abstains from those things should offer 
<margin>34</margin> first-fruits <note>original: "aparchesthai"; the traditional act of dedicating the first portion of a harvest or meal to the divine</note> only of those things which he touches. We too, therefore, shall <margin>5</margin> 
sacrifice; but we shall sacrifice as is fitting, bringing different 
sacrifices to different powers. To the God who is over 
all—as a certain wise man said <note>Likely referring to Apollonius of Tyana, a famous Neopythagorean philosopher</note>—we should offer nothing 
perceivable by the senses, neither burning incense nor 
naming Him with spoken words. For there is nothing 
material <term>enulon</term> which is not immediately impure <margin>10</margin> 
to the Immaterial <term>aulō</term>. For this reason, neither 
the spoken word is appropriate for Him, nor even the 
internal word when it is defiled by the passions of the soul; 
instead, we worship Him through pure silence and through 
pure thoughts about Him. It is necessary, therefore, that having 
joined and likened ourselves to Him, we offer our own <margin>15</margin> 
ascent <term>anagōgēn</term> <note>the philosophical process of the soul "rising up" to the divine</note> as a sacred sacrifice to God—this being both 
our hymn of praise and our salvation. This sacrifice is 
perfected in the soul's freedom from passion <term>apatheia</term> 
and in the contemplation <term>theōria</term> of God. 
But to His offspring—the intelligible gods <note>secondary divine beings that exist in the realm of Pure Intellect</note>—we should <margin>20</margin> 
now add the hymnody of the spoken word. For a sacrifice 
is a first-fruit for each of the things they have given, and through 
which they nourish us and hold our essence together in being. 
Just as a farmer offers first-fruits of the sheaves and the 
fruit-trees, so we shall offer to them the first-fruits of <margin>25</margin> 
beautiful thoughts about them, giving thanks for the 
contemplation they have granted us, and because they 
truly nourish us through the vision of them, being present 
with us, appearing to us, and shining upon our 
<margin>35</margin> salvation. But now, many even of those who have sought 
to study philosophy hesitate to do this; seeking 
reputation <note>original: "doxokopountes"; literally 'clapper-hunting' or seeking public applause</note> rather than honoring the Divine, they occupy <margin>30</margin> 
themselves with physical statues <note>original: "aphidrumata"; consecrated images or shrines</note>, without even considering 
how they ought to approach the gods, nor having learned 
it from those wise in divine matters...

<meta>Continuing the discussion of the hierarchy of sacrifice, Porphyry transitions from the silent, mental worship of the Supreme God to the intellectual offerings of the Pythagoreans and the specific bloodless rituals required for the celestial deities (the stars and planets). ### ON ABSTINENCE II.

...having been diligent to see how far and to what extent we must make comparisons here. But we shall not differ from these men, lest we ourselves also strive to make such distinctions; instead, we shall imitate those holy and ancient people, offering the greater part of our first-fruits from the contemplation <term>theōrias</term> <note>deep philosophical study or "vision"</note> <margin>5</margin> which they themselves have handed down to us, and which we now find necessary for our true salvation.

<margin>36</margin> The Pythagoreans <note>followers of Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the building blocks of the universe</note>, for instance, being devoted to numbers and geometric lines, offered the greater part of their first-fruits to the gods from these studies. They <margin>10</margin> called a certain number "Athena," and another "Artemis," just as they called another "Apollo." Again, they identified one number with "Justice" and another with "Temperance"; they did the same with geometric diagrams. In this way, they pleased the gods with such first-fruits, even encountering them by calling <margin>15</margin> upon each deity through these dedicated objects, often using them for divination <term>manteian</term> or whenever they needed to conduct a philosophical investigation.

To the gods within the heavens—both the wandering stars <note>the planets</note> and the fixed stars—among whom the Sun must be placed as the leader of all and the Moon as second, we should kindle a kindred fire <margin>20</margin> and perform the actions described by "the theologian" <note>likely referring to Orpheus, the legendary poet-priest</note>. This authority says to sacrifice not a single living thing <note>original: "empsychon"; a creature with a soul</note>, but rather to offer first-fruits of barley meal, honey, the fruits of the earth’s trees, and various flowers. He says the sacrificial fire must not be taken from <margin>25</margin> a blood-stained hearth, along with his other instructions—for why is it necessary for me to transcribe them here? He who cares for piety knows that no living thing is sacrificed to the true gods, but rather to spirits <term>daimosi</term> <note>daemons or intermediary beings, ranging from divine to "base"</note>—whether they be good or even base—and he knows which people sacrifice to these beings and how far <margin>30</margin> the spirits require such offerings. As for me, let other matters "remain well-spoken" <note>original: "eustoma"; a ritual term for maintaining a holy silence about sacred mysteries</note>...

### ON ABSTINENCE II.

...Since some of the Platonists <term>Platōnikōn</term> <note>philosophers following the school of Plato, whose ideas Porphyry synthesized</note> have made these matters public, it is not offensive to present them to intelligent readers to explain our subject. They speak as follows: The first god <note>The "One," the supreme, transcendent source of all existence</note>, being incorporeal <term>asōmatos</term>, unmoved, and indivisible, neither existing within anything else nor being bound <insert>5</insert> to himself, has no need for anything external, as has been said. Neither does the Soul of the World <term>psychē tou kosmou</term> <note>the spiritual force that animates and organizes the physical universe</note> [have need of anything]; though she possesses three-dimensional extension and is naturally self-moving, she is designed by nature to choose to move beautifully and orderly, and to move the body of the universe according to the highest principles. She has <insert>10</insert> received the world’s body into herself and encompassed it, despite being incorporeal and entirely free from any passion <term>pathous</term> <note>in this sense, "passion" means being affected or changed by external physical forces</note>.

To the other gods—the universe itself, the fixed stars, and the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>—who are visible gods composed of both soul and body, <insert>15</insert> we must show gratitude in the manner already described: through inanimate <note>original: "apsychōn," meaning bloodless or "without soul," such as plants, grains, or incense</note> sacrifices.

There remains for us, then, the multitude of invisible beings, whom Plato called "daemons" <term>daimonas</term> <note>intermediary spirits; in this period, the term was neutral and included both helpful and harmful spirits, not just "demons" in the modern sense</note> without making further distinctions. Some of these have been given names by humans and <insert>20</insert> receive honors equal to the gods and other forms of service in various places. Others, for the most part, have not been named at all, but receive names and worship obscurely from certain people in villages or particular cities.

As for the rest of the multitude, they are addressed collectively by the general <insert>25</insert> name of "daemons." There is a widespread belief regarding all of them that they might cause harm if they are angered by being overlooked or by failing to receive their customary service; and conversely, that they might benefit those who appease them with prayers, <insert>30</insert> supplications, sacrifices, and the accompanying rituals. 
<margin>38</margin> Because the common understanding of them is confused and leads to much slander <note>or "disrepute"</note>, it is necessary to use reason to distinguish their true nature. Perhaps...

<summary>Porphyry outlines the celestial hierarchy, from the self-sufficient Supreme God and World Soul down to visible celestial bodies and invisible daemons. He explains that while higher beings need nothing, humans believe daemons must be appeased with rituals to prevent harm.</summary>

<meta>On the previous page, Porphyry described the highest gods as transcendent and requiring only pure, intellectual worship or bloodless offerings. ### ->DE ABSTINENTIA II.<-

...for they say it is necessary to reveal the origin of the error that has arisen among men concerning these beings. Therefore, a distinction must be made in the following manner. Those souls that have branched off from the Whole and manage the great parts of the sublunary <note>the regions between the Earth and the Moon, traditionally considered the realm of change and decay</note> <margin>5</margin> regions—supporting themselves upon a spirit-substance <term>pneuma</term> <note>original: "pneuma," a subtle, airy matter that serves as a "vehicle" or body for the soul</note> but ruling over it according to reason—these must be considered **good daemons** <term>daimones</term>. We should believe that they occupy themselves with the benefit of everything under their care, whether they preside over certain animals, or specific crops, or the things that exist for the sake of these, <margin>10</margin> such as rains, moderate winds, fair weather, and all other things that assist these ends—namely, the balanced temperament of the seasons of the year. For us, they also oversee the arts and all that pertains to music, education, medicine, gymnastics, or anything similar. For it is impossible for these <margin>15</margin> to provide benefits and yet, in turn, be the causes of harm in these very same matters.

Among these we must also number the "messengers" <note>original: "porthmeuontas," literally "ferrymen"</note>, as Plato says <note>a reference to Plato’s *Symposium*, where daemons act as intermediaries between the human and divine</note>, who announce things from humans to gods and from gods to humans. They carry our prayers <margin>20</margin> to the gods as if to judges, and they bring back to us the gods' advice and warnings along with prophecies.

But those souls that do not rule over the spirit-substance that attaches to them, but for the most part are ruled by it—for this very reason they are driven and carried away excessively <margin>25</margin> whenever the angers and desires of the spirit-substance take hold. These souls are also daemons, but they should rightly be called **evil-doers** <term>kakoergoi</term>. Both these and those of the opposite power <margin>39</margin> are invisible and entirely imperceptible to human senses. <margin>30</margin> For they are not clothed in a solid body, nor do they all possess a single form; rather, the shapes that characterize the spirit-substance are imprinted in many forms...

<summary>Porphyry distinguishes between good daemons, who manage the natural world and human arts for our benefit, and "evil-doing" daemons who are governed by irrational passions and spirit-substance (pneuma).</summary>

### ->DE ABSTINENTIA II.<-

Their forms sometimes appear, and sometimes they are invisible; sometimes those who are of the worse sort even change their forms. The spirit-substance <term>pneuma</term> <note>original: "pneuma"; here referring to a subtle, airy matter that serves as a vehicle or "body" for the soul</note>, insofar as it is bodily, is <margin>5</margin> subject to passions and is perishable. However, because it is bound by souls in such a way that their form persists for a longer time, it is nevertheless not eternal. For it is likely that something flows away from it continuously and is transformed. In the case of good beings, then, this substance exists in symmetry, just as the bodies of visible things do; but in the malevolent ones, it is asymmetrical. <margin>10</margin> These latter beings, assigning more to the passible <note>subject to emotion and physical sensation</note> part of their nature and occupying the region near the Earth, attempt to perform every kind of evil. For possessing a character that is entirely violent and deceitful, and being deprived of the protection provided by the superior divinity, they mostly <margin>15</margin> make their attacks with sudden and violent force, like ambushes—trying in one way to remain hidden, and in another to act by force.

Hence, the sufferings caused by them are sharp and acute; whereas the healings and corrections that come from the superior daemons seem to happen more slowly. For everything good, being easy to manage and smooth, proceeds in <margin>20</margin> order and does not overstep what is necessary. If you hold these opinions, you will never fall into the ultimate absurdity: that of believing evil things about the good beings, or good things about the evil ones. For not only is such a line of reasoning <margin>25</margin> absurd, but many people, by adopting the most degraded conceptions about the gods, spread them to the rest of mankind. Indeed, one must consider this as one of the greatest harms <margin>40</margin> caused by the malevolent daemons: that while they themselves are the causes of earthly disasters—such as plagues, crop failures, earthquakes, droughts, and the like— <margin>30</margin> they persuade us that those who are the causes of the exact opposite <note>meaning the good gods and daemons</note> are actually responsible for these things [namely, for abundance...

### ->DE ABSTINENTIA II.<-

...as according to <term>Plato</term> <note>Referring to Republic 335d: "It is not the property of heat to chill, but of its opposite... nor is it the property of the just man to harm."</note>, it is not the nature of heat to chill, but of its opposite; so it is also not the nature of the just to do harm. Now, surely the divine is by nature the most just of all things, for otherwise it would not even be divine. Therefore, this power and role [of harming] must be cut off from the <term>beneficent demons</term> <note>original: "agathoergōn daimonōn"; spirits who perform good deeds and maintain the order of the cosmos</note>. For a <margin>5</margin> nature that is naturally disposed to and willing to harm is the opposite of a beneficent one; and opposites can never exist within the same subject. While these [malevolent spirits] ruin the mortal realm in many respects, and sometimes in great matters—for there is never a time <margin>10</margin> when the good spirits do not carry out their own duties—they even signal, as far as they are able, the dangers hanging over us from the <term>evil-doers</term> <note>original: "kakoergōn"; referring here to malevolent spirits</note>, revealing them through dreams, through a divinely inspired soul, and many other means. And if someone <margin>15</margin> were capable of interpreting the signs, everyone would know and be on guard. For they give signs to all, but not everyone understands what is signified, just as not everyone can read what is written, but only he who has learned his letters.

Furthermore, all <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: "goēteia"; a term for low magic or witchcraft associated with deception and the manipulation of lower spirits</note> is carried out through these <margin>20</margin> opposite spirits. For those who perform evil deeds through sorceries especially honor these spirits and their leader. These beings are full of <margin>42</margin> every kind of phantom and are capable of deceiving through <term>wonder-working</term> <note>original: "teratourgias"; the performance of marvels or magic tricks meant to astonish</note>. It is through them that the <term>malevolent spirits</term> <note>original: "kakodaimones"</note> prepare potions and love-charms. <margin>25</margin> For all licentiousness and the hope for wealth and glory is through these beings, and most especially, deception. For falsehood is natural to them; they wish to be gods, and their presiding power wishes to seem to be the Greatest God. These are the ones who delight in:
> “libation and the smell of roasting fat,” <note>original: "loibē te knisē te"; a quote from Homer's Iliad 9.499, describing the offerings that appease the gods</note>
by which their <term>spiritual and physical nature</term> <margin>30</margin> <note>original: "pneumatikon kai sōmatikon"; the "astral" or subtle body that Neoplatonists believed demons possessed, which was composed of vaporous matter</note> is fattened. But we, to the extent of our power, will not require what these beings provide; rather, from both the soul and external things, we make every effort to become like God and those around Him—which happens through <term>freedom from passion</term> <note>original: "apatheia"; not a lack of feeling, but the state of being undisturbed by irrational emotions or worldly desires</note> and the clearly articulated understanding of <term>true reality</term> <note>original: "tōn ontōs ontōn"; literally "the things that really are," referring to the eternal, Platonic Forms rather than the changing physical world</note>, <margin>15</margin> and the life directed toward these very things—and to become unlike evil men and demons, and generally everything that delights in the mortal and material. 

So, according to what was said by <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A student of Aristotle who wrote on piety and argued that the gods prefer simple, bloodless offerings like grain and fruit</note>, we too shall sacrifice. With him the <term>theologians</term> <note>original: "theologoi"; Porphyry likely refers to ancient authorities on sacred rites, such as the Orphic or Pythagorean traditions</note> <margin>20</margin> also agreed, knowing that insofar as we neglect the removal of passions from the soul, to that extent we are joined to the evil power, and it will be necessary to appease this power as well. For as the theologians say, for those bound by external things and not yet masters <margin>25</margin> of their passions, it is necessary to turn away <note>original: "apotrepesthai"; to perform a ritual to ward off or divert a malevolent force</note> even this power; otherwise, they will not find rest from their labors. <margin>44</margin>

Let what has been said concerning sacrifices suffice up to this point. Except for what we were saying from the beginning: that it is not necessary that, if animals must be sacrificed, they must also be eaten; now, it is demonstrated <margin>30</margin> by necessity that one must not eat, even if it is ever necessary to sacrifice. For all the theologians agreed on this point: that one must not touch the meat in sacrifices intended to ward off <note>The text breaks off at "apotro-", clearly part of "apotropais" or "apotropaiois," referring to apotropaic rituals meant to turn away evil spirits.</note>...

### ->DE ABSTINENTIA II<-

...the remaining sacrifices of those being offered, and purifications must be used. For they say that one should not enter a city or one’s own house without first <term>cleansing</term> <note>original: "apokathēras"; to wash away ritual pollution</note> the clothing and the body in rivers or a spring. So, even to those whom they permitted to sacrifice, <margin>5</margin> they commanded them to abstain from the things being sacrificed; they were ordered to purify themselves beforehand by fasts and especially by <term>abstinence</term> <note>original: "apochais"; the root of the book's title, referring here specifically to refraining from eating animal flesh</note> from animal food. 

For they believed that <term>purity</term> <note>original: "hagneia"; a state of being ritually and morally "unpolluted" and fit for the presence of the gods</note> is a safeguard for caution, serving as a symbol or a <term>divine seal</term> <note>original: "sphragis theia"; a mark of protection, often used in ancient mystery religions to denote one who is under a god's protection</note> to ensure one suffers nothing from those beings whom he approaches and <margin>10</margin> seeks to appease. For by being disposed in a manner opposite to the spirits he deals with—being more divine because he is more pure—he remains unharmed in both body and in the <term>passions of the soul</term> <note>original: "pathē tēs psychēs"; the irrational drives like anger, lust, and fear that Neoplatonists believed weighed the soul down</note>, having wrapped <term>purity</term> around himself like a <margin>45</margin> fortress. 

For this reason, even <term>sorcerers</term> <note>original: "goētōn"; those who practice low magic or "goetia," often by manipulating lower spirits for selfish ends</note> have found such precaution necessary. However, they cannot maintain it <margin>15</margin> consistently; for the sake of their own licentiousness, they disturb evil <term>demons</term> <note>original: "daimonas"; in this context, the lower, malevolent spirits that inhabit the thick air near the earth</note>. Thus, true purity does not belong to sorcerers, but to divine and "God-wise" men; it brings a safeguard everywhere to those who use it through their kinship with the divine. 

If only sorcerers would use it <margin>20</margin> consistently! They would then have no desire to practice sorcery, as they would be barred by this very purity from enjoying the things for which they act impiously. Since they are full of passions and abstain from "unclean" foods for only a short time, they remain filled with impurity and pay the penalty for their <margin>25</margin> lawlessness against the whole of nature—partly from the very spirits they irritate, and partly from **Justice**, who oversees all mortal works and thoughts. 

The <term>divine man</term>, therefore, practices both internal and external purity. He strives to "fast" from the passions of the <margin>30</margin> soul and likewise to fast from those foods that stir the passions. Instead, he feeds upon <term>divine wisdom</term> <note>original: "theosophian"; a deep, direct knowledge of the divine</note>, making himself like the right thoughts concerning the divine. He is consecrated by the <term>intellectual sacrifice</term> <note>original: "noerā thysia"; a spiritual offering of the mind and soul rather than a physical animal</note> and, clothed in white garments...

### ->DE ABSTINENTIA II.<-

...presence (since it often appears that the presence of the impure is what disturbs the diviner <note>original: "hieroskopon"; a priest who inspects sacrifices to discern the will of the gods</note>; for which reason they say that sacrificing at the wrong time brings greater harm than benefit), surely then will the priest of the Father himself endure <margin>5</margin> to become a tomb of dead bodies <note>A famous Orphic and Pythagorean play on words: "sōma" (body) and "sēma" (tomb)</note>, being himself full of pollutions <note>original: "miasmatōn"; ritual defilement that prevents contact with the divine</note>, while he is eager to become a companion to the Superior Being? It is enough that we receive the parts of death through the fruits of the earth for our life here. But let us not speak of these things yet; we must still distinguish the matters <margin>10</margin> regarding sacrifices. For someone might say that we take away <margin>51</margin> a large part of divination through entrails <note>original: "splagchnōn"; the practice of extispicy, or reading the guts of animals</note> by abstaining from the slaughter of animals. Therefore, let such a person also slaughter human beings; for the future is revealed even more clearly, so they say, in their entrails; <margin>15</margin> and many of the barbarians indeed practice divination through human sacrifice. But just as it was a mark of injustice and greed to slaughter one of the same race for the sake of divination, so too is it unjust to slaughter an irrational animal for the sake of divination. Whether the gods reveal <margin>20</margin> these signs, or demons, or whether the soul of the animal as it is released responds to the inquiry through signs in the entrails, is not the subject of the present discourse to investigate.

For those whose life is rolled about in external things <margin>52</margin>, we allow them, having once committed impiety against themselves, to be carried along wherever <margin>25</margin> they are indeed carried. But for the one we describe as a philosopher, who withdraws from external things, we reasonably say that he will not trouble demons, nor will he need diviners or animal entrails. For the very things for which divinations are sought, this man has <margin>30</margin> practiced withdrawing from. For he does not enter into marriage, so as to trouble the diviner about marriage, nor into commerce...

### ->ON ABSTINENCE II.<-

...supposition, we shall bring the book to a close. At any rate, even those poets who are wise for a short time say:

> Who is so foolish and so utterly slack
> Among men as to believe the gods—
> In bare bones and smoldering gall,
> Which even hungry dogs would not eat—
> Rejoice in such first-fruits and receive this as their prize?

> Barley cakes, frankincense, sacrificial cakes; these I shall buy.
> For I am not sacrificing to my friends, but to the gods
> at this time.

<margin>59</margin> Since Apollo also advises sacrificing "according to ancestral custom"—that is, according to the habit of our fathers—he seems to be leading us back to the ancient custom. And the ancient custom was through sacrificial cakes and fruits, as we have demonstrated. Hence, they were called *thusiai* <note>sacrifices</note>, *thuēlai* <note>sacrificial offerings</note>, and *thumelai* <note>altars for incense</note>, and the word "to sacrifice" <term>thuein <note>originally meaning to burn or fumigate</note></term> itself was linked to "to burn incense" <term>thumian</term> and to what we now call "to offer a sacrifice" <term>epithuein</term>. For what we now call "sacrificing" <term>thuein</term>, they used to call "performing" <term>erdein <note>literally "to do" or "to work," used in religious contexts for performing a rite</note></term>.

> And they offered <note>original: *erdon*</note> to Apollo perfect hecatombs <note>literally a "hundred-ox sacrifice," but used for any large-scale offering</note>
> of bulls and goats.

<margin>60</margin> But those who introduced extravagance into sacrifices are unaware how they introduced a swarm of evils along with it: superstition, luxury, and the idea that one can bribe the divine and heal injustice through sacrifices. Otherwise, from where did some get the practice of sacrificing "triplets with gilded horns" <note>a rare and expensive ritual involving three animals</note>, and others hecatombs, and why did Olympias, the mother of Alexander, sacrifice a thousand of everything, once extravagance had led the way toward superstition? When a young man learns that the gods rejoice in extravagance and, as they say, in the feasts of oxen and other animals, when would he ever choose to be temperate <note>original: *sōphronēseien*</note>? And how, believing that he offers things pleasing to the gods...

### ->DE ABSTINENTIA III.<-

...those who dispute what the ultimate goal <note>original: *telos*</note> of life is; he said that not even if all the pigs and goats in the world were to agree with it, would we be persuaded that our happiness consists in pleasure, so long as Intellect <note>original: *nous*</note> holds sway over all things. And we, likewise, even if all the wolves
<margin>5</margin>

Transitioning, then, to the discourse on justice <term>dikaiosynē <note>The moral virtue of giving each their due and acting rightly toward others</note></term>, since
<margin>10</margin>
those who argue against us have said that this should be extended only toward those similar to ourselves, and for this reason they exclude the irrational <term>aloga <note>Literally "without logos," meaning beings that supposedly lack reason or speech</note></term> animals—come now, let us present the true and Pythagorean <note>Refers to Pythagoras and his followers, who believed in the kinship of all living things and the transmigration of souls</note> opinion, demonstrating that every soul which participates in sensation and memory is rational <term>logikē <note>Possessing the faculty of reason and the ability to organize thoughts</note></term>. 
<margin>15</margin>
For once this is proven, we shall, in accordance with their own logic, rightly extend justice toward every living being. We shall speak by briefly summarizing the arguments found among the ancients.

<margin>2</margin> Since there are two kinds of reason <term>logos <note>A multifaceted Greek term meaning both "internal thought" and "external speech"</note></term> according to the Stoics <note>A school of philosophy that argued only humans and gods are rational beings</note>—one being internal <term>endiathētos <note>The "reason" held within the mind or soul before it is spoken</note></term>, and the other expressed
<margin>20</margin>
<term>prophorikos <note>Reason as it is externalized through spoken language</note></term>—and again, one being correct and the other erroneous, it is necessary to distinguish which of these they deprive animals of. Is it only "right reason" <note>perfected or virtuous reason</note> they deny them, and not reason in its simple sense? Or is it a total deprivation of all reason, both that which stays within and that which
<margin>25</margin>
is projected outward? They seem to allege a complete deprivation of reason, not just the deprivation of its perfected form. For if they only lacked perfected reason, animals would still be rational <term>logika</term> beings, just as almost all men are in the Stoic view. For they say that only one or two wise men have ever existed in whom reason has been
<margin>30</margin>
perfected, while all other men are "base"—even if some are making progress and others are drowning in a flood of baseness—yet all are nonetheless equally rational. It is only because of self-love...

### ->DE ABSTINENTIA III.<-

...those who take the lead call animals "irrational" <note>original: *aloga*</note>, along with all other living creatures, wishing to indicate a complete deprivation of reason through the term "irrationality." Yet, if one must speak the truth, reason <term>logos <note>A central Greek philosophical term meaning both "speech/language" and the "faculty of reason." Porphyry argues that animals possess both.</note></term> is not only simply observed in all animals, but in many of them, it even possesses the foundations 
<margin>5</margin>
toward perfection. Since, then, reason is twofold—one kind being in utterance <term>prophorikos <note>Externalized speech or vocal expression</note></term> and the other in disposition <term>endiathetos <note>Internal thought or the mental "arrangement" of ideas before they are spoken</note></term>—let us first begin with the reason that is uttered and ordered according to the voice. 

If, indeed, uttered reason is a 
<margin>10</margin>
vocal sound made by the tongue that signifies internal states and the experiences of the soul—for this is the most common definition and one not yet tied to any specific philosophical sect, but is simply the general concept of reason—what part of this is missing from animals that make sounds? Why is it not the case that what an animal experiences, it first considers 
<margin>15</margin>
before speaking what it intends? I call "thought" <term>dianoia <note>The mental process of thinking things through</note></term> that which is voiced within the soul in silence. Therefore, regarding that which is voiced by the tongue, in whatever way it might be voiced—whether in the manner of a barbarian, a Greek, a dog, or an ox—all vocalizing 
<margin>20</margin>
animals participate in reason. For while humans speak according to human laws <note>In this context, "laws" (nomoi) refers to the conventions and rules of specific human languages</note>, animals speak according to the laws which each has received from the gods and nature. 

And if we do not understand them, what of it? For those raised in Attica <note>The region surrounding Athens, known for the "purest" Greek dialect</note> do not understand the language of the Indians, nor of the Scythians, Thracians, or Syrians; 
<margin>25</margin>
instead, the sound of one group strikes the ears of another like the "clangor of cranes" <note>original: *klangē geranōn*. This is a classical literary reference to Homer’s Iliad, where the speech of foreigners or the noise of battle is compared to the loud, unintelligible cries of migrating birds.</note>. And yet, their own speech is writable and articulate to them, just as ours is to us; but the speech of Syrians, for example, or 
<margin>30</margin>
Persians, appears inarticulate and unwritable to others, just as animal speech does to everyone. For just as we perceive only noise and sound, being unable to understand, say, the conversation of Scythians, and [the sound of] clang...

### ->DE ABSTINENTIA III.<-

...[they] seem to [merely chatter] and articulate nothing, but use a single sound, whether longer or shorter, and its variation never strikes us as having meaning. Yet, for them, their utterance is easy to understand and possesses much variation, just as our customary speech does for us. 
<margin>5</margin>
So it is with animals: understanding belongs to them specifically according to their kind, while to us only the sound is audible, the meaning being lost on us. This is because no one who has been taught their language has taught us, through our own tongue, the interpretation of what is said by animals. 
<margin>10</margin>
And yet, if we are to believe the ancients and those who lived in our time or our fathers' time, there are some who are said to have listened to and understood the speech of animals. Among the ancients, there were Melampus 
<margin>15</margin>
and Tiresias <note>Melampus and Tiresias were legendary Greek seers famous for their ability to understand the language of birds and animals, often used for prophecy.</note> and others like them; and not long ago, there was Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and wonder-worker of the 1st century AD, often compared to Pythagoras or Jesus in antiquity.</note>, of whom it is said that while he was with his companions, a swallow flew up and chirped. He told them that the swallow was informing the others 
<margin>20</margin>
that a donkey had fallen outside the city while carrying a load of grain, and that the grain had been spilled on the ground when the beast of burden fell. A companion of ours used to relate that he met a servant boy who understood all the cries of birds; everything they said was 
<margin>25</margin>
prophetic and announced what was about to happen shortly. However, he was deprived of this understanding because his mother—fearing that she might have to send him as a gift to the King—urinated into his ears while he was sleeping <note>In ancient folklore, hearing could be opened or closed to the divine or the animal world through specific rituals involving the ears.</note>. But even if we 
<margin>30</margin>
pass over these stories because of our innate tendency toward disbelief, surely no one, I think, is ignorant that even until now certain nations have a kinship with the understanding of the speech of certain animals. The Arabs listen to ravens, and the Tyrrhenians <note>The Etruscans of Italy, who were renowned throughout the Mediterranean for their expertise in "augury," the art of interpreting bird signs.</note> to eagles; and perhaps also...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animal vocalizations are a structured language that humans simply fail to understand, citing historical figures and cultures—like the Arabs and Etruscans—who were reputed to have mastered animal communication.</summary>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

We and all people would be understanding of all animals if a serpent <note>original: *drakon*. In Greek folklore, having one's ears licked by a serpent or dragon was a ritual that granted the person the supernatural ability to understand the language of birds and beasts.</note> had licked our ears. Truly, the variety and diversity of their vocalizations demonstrate that their speech is meaningful. At any rate, they sound one way 
<margin>5</margin> 
when they are afraid, another way when they call out, another when they summon one another to food, another when they are being affectionate, and another when they are challenging one another to a fight. And the difference is so great that these variations are extremely difficult to track—even for those who have dedicated their lives to the observation of these creatures—due to their sheer 
<margin>10</margin> 
abundance. Augurs <note>Individuals who practiced divination by observing the flight and cries of birds.</note>, for instance, have noted the differences in the cries of the crow and the raven up to a certain point, but they abandoned the rest of the study, as it was not easily grasped by a human being. But when animals speak to one another in ways that are clear and distinct, 
<margin>15</margin> 
even if they are not familiar to us, and when they are seen to imitate us and even learn the Greek language and understand their masters—who is so shameless as not to admit that they are rational creatures <term>logika: creatures possessing the faculty of reason and speech</term> just because he himself does not understand what they are saying? Ravens, at any rate, and jays, 
<margin>20</margin> 
robins, and parrots imitate humans; they remember what they have heard and, when being taught, they obey their teacher. Many of them have even used what they were taught to report those who were committing crimes in the household. Then there is the Indian hyena, which the 
<margin>25</margin> 
locals call the *corocotta* <note>A mythical or semi-mythical animal often described in antiquity as a hybrid of a dog and a wolf, or a hyena, said to be able to mimic human speech to lure people into the woods.</note>; even without a teacher, it speaks in such a human-like way that it approaches houses and calls out to whomever it sees as easy prey. It imitates the voice of the person's dearest friend—someone the person would surely answer. The result is that even though the 
<margin>30</margin> 
Indians know about this, they are still deceived by the similarity and are killed when they come out in response to the voice. If animals do not imitate everything, or if they are not all quick learners...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animal vocalizations are a complex, meaningful form of speech that expresses emotions and intentions, and he uses the mimicry of birds and the mythical corocotta to prove they possess rational intelligence.</summary>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...of our own [language], what of it? For not every human is a quick learner or capable of mimicking—I do not mean the speech of animals, but not even five of the human dialects. 
<margin>5</margin> 
And some animals perhaps do not speak because they have not been taught, or perhaps because they are hindered by their vocal organs. We ourselves, for instance, while in Carthage, raised a tame partridge that flew to us. As time passed and familiarity turned it into a state of great tameness, 
<margin>10</margin> 
we noticed it not only fawning over us, tending to us, and playing with us, but eventually even answering back to our own speech and responding as much as was possible—in a manner quite different from how partridges are accustomed to call to one another. 
<margin>5</margin> 
It did not merely respond while we were silent, but answered back specifically when we spoke. It is also recorded that even some voiceless animals obey their masters so readily that not even a close human associate could do better. For instance, the moray eel of Crassus the Roman <note>Likely Lucius Licinius Crassus, a famous orator who was teased by his rival Domitius for weeping over a dead fish; Crassus famously retorted that he wept for a fish more than Domitius had wept for his three wives.</note> would come to Crassus when called by name; he was so moved by the creature that he mourned its death, 
<margin>20</margin> 
even though he had previously borne the loss of three of his own children with great composure. Many have also recorded that the eels in Arethusa <note>A famous spring, most likely the one in Syracuse, Sicily, known for its sacred fish.</note> and the *saperdas* <note>original: *saperdas*. A type of small fish, likely a variety of perch or a salted fish from the Black Sea region, mentioned in the context of the Meander River.</note> around the Meander river obey those who call them. Therefore, is the mental impression <term>phantasia: the internal mental image or thought that precedes speech</term> not the same as that of the speaker, whether it reaches the tongue or not? 
<margin>25</margin> 
How then is it not unreasonable to claim that only human speech constitutes reason <term>logos: both the faculty of thought and the expression of it through speech</term> simply because it is intelligible to us, while rejecting the speech of other animals? This is much the same as if crows were to claim that only their own vocalization was true speech, and that we were irrational <note>original: *alogous*. In Greek, this literally means "without reason" or "without speech."</note> because we do not speak in a way that is clear to them. 
<margin>30</margin> 
Or as if the inhabitants of Attica <note>The region of Greece including Athens, whose residents considered their dialect the most refined and the standard of "correct" Greek.</note> were to say that only the Attic dialect was true speech, considering everyone who lacked an Attic vocabulary to be irrational. And yet, one might sooner [learn the speech] of a crow...

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...would an Athenian understand a Syrian or a Persian speaking Syriac or Persian? <margin>5</margin>

Having understood, the birds report these signs as best they can, serving as heralds for the various gods: 
<margin>10</margin> 
the eagle for Zeus, the hawk and the raven for Apollo, the stork for Hera, and for Athena, the corncrake and the owl; just as the crane serves Demeter, and others serve other gods. Furthermore, those of us who are observers and companions to animals recognize the meaning of their vocalizations. 
<margin>15</margin> 
The hunter, for instance, perceives from the specific tone of the dog’s barking <note>original: "hypokriseos," meaning the 'delivery' or 'acting out' of the sound</note> whether it is searching for the hare, has found it, is chasing it, has caught it, or—if the dog has lost the scent—that it is wandering. So too, the cowherd 
<margin>20</margin> 
knows if the cow is hungry, thirsty, exhausted, in heat, or searching for her calf. The roaring lion makes it clear that he is threatening; the howling wolf shows he is in distress; and bleating sheep do not fail to let the shepherd know exactly what they need. 
<margin>6</margin> <note>Note: The original manuscript numbering repeats here.</note>

<margin>25</margin> 
friendship, or are calling out—whether the voice is one of chasing, asking, or giving—they do not miss a single nuance, but respond appropriately to each one. This would be impossible if a like understanding were not operating upon a like understanding. 
<margin>30</margin> 
They are even disciplined by musical melodies; thus deer, bulls, and other animals are transformed from a wild state to a tame one. Even those who "vote against" animals possessing reason <note>A reference to the Stoic philosophers, who were Porphyry's primary intellectual opponents on the status of animals.</note> admit that dogs understand dialectic <note>The art of logical argument; the Stoic Chrysippus famously argued that a dog chasing a scent at a three-way crossroads uses a "disjunctive syllogism" to decide which path to take.</note> and make use of it...

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...tracking their prey through multiple diverging paths, they show their reasoning when they arrive at a three-way crossroad. <margin>5</margin>

<margin>10</margin>

<margin>15</margin>

<margin>25</margin>

<margin>7</margin>

<margin>30</margin>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...the precision or lack thereof of reason <term>logos; the capacity for rational thought</term>. And that they [animals] are disposed similarly to us, at least in regard to perception and the rest of their physical organization—both in their sense organs and their flesh—almost everyone has conceded. 

<margin>5</margin> 
For not only have they shared with us natural passions and movements through these organs, but even those states observed in them that are contrary to nature and diseased. No person of sound mind would say that, because of the difference in physical constitution, animals are incapable of a rational disposition,

<margin>10</margin> 
seeing as there is much variation in constitution even among humans, according to their lineage and nation <note>original: *ethne*; referring to various ethnic or cultural groups</note>, and yet we allow that all are rational. A donkey, for instance, is afflicted by catarrh <note>original: *katarrho*; a discharge of fluid from the respiratory tract</note>, and if the disease flows into its lungs, it dies just like a human. A horse can develop an abscess 

<margin>15</margin> 
or waste away from consumption <note>wasting disease, often associated with tuberculosis</note>, just like a human; and a horse may be seized by tetanus, gout, fever, and rabies <term>lyssa; a state of madness or rage</term>, at which point it is said to "look downward." And a pregnant mare, if she catches the scent of a lamp being extinguished, 

<margin>20</margin> 
miscarries just as a woman does. A bull also suffers from fever and goes mad, as does the camel. A crow suffers from mange and leprosy, as does a dog; and the dog also suffers from gout and rabies. A pig suffers from quinsy <note>original: *brangcha*; a sore throat or inflammation of the windpipe</note>, and even more so the dog; indeed, the ailment in humans 

<margin>25</margin> 
is named "cynanche" <note>original: *kynanche*; literally "dog-strangle," a severe sore throat</note> after the dog. These things are well-known because these animals live alongside us, but we are ignorant of the others because of our lack of familiarity. When castrated, they also become softened: roosters no longer sing, 

<margin>30</margin> 
but change their voice to a feminine tone just like [castrated] men; and one cannot distinguish the horns or the voice of a castrated bull from a female. Stags no longer shed their horns but keep them, just as eunuchs keep their hair <note>Porphyry suggests that castrated men do not go bald</note>; and if they did not have horns...

<summary>Porphyry argues for the kinship between humans and animals by demonstrating that they share nearly identical physical organs and suffer from the same diseases, such as fever, gout, and rabies. He concludes that if humans vary physically but remain rational, then the physical differences of animals should not be used to deny them a share of reason.</summary>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...they grow <note>referring to physical features like hair</note> just as those do who were castrated before growing a beard. Thus, the bodies of nearly all animals are similar to ours in terms of their passions and physical experiences.

<margin>8</margin>
Now, consider whether the passions of the soul are not also entirely similar; and let us look first at perception <term>aisthesis; the ability to perceive through the senses</term>. For it is certainly not the case that in humans, taste perceives flavors, sight perceives colors, and smell perceives odors—or that hearing catches sounds and touch perceives heat, cold, or textures—while this does not happen similarly in all other animals. 

<margin>10</margin>
Nor are animals deprived of this perception just because they are not human, any more than they should be said to lack reason for that same reason. For if that were the case, the gods themselves would be deprived of reason because they are not human; or perhaps we would be the ones lacking it, if we assume only gods are truly rational. Indeed, in matters of sense perception, animals actually seem to have the advantage. 

<margin>15</margin>
For which human sees as clearly as a serpent? Not even the legendary Lynceus <note>In Greek myth, Lynceus was an Argonaut with sight so keen he could see through trees, stones, and underground</note> could see as well as a "dragon." This is why the poets use the word *drakein* <note>original: "δρακεῖν"; a poetic verb for seeing or glancing</note> to mean "to see." And of the eagle, they say: "Even from high above, the cowering hare did not escape his notice." <note>A reference to Homer’s Iliad, describing the eagle's legendary eyesight</note> 

<margin>20</margin>
And who has sharper hearing than the cranes? They hear from such a distance that no human could even see that far. In the sense of smell, nearly all animals so excel us that they are struck by scents that escape us entirely; they can recognize each creature by its kind and even track them by scent alone. 

<margin>25</margin>
Indeed, humans must use dogs as guides when they need to pursue a boar or a deer. Furthermore, the changing state of the air affects us only after some time, but it affects other animals immediately, so that we use them as signs to predict what is coming. 

<margin>30</margin>
As for the distinction of flavors, they know them so well that they can accurately distinguish the harmful from the healthy and the poisonous—a task that not even human doctors can manage so well. Aristotle even says that those creatures with more acute senses are more intelligent. Differences in bodies make them susceptible...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animals possess superior sensory perceptions compared to humans, citing their keen sight, smell, and hearing as evidence of a sophisticated "soul" and intelligence.</summary>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...can indeed make the soul suffer, and make reason <term>logos; the capacity for rational thought and speech</term> more or less readily available, but they cannot change the soul in its essence, especially since they have not even altered the senses or the passions, nor have they caused them to deviate completely <note>literally "to have stepped out of" their natural state</note> from their nature. 

Therefore, let the difference be admitted as a matter of "more and less," but not as a total deprivation; not as a case where one has it entirely and the other not at all. Rather, just as within a single category one body is healthier and another less so—and similarly in illness there is much variation, as there is in natural talent and the lack of it—so too it is in souls. 

<margin>10</margin>
One soul is good and another base; and of the base, one is more so and another less. Even among the good, there is not the same equality: Socrates, Aristotle, and Plato are not good in the same way, nor is there identity even among those who hold the same opinions. 

<margin>15</margin>
Therefore, even if we think more than the animals do, we should not on that account strip the animals of thinking <term>noein; the act of intellection or understanding</term>, just as we would not deny that partridges fly simply because hawks fly better than they do—nor should we deny it to other hawks just because the pigeon-killer <note>original: "phassophonos"; likely referring to the Goshawk or Peregrine Falcon</note> flies better than them and all the others.

<margin>20</margin>
One might grant that the soul "sympathizes" with the body and is affected by it—whether the body is in a good or bad state—but the soul never changes its own nature. If it only sympathizes and uses the body as an instrument, it might perform many actions through it; but because the body is organized differently than ours, the animal may do things that we are incapable of doing. While the soul might suffer in accordance with the body's condition, it would not alter its own nature. 

<margin>26</margin>
Therefore, we must demonstrate that reason <term>logikē; the faculty of logic or rationality</term> exists in them and that they are not deprived of wisdom <term>phronēsis; practical wisdom or prudence</term>. 

First, each animal knows whether it is weak or strong, and it guards certain parts of itself while using others: for instance, the leopard uses its teeth, the lion uses its claws and teeth, the horse its hoof, the bull its horns, the cock its spur, and the scorpion its [sting]...

<summary>Porphyry argues that rationality is a matter of degree rather than a binary "have or have-not" trait, comparing the differing intelligence of animals to the differing genius of philosophers like Socrates and Plato. He concludes that animals demonstrate practical wisdom by understanding their own physical strengths and weaknesses.</summary>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...with a sting. The snakes in Egypt use their spit (which is why they are called "spitters" <note>original: *ptyades*; likely referring to spitting cobras</note>) to blind the eyes of those who approach them. Different creatures use different means, but each acts to save itself.

Furthermore, strong animals tend to live far away from humans, while those that are less powerful <margin>5</margin> avoid stronger beasts and instead seek out human company. Some keep a slight distance, such as sparrows nesting under eaves or swallows, while others live directly with us, like dogs. They even change their locations according to the seasons, doing whatever they know will be to their advantage.

<margin>10</margin> One can observe this same kind of reasoning <term>logismos; the process of weighing options or calculating</term> in fish and birds as well. The ancient authors collected many such examples in their works on the "wisdom of animals." Aristotle—who investigated these matters more extensively than most—states that every animal has its own <margin>15</margin> devised way of living and dwelling to ensure its survival.

<margin>10</margin> Anyone who claims that these traits belong to animals "by nature" <term>physis; the innate constitution of a being</term> while implying they lack reason is mistaken. To say they are rational "by nature" is no different <margin>11</margin> from saying that reason in humans is also a natural development. It is wrong to suggest that our own growth toward perfection does not <margin>20</margin> also follow our natural constitution. 

After all, the Divine <note>referring to the gods or the cosmic intellect</note> did not become rational through learning <term>mathesis; the acquisition of knowledge or schooling</term>. There was never a time when the Divine was irrational; it has always been simultaneously existent and rational. We do not deny that the Divine has reason just because it never had to be <margin>25</margin> taught. 

And yet, just as with humans, nature teaches animals certain things, while learning provides others. They learn some things from one another and other things, as we have mentioned, from human beings. Furthermore, animals possess memory, which is the most essential faculty for the <margin>30</margin> development of reasoning and practical wisdom <term>phronesis; practical intelligence or prudence</term>. They even exhibit many vices, though these are not as widespread as they are among humans; indeed, the wickedness found in animals is far milder than our own.

<summary>Porphyry argues that animals display rational calculation through their survival strategies, habitat choices, and capacity for memory. He refutes the idea that "natural" behavior is separate from "rational" behavior, using the inherent reason of the Divine as a primary example.</summary>
