### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

For instance, a man who is a builder would not lay the foundations of a house unless he were sober, nor would a shipwright lay a ship’s keel unless he were in his right mind, nor would a farmer plant a vine without focusing his attention on the task. Yet, almost all men <margin>5</margin> engage in procreation while they are drunk. But animals do not; they produce life for the sake of offspring, and for the most part, once the male has made the female pregnant, he does not attempt to mate with her, nor does the female allow it. The sheer insolence and lack of restraint found in humans in these matters is obvious. <margin>10</margin> Among animals, the mate recognizes the labor pains of the mother and, in many cases, shares in those pains—just as roosters do. Some even help hatch the eggs, like male pigeons, and they take care to choose a place where they intend to give birth. <margin>15</margin> Once the young are born, each parent cleans both the newborn and themselves.

If one observes closely, one can see that they all move with order and greet their caregivers by wagging their tails; they recognize their masters and <margin>11</margin> signal when an intruder <note>original: *epiboulon*; one who plots against another</note> is near. As for social animals, who is unaware of how they maintain justice toward one another? <margin>20</margin> This is true of every single ant, as well as bees and similar creatures. And what of the self-control <term>sōphrosynē; a cardinal Greek virtue involving moderation and self-mastery</term> of wood-pigeons toward their mates? If they catch them in adultery, they will even kill the offender. Or who has not heard of the <margin>25</margin> justice of storks toward their parents? <note>Ancient Greeks believed storks were the model of filial piety, claiming they fed and carried their elderly parents.</note>

In each species, a specific virtue <term>aretē; excellence or moral virtue</term> stands out, for which it is naturally endowed. This does not strip them of reason <term>to logikon; the faculty of logic or rational thought</term>, nor does it mean their nature is simply fixed. For we must examine whether their actions are not consistent with virtue and the exercise of reason. If we do not understand exactly how these actions are <margin>30</margin> performed because we cannot enter into their thoughts <term>logismos; the internal process of reasoning or calculation</term>, we should not, therefore, accuse them of lacking reason. After all, no one can enter into the mind of God...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animals display higher moral standards than humans in procreation and social justice, citing the fidelity of pigeons and the filial piety of storks. He concludes that our inability to see into an animal's mind does not prove they lack the power of reason.</summary>
<keywords>animal ethics, procreation, sobriety, parental care, social justice, ants, bees, pigeons, storks, virtue, aretē, logismos</keywords>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...is able to give; from the works of God, we have agreed with those who declare that the Divine is intellectual and rational. <margin>12</margin> One might wonder at those who establish justice <term>dikaiosynē; the Greek concept of moral rightness and the fair distribution of duties and rights</term> on the basis of reason, and who call those animals that do not live in community "wild" and "unjust," yet they fail to extend the reach of justice to those animals that *do* live in community with us. For just as life perishes for humans if community is removed, so it is for those creatures. <margin>10</margin> At any rate, birds and dogs and many of the four-footed animals—such as goats, horses, sheep, donkeys, and mules—perish if they are deprived of their community with humans. And the Nature that created them placed them in a state of needing humans, just as it made humans in need of them; it established an innate sense of justice in them toward us and in us toward them. <margin>15</margin> If some animals act wildly toward humans, it is no wonder; for the saying of Aristotle is true: if all animals possessed an abundance of food, they would be wild neither toward each other nor toward humans. <note>original: Aristotle, *History of Animals* 608b. Porphyry frequently cites Aristotle to support his observations of nature.</note> For it is for the sake of food—though it is a necessary and humble thing—that their enmities <margin>20</margin> and friendships exist, as well as for the sake of territory. If humans were shut up in such narrow and desperate circumstances as animals are, how much wilder would they have become than even those creatures we consider "wild"? War and famine have shown this to be true, where humans do not even spare tasting one another; <margin>25</margin> and even without the pressure of war and famine, they still devour animals that have been raised alongside them and are tame. <margin>13</margin> But someone might say that while animals are indeed rational <term>logika; possessing logos, which can mean both "reason" and "speech"</term>, they nevertheless have no relation to us. And yet, it was by claiming they were "irrational" that people used to remove any moral relation to them. They made them out to be irrational, and then they claimed our community with them was based on utility <margin>30</margin> rather than reason. But if they are rational to us...

<summary>Porphyry argues that many domestic animals share a natural social bond (koinonia) and innate sense of justice with humans, suggesting that their occasional "wildness" is merely a result of scarcity, a trait they share with humans.</summary>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...the goal was to show, not whether animals have made contracts with us; for even among humans, not every person makes a contract with us, yet no one would call a person who has not entered an agreement "irrational" <term>alogon; literally 'without speech' or 'without reason'</term>. <margin>21</margin> And yet, most animals have even served humans, and as someone rightly said—speaking correctly—though they serve because of the thoughtlessness <margin>5</margin> of humans, they have nonetheless, through their own wisdom and justice, made their masters into their own servants and caretakers. Furthermore, their vices <term>kakiai; moral failings or defects</term> are clearly visible, and it is from these that their rationality <term>to logikon; the capacity for reason</term> is most apparent; <margin>10</margin> for they feel envy and they are jealous over their females, and the females likewise over the males. But one vice does not exist among them: plotting against a benefactor. Instead, they happen to possess nothing but goodwill for everyone; <margin>15</margin> and they trust a benefactor so much that they follow wherever he may lead, even to slaughter and obvious danger. For even if someone feeds them not for their own sake, but for his own, the animal still feels goodwill toward the owner. <margin>14</margin> Humans, however, plot against no one so much as the one who feeds them, and they pray for no one's death as much as his.

Animals are so calculating <margin>20</margin> in what they do that often, even when they recognize that baits are traps, they approach them anyway out of a lack of self-control <term>akrasia; acting against one's better judgment due to passion or appetite</term> or because of hunger. Sometimes they do not approach immediately; at other times they hesitate and try to see if they can <margin>25</margin> take the food without falling into the trap. Often, when their reason has conquered, their desire departs. <margin>21</margin> Some animals even go so far as to insult and urinate upon the clever tricks of humans; others, though they know they will be caught, are so overcome by greed that—no worse than the companions of Odysseus—they choose <note>original: "περιεῖδε" - to overlook or allow. Porphyry compares the animals' calculated risk for food to the crew of Odysseus who, in Homer's Odyssey, often succumbed to their hunger despite warnings.</note> to die after they have eaten. <margin>30</margin> Some writers have also quite successfully attempted to show, from the very environments animals have been allotted, that many are even more prudent than we are. For just as the beings dwelling in the upper air <note>original: "aithera" - the ether, the home of divine or celestial beings</note> are rational, so they say...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animals demonstrate reason through their social behaviors, loyalty, and even their vices (like jealousy). He contrasts animal gratitude with human treachery and describes how animals consciously weigh the risks of traps against their hunger.</summary>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...those things which dwell in the region immediately adjacent to that [the divine realm], such as the creatures in the air, then those in the water differ from them, and then likewise the land animals; of which we inhabit the very dregs <note>original: "hypostathmēn," literally the sediment or lees of a liquid; here referring to the lowest, most material level of the cosmos</note>. <margin>5</margin> For surely we do not conclude that the gods are superior simply because of their location, yet refuse to apply the same logic to mortals. Furthermore, when animals take up arts <term>technas; skilled crafts or disciplines</term>, and even those of humans—learning to dance <margin>15</margin> and drive chariots, to fight as gladiators and walk on ropes, <margin>10</margin> and even to write and read, to play the flute and the lyre, to shoot arrows and to ride horses—will you still dispute whether the recipient of these skills possesses reason, when the thing received is clearly seen within them? <margin>15</margin> Where could the animal receive these things if reason <term>logos</term>—in which the arts consist—were not already present? For an animal does not hear our voice as mere noise; rather, they have a perception of the difference between signs <note>original: "sēmeiōn," referring to the distinct meanings or signals in human speech</note>, which surely <margin>15</margin> arises from a rational understanding. 

But, they say, the animals perform these human tasks poorly. Well, not even all humans perform them well; otherwise, the contests would be in vain, as there would be no winners <margin>20</margin> or losers. But, they say, animals do not deliberate, nor do they hold assemblies or sit in judgment. Tell me, do all humans do these things? Is it not true that for many people, their actions come before they ever deliberate? How could <margin>25</margin> anyone demonstrate that animals do not deliberate? No one can provide proof of this; on the contrary, those who have written detailed accounts of animals have shown the opposite to be true. 

As for the rest, the other rhetorical arguments against them are stale; for instance, that they have no cities. I would say that neither do the <margin>30</margin> wagon-dwelling Scythians <note>A nomadic people of Central Asia often cited by Greeks as an example of a culture without fixed cities</note>, nor do the gods. They also say that there are no written laws among animals; but there were no written laws among humans either, as long as they were happy. It is said that Apis <note>A legendary figure in Greek mythology sometimes identified as an early king of Argos or a son of Apollo</note> was the first to legislate for the Greeks, only when they stood in need of it. <margin>16</margin> Thus, it was for humans, on account of their gluttony...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animals possess a rational mind because they can learn complex human arts and understand meaningful speech, refuting the idea that lacking cities or written laws proves a lack of reason.</summary>
<keywords>animal intelligence, logos, education of animals, Scythians, law-giving, Apis, Porphyry</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument that animals are rational beings. Having previously discussed their ability to learn human skills and respond to speech, he now turns to the religious and mythological evidence from both Egyptian and Greek traditions to show that animals have historically been treated with the same reverence as humans or even the gods themselves.</meta>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...it seems that animals possess reason; indeed, they have been honored by the gods and by divine men on equal footing with human suppliants <note>original: "hiketais," individuals seeking protection or sanctuary at a temple</note>. Indeed, the god <note>the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi</note> gave a response to Aristodicus of Cyme, declaring that the sparrows were his own suppliants. Socrates used to swear oaths <margin>5</margin> by them, and even before him, Rhadamanthus <note>a legendary judge of the underworld known for his absolute fairness</note>. The Egyptians even considered them to be gods—whether they truly believed them to be divine, or whether they intentionally fashioned the images of the gods with the faces of bulls, birds, or other creatures so that people might abstain from harming them just as they would abstain from humans, <margin>10</margin> or perhaps for other more mystical reasons. In the same way, the Greeks attached the horns of a ram to the statue of Zeus, and those of a bull to the statue of Dionysus. They composed the image of Pan from both a man and a goat, and they gave wings to the Muses and the Sirens, <margin>15</margin> and likewise to Nike <note>Victory</note>, Iris, Eros, and Hermes. Pindar, in his processional songs, described how all the gods—when they were being pursued by the giant Typhon—took on forms not resembling humans, but those of "irrational" animals <note>original: "alogois zoiois"; Porphyry is highlighting the irony that gods chose animal forms for safety</note>. He also says that Zeus, <margin>20</margin> when in love with Pasiphae, became a bull, and at other times an eagle and a swan. Through these stories, the ancients demonstrated the honor they held for animals—and even more so when they say that a goat nursed the infant Zeus. Among the Cretans, there was a law of Rhadamanthus that one should take an oath by all the animals. Nor <margin>25</margin> was Socrates merely joking when he swore by the dog and the goose; rather, he was making his oath according to the law of the son of Zeus and Justice <note>referring again to Rhadamanthus</note>. Nor was he joking when he called the swans his "fellow-servants" <term>homodoulous; implying that both humans and animals serve the same divine master</term>. Myth also hints that animals share the same kind of soul as we do <margin>30</margin> <note>original: "homopsycha," literally "same-souled"</note>, suggesting that by the anger of the gods, humans changed into animals, and having changed, they are thereafter pitied and loved. Such are the stories told about dolphins, and those concerning kingfishers and nightingales.

<summary>Porphyry argues that animals deserve moral consideration by citing historical and mythological precedents where gods took animal forms or where animals were treated as sacred suppliants and "fellow-servants" to humanity.</summary>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

<margin>17</margin> ...and swallows. Each of the ancients also boasts—whoever was lucky enough to have been raised by animals—not so much of their biological fathers as of their foster parents: one by a she-wolf, another a deer, another a goat, another a bee. Semiramis was raised by doves, Cyrus by a dog, and a certain Thracian by a swan; they even bore the names of their foster parents. <margin>i</margin> This is also the source of the epithets given to the gods: Dionysus is called Eiraphiotes <note>original: "Eiraphiotes"; an epithet of Dionysus often linked by ancient etymologists to the "kid" or young goat, though also traditionally meaning "sewn-in" to Zeus's thigh</note>, <margin>l</margin> Apollo is called Lykeios <note>Wolf-god</note> and Delphinios <note>Dolphin-god</note>, Poseidon is called Hippios <note>Horse-god</note>, and Athena is called Hippia <note>of the Horse</note>. Even Hecate <margin>10 k</margin> is said to be more inclined to listen when she is addressed as a bull, a dog, or a lioness.

<margin>l</margin> But if, because they sacrifice and eat them, men call them "irrational" <term>alogos</term> <note>meaning both "without speech" and "without reason"</note> <margin>r</margin> as a way of comforting themselves, then those Scythians who feast upon their own fathers might just as well claim <margin>i 18</margin> that their fathers were "irrational." <margin>15</margin> Through these points and others which we shall mention in order as we survey the traditions of the ancients, it is demonstrated that animals are rational beings <term>logika</term>; though their reason is imperfect in most cases, it is certainly not entirely absent. Since justice applies to rational beings—as our opponents themselves claim—how <margin>20</margin> could justice not also apply to these creatures? For we do not extend the scope of justice to plants, because they appear to be utterly disconnected from reason. And yet, even there, we are accustomed to use their fruits, but certainly not to cut <margin>25</margin> down the trunks along with the fruits. We gather the grain and the pulses <term>chedropa</term> <note>a general term for legumes like beans, peas, and lentils</note> after they have withered, fallen to the ground, and died. But no one would consume the meat of animals that died naturally <note>original: "thneseidia," referring to animals that have died of old age or disease rather than being slaughtered</note>; therefore, there is great injustice in these matters. To begin with, as Plutarch says, just <margin>30</margin> because our nature requires certain things and we make use of them, it does not mean we should extend injustice to everything and everyone. For nature grants and provides for our necessities...

<summary>Porphyry argues that animals are rational beings because they have fostered legendary heroes and share epithets with the gods. He concludes that since they possess reason, humans are morally obligated to treat them with justice, unlike plants which lack reason and can be harvested without being killed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument that while some harm to the natural world is inevitable for survival, the slaughter of animals for food is a choice of luxury rather than necessity. ### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...limited harm, if indeed taking something from plants is "harm," especially since they remain alive after the harvest. But to destroy and ruin other living things out of luxury and for the sake of pleasure is a mark of total savagery and injustice <term>adikia</term> <note>original: "adikia"; the opposite of justice, implying a violation of the natural order</note>. Abstaining from these things does not diminish us either in terms of basic survival or in "living well" <note>This refers to the Greek concept of *eudaimonia*, or flourishing</note>. 

For if we required the slaughter of animals and the eating of flesh for our lives, just as we need air, water, plants, and fruits—without which life is impossible—then nature would be bound by a necessary entanglement with this injustice. 

But since many priests of the gods and many kings of foreign nations maintain their purity through abstinence, and since countless species of animals live without ever touching such food and yet reach their natural end <term>telos</term> <note>the "end" or purpose of a thing's nature</note>, how is it not absurd to claim that because we are forced to be at war with some creatures, we should not even live peaceably with those for whom it is possible? Is it really the case that we must either live without practicing justice toward anything, or practice it toward everything and cease to live? 

<margin>31</margin> Just as among men, the person who—for the sake of his own safety, or for his children or country—seizes the property of others or ravages a territory and a city, has a pretext of necessity for his injustice. But whoever does these things for the sake of wealth, or through greed, or for luxurious pleasures and the satisfaction of non-essential desires, is judged to be unsociable, unrestrained, and wicked. 

In the same way, God grants forgiveness for the harm done to plants, the consumption of fire and spring water, the shearing of sheep, the milking of cows, and the taming and harnessing of oxen for the survival and preservation of those who use them. But to lead animals to slaughter and to cook them, becoming saturated with murder—not for the sake of nourishment or filling a void, but for pleasure and gluttony...

<summary>Porphyry argues that killing animals for food is an act of luxury and injustice, distinguishing it from the necessary use of plants or animal products like milk and wool. He refutes the idea that humans must either be completely just to all things or completely unjust, advocating for a middle path of peace where possible.</summary>

<keywords>justice, necessity vs luxury, animal ethics, Porphyry, abstinence, nature, divine forgiveness</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument from Book III of "On Abstinence from Animal Food." He is mid-sentence, contrasting those who kill out of necessity with those who kill for luxury. He moves into a critique of Stoic philosophy, specifically their denial of justice toward animals.</meta>

### ->ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...seeking such an end <term>telos</term> <note>original: "telos"; the ultimate goal or purpose of an action</note> is exceedingly lawless and terrible. For it is surely enough that we make use of those who must labor—those who toil and work on our behalf—

> The breeds of horses and donkeys, and the offspring of bulls,

<margin>5</margin> as Aeschylus says, 

> to serve as slaves in our place and to take upon themselves our labors,

once we have mastered and yoked them. <margin>19</margin> But as for the person who demands that we do not treat the ox as a meat dish <note>The Greek "opson" refers to anything eaten with bread, specifically delicacies or meat</note>, and that we should not destroy "breath and life" by adding the seasonings of gluttony and the decorations of the table—what is he taking away from life <margin>10</margin> that is necessary for our survival, or what that is noble for the cultivation of virtue? 

Furthermore, to compare plants to animals is entirely forced. For animals are by nature capable of perception, of feeling pain, of feeling fear, and of being harmed—which is exactly why they can be treated unjustly <term>adikia</term>. <margin>15</margin> But for plants, there is no perception; consequently, nothing is "alien" to them, nor "bad," nor is there any harm or injustice involved. Indeed, the very origin of all kinship and alienation <note>original: "oikeiosis" and "allotriosis"; "oikeiosis" is a central Stoic term meaning the recognition of something as belonging to oneself</note> is the ability to perceive. And those from the school of Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium was the founder of Stoicism</note> <margin>20</margin> place this sense of kinship as the very foundation of justice. 

How, then, is it not irrational to observe many humans who live by perception alone, possessing neither intellect nor reason <term>logos</term>, and many others who exceed the most terrifying wild beasts in cruelty, anger, and greed—child-killers, murderers of parents, <margin>25</margin> tyrants, and the lackeys of kings—and yet believe that we owe some form of justice to *them*, while we owe nothing at all to the plow-ox, the companion dog, and the livestock that nourish us with their milk and clothe us with their wool? How is this not utterly illogical? 

<margin>20</margin> But, by Zeus, that argument of Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus was the third head of the Stoic school and its most prolific theorist</note> <margin>30</margin> was supposedly "persuasive": that the gods created us for their own sake and for one another, but that they created animals for *our* sake—horses to go to war with us, dogs to hunt with us...

<summary>Porphyry argues that while using animals for labor might be justified by necessity, killing them for food is a luxury that violates natural justice. He critiques the Stoic view that we only owe justice to rational beings, pointing out the hypocrisy of protecting cruel humans while slaughtering helpful animals.</summary>

<header>DE ABSTINENTIA III.</header>

...[training] grounds, while leopards, bears, and lions serve as exercises for human courage. And then there is the sow—for here is the "sweetest of the Graces" <note>Porphyry is speaking ironically here, mocking those who view the pig only as a source of pleasure</note>—which was born for no other reason than to be sacrificed. To its flesh, God mixed in a soul like a pinch of salt <note>This is a famous Stoic joke, often attributed to Chrysippus: the soul of a pig is merely salt to keep the meat from rotting before it is eaten</note>, <margin>5</margin> engineering a delicacy for our benefit. And so that we might have an abundance of broth and side-dishes <term>paradeipnia</term>, He prepared all kinds of oysters, purple-fish, sea-nettles, and various breeds of birds. He did this not from any other source, but by turning a great part of His own essence into these "sweet-hearted" things, <margin>10</margin> surpassing even the care of wet-nurses by packing this terrestrial region with pleasures and enjoyments.

If anyone truly thinks that these ideas possess any probability or are fitting for a god, let him consider how he will answer the argument that Carneades <note>Carneades (c. 214–129 BCE) was a skeptical philosopher who famously argued against Stoic dogmatism</note> used to pose: <margin>15</margin> "Every creature produced by nature is benefited when it attains the end <term>telos</term> <note>The ultimate purpose or 'finishing point' for which a thing exists</note> for which it was naturally born." We must understand "benefit" in a general sense, which these people call utility <term>euchrestia</term>. <note>original: "euchrestia"; a technical Stoic term for things that are useful or provide service</note> Now, if the sow was born by nature to be slaughtered and <margin>20</margin> devoured, then in suffering this fate, it attains the very purpose for which it was born, and thus it is "benefited." 

Furthermore, if God engineered animals for the use of human beings, what use shall we make of flies, mosquitoes, bats, beetles, scorpions, and vipers? Some of these are <margin>25</margin> hideous to look at, filthy to touch, unbearable in their smell, and possess voices that are terrifying or unpleasant; others are outright deadly to those who encounter them. And what of the whales, the sawfish, and the other sea-monsters of which Homer says "deep-moaning Amphitrite <note>A sea goddess and wife of Poseidon; here she personifies the ocean</note> feeds ten thousand"? <margin>30</margin> Why did the Creator not teach us in what way these creatures were born useful to our nature? 

If they respond that not everything was born for us or because of us, then besides the fact that this distinction creates great confusion and obscurity, we still do not escape the charge of injustice <term>adikia</term> when we attack and use...

<summary>Porphyry mocks the Stoic claim that animals like pigs exist only to be eaten, using Carneades' logic to show how absurd it is to claim slaughter is "beneficial" for the victim. He further challenges the idea of a human-centered world by pointing to "useless" or dangerous creatures like scorpions and sea monsters.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument against the Stoic claim that animals exist solely for human use. The previous page ended mid-sentence, discussing Carneades’ skeptical challenge: if everything is "benefited" by fulfilling its natural purpose, then a pig is "benefited" by being slaughtered for food. Porphyry is now showing the logical endpoint of such anthropocentric reasoning.</meta>

<page-num>143</page-num>
<header>ON ABSTINENCE III.</header>

...[acting] harmfully toward those things which were not made for our sake, but which, just like us, were brought into being according to nature. I will omit saying that if we define our relationship to the world solely by utility, we would soon find ourselves conceding that *we* were created for the sake of the most destructive animals—such as crocodiles, <margin>5</margin> whales, and serpents <note>original: δράκοντες (drakontes). While often translated as "dragons," in this context it refers to large, dangerous snakes or sea-monsters</note>. For we receive no benefit at all from those creatures; yet they, by snatching and destroying any humans who happen upon them, use us for food. In this, they act no more cruelly than we do, except <margin>10</margin> that they are driven to this injustice by necessity and hunger, whereas we, out of insolence <term>hybris</term> and for the sake of luxury, slaughter the majority of animals for sport in theaters and during hunts. 

From these practices, our murderous and beastly nature is strengthened, as is our apathy toward pity. Those who <margin>15</margin> first dared to do this blunted the greater part of our civilized humanity. The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who were famous in antiquity for their vegetarianism and belief in the transmigration of souls</note>, however, made gentleness toward beasts a training ground for the love of mankind and compassion. Therefore, how is it that they did not rouse men toward justice more effectively <margin>20</margin> than those who claim that our common justice is corrupted by such kindness? For habit is a powerful force; once a person is gradually made familiar with these violent passions, habit leads them much further. 

"Yes," they <note>Porphyry is here voicing a Stoic counter-argument</note> say, "but just as the immortal is the opposite of the mortal, and the incorruptible the opposite of the corruptible, <margin>25</margin> and the incorporeal the opposite of the body, so too there must exist an 'irrational' <term>alogon</term> to stand as an opposite and counterpart to the 'rational' <term>logikon</term>. It would be wrong for this pair <note>original: συζυγίαις (syzygies). A philosophical term for pairs of fundamental opposites that balance the universe</note> alone, among so many others, to be left incomplete and unfulfilled." 

As if we were not already conceding this! We point out that there is a vast amount of the irrational <margin>30</margin> in existence. For there is surely a great and abundant amount of it in all things that lack a soul <note>Porphyry argues that plants and inanimate objects provide the "irrational" contrast to human reason, so we don't need to categorize animals as irrational to balance the scales</note>, and we require no other opposition to the rational. But all well...

<summary>Porphyry argues that if utility determines purpose, humans could be seen as food for predators; he contrasts Pythagorean compassion with the desensitizing effect of hunting and blood sports.</summary>

-># ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...[immediately] the inanimate <note>original: ἄψυχον (apsychon), literally "soulless"</note>, being without a soul and without intellect, stands in opposition to that which possesses a soul, reason <term>logos: both "speech" and "reasoned thought"</term>, and thought. But if one claims that nature is not "mutilated" <note>meaning incomplete or lacking a necessary counterpart</note>, but rather that within animate nature there is a rational part and an irrational part, <margin>5</margin> another will then demand that animate nature also contains a part capable of imagination <note>original: φανταστικόν (phantastikon), the faculty of mental representation</note> and a part incapable of it, or a part with sensation and a part without sensation, so that nature might hold these balanced pairs of opposing states and privations within the same genus, as if on a scale. But <margin>10</margin> this is certainly absurd. 

For if it is absurd to seek a part of the animate that perceives and another that is insensitive—or one with imagination and another without—it is because every animate being is naturally endowed with sensation and imagination. Likewise, it is not reasonable to demand <margin>15</margin> that one part of the animate be rational and the other irrational. This is especially true when speaking to those who believe that nothing partakes in sensation without also partaking in understanding, nor that any animal exists that does not naturally possess a degree of opinion and reasoning <term>logismos: the process of calculation or logical thought</term>, just as it possesses sensation and impulse. 

<margin>20</margin> For nature—which they rightly say does everything for a purpose and toward an end—did not make the animal sensitive for the mere sake of experiencing or perceiving. Rather, since many things are favorable to it and many are alien, it would not be able to survive for even a moment if it did not learn to guard against some things <margin>25</margin> and associate with others. 

Sensation provides the knowledge of both to each creature; but the actions that follow sensation—the seizing and pursuing of the beneficial, and the repelling and fleeing of the destructive and painful—could never be achieved by creatures that are <margin>30</margin> not naturally inclined toward calculation, judgment, memory, and attention. For if you entirely remove expectation, memory, purpose, preparation, and hope...

<summary>Porphyry argues that because animals possess sensation (sight, touch, etc.) and must make choices to survive, they logically must possess a form of reason and memory. He rejects the idea that animals can be "animate" yet "irrational," as sensation and judgment are inextricably linked.</summary>

<margin>1</margin>to feel fear, to desire, or to be distressed. Neither the presence of eyes nor ears is of any use—nor is there any benefit to any sensation or imagination <term>phantasia: the ability to form mental images</term>—if the faculty that uses them is not present. Indeed, it would be better to be rid of these senses than to suffer, grieve, and feel pain <margin>5</margin> without the means to ward them off when the mind is absent. Furthermore, there is an argument by Strato the Physicist <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a scientist-philosopher who led Aristotle's school</note> demonstrating that it is impossible to perceive anything at all without the act of thinking <term>noein: the active processing of the mind</term>. But later, the mind returns and pursues each of the things previously mentioned, gathering them up by recollection. This is why it has been said,
> The mind sees, the mind hears; everything else is deaf and blind. <note>original: νοῦς ὁρᾷ, νοῦς ἀκούει, τὰ δ' ἄλλα κωφὰ καὶ τυφλά. Though often attributed to the poet Epicharmus, the footnote below suggests another source.</note>

From this, it follows that in all beings where sensation exists, thinking must also exist.

-># ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

In introductory textbooks, whenever they define <term>prothesis: purpose or intention</term> as a "sign of completion," or <term>epibolē: application</term> as "impulse before impulse," or <term>paraskeuē: preparation</term> as "action before action," and <term>mnēmē: memory</term> as the "apprehension of a past proposition <margin>5</margin> whose presence was originally apprehended through sensation"—they are describing things that are inherently rational. Yet all of these qualities belong to every animal. This is exactly the same as with <term>noēseis: thoughts</term>, which are called <term>ennoiai: concepts</term> when they are stored in the mind, and <term>dianoēseis: active reasonings</term> when they are in motion. Furthermore, given that they commonly admit that all <term>pathē: passions or emotions</term> are <margin>10</margin> "corrupt judgments" and "opinions," it is strange that they overlook the deeds and movements in wild beasts that stem from many types of rage and fear—and by Zeus, even from envy and jealousy. Indeed, these people themselves punish dogs and horses that make mistakes—not for no reason, but for <margin>15</margin> <term>sōphronismos: correction or discipline</term>, creating a sense of grief in them through pain, which we call <term>metanoia: repentance or remorse</term>.

When pleasure comes through the ears, it is called enchantment; through the eyes, it is called fascination. People use both of these against wild animals. <margin>20</margin> Deer and horses are enchanted by pan-pipes and flutes; fishermen call crabs out of their crevices by piping to them on pan-pipes; and they say that the shad <note>A type of migratory fish common in the Mediterranean</note> rises up and comes forward when people sing. 

Those who speak foolishly about these matters claim that animals do not actually feel pleasure, or anger, <margin>25</margin> or fear, or make preparations, or remember. Instead, they claim the bee "as-if" remembers, the nightingale "as-if" prepares, the lion "as-if" feels anger, and the deer "as-if" feels fear. I do not know what these people will do when faced with someone who says animals do not <margin>30</margin> even see or hear, but only "as-if" see and "as-if" hear; or that they do not make sounds, but only "as-if" make sounds; or that they do not live at all, but only "as-if" live. These latter claims are no more absurd than the former.

<summary>Porphyry argues that the cognitive and emotional states of animals—such as memory, preparation, and regret—are identical in nature to human ones. He ridicules the Stoic "as-if" (hōsanei) argument, which attempts to deny animals true rationality and emotion by using purely metaphorical language for their behaviors.</summary>

<keywords>animal psychology, Stoicism, memory, emotion, repentance, enchantment, hōsanei, Porphyry</keywords>

-># ON ABSTINENCE III.<-

...occurring in accordance with clear evidence, just as a fair-minded person would be persuaded. But when I compare the lives, habits, and diets of animals with those of humans and see much baseness—and no clear aim, progress, or desire among animals toward that <margin>5</margin> virtue for which <term>logos: reason</term> was created—I might be at a loss as to why Nature gave a starting point to those who are unable to reach the final goal. Yet, this does not seem strange even to those [opposing] philosophers. For instance, they establish that parental affection <margin>10</margin> (<term>philostorgia: natural love for offspring</term>) is the very origin of our own social community and justice; but even though they see this affection is present in animals to a great and powerful degree, they still claim animals have no share in justice. Consider also whether it is not ridiculous for those followers of the Stoics to say that men like Socrates, Plato, and Zeno lived with a "vice" no <margin>20</margin> lighter than that of a common slave, claiming they were all equally foolish, intemperate, and unjust <note>Porphyry is mocking the Stoic "paradox" that all sins are equal and anyone who is not a perfect Sage is equally "vicious."</note>. If they say this of the great sages, how can they then blame wild beasts for not being pure or perfected in virtue? They suggest that animals possess a "deprivation" rather than a "baseness" of reason, or a mere weakness—and this despite <margin>25</margin> admitting that "vice" is a rational quality, and that every beast is full of it! For we see cowardice, intemperance, injustice, and malice existing in many of them. <margin>27</margin> However, the person who claims that a creature which does not naturally receive "correctness" of reason does not possess reason at all, <margin>30</margin> is no different from someone claiming that a monkey is not naturally "ugly" or a turtle is not naturally "slow" simply because they are not capable of [human] beauty or speed. He fails to see the obvious distinction between the two.

-># ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK III<-

Reason (<term>logos: the faculty of reason and speech</term>) exists by nature, but excellent and perfect reason comes from care and instruction. For this reason, all living beings share in the rational faculty, but [the Stoics] cannot even claim that a [single] human has attained rightness of mind and <margin>5</margin> wisdom, though there be ten thousand of them. Just as there is a difference between one sight and another, or one flight and another—for hawks do not see in the same way cicadas do, nor do eagles fly like partridges—so too does every rational being not share in the same degree of agility and sharpness that <margin>10</margin> reaches the highest peak. There are many examples of community, courage, and cleverness in providing for oneself and managing a household, just as there are examples of the opposites: injustice, cowardice, and stupidity. From this, certain debates arise, with some saying land animals are more advanced <margin>15</margin> and others saying sea animals are. This is clear when comparing land-horses to river-horses <note>original: "potamiois," referring to the hippopotamus</note>: for the former care for their parents, while the latter kill them in order to mate with their mothers. Or compare doves with partridges: for [male partridges] hide <margin>20</margin> and destroy the eggs when the female is brooding and does not accept mating; but [male doves] take their turn in the care, warming the eggs, and are the first to feed the chicks. If the female wanders away for too long, the male pecks at her and drives her back <margin>25</margin> to the eggs and chicks. Antipater <note>Antipater of Tarsus, a Stoic philosopher who argued that animals lack reason because they are "unclean" and lack social instinct.</note> accused donkeys and sheep of lacking cleanliness, but I do not know how he overlooked lynxes and swallows. Furthermore, we do not say one tree is more ignorant than another, as we say a sheep is more ignorant than a dog, nor...

<summary>Porphyry argues that reason is a natural faculty shared by all animals, though it manifests in varying degrees of "sharpness" and skill. ...one vegetable is not more "unmanly" than another <note>original: "anandroteron." <margin>10</margin> animals in his capacity for learning, sharpness of mind, and in matters of justice and social bonding. <margin>24</margin> troubled. If many examples had not been collected and spoken of by many authors, I could bring forth ten thousand more to 
<margin>25</margin> demonstrate the natural cleverness of animals. But one further point must be considered. It seems that whatever part or power is naturally capable of receiving a certain state is also, by its very nature, capable of falling into the opposite, unnatural state when it is maimed or diseased. For instance, the eye can fall 
<margin>30</margin> into blindness, the leg into lameness, and the tongue into stammering, but nothing else can. For there is no such thing as "blindness" in something not naturally made to see, nor "lameness" in something not naturally made to walk...

<summary>Porphyry argues that reason exists in degrees; just because animals have "clouded" or weaker reasoning compared to humans, it does not mean they lack it entirely, much as a slow runner still possesses the faculty of movement.</summary>

-># ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK III<-

...one will not hate the species as a whole, but rather, the more encompassing the genus of living beings is, the more one will preserve this kindness toward both the individual part and that which is familiar. Therefore, the person who has established a sense of kinship <note>original: "oikeiōsis"—a technical term for the process of recognizing others as belonging to one’s own circle of concern</note> with living beings in general <margin>5</margin> will not treat any specific animal with injustice. However, the person who limits the scope of justice only to humans is ready to cast aside the restraint against injustice as if he were operating within a narrow, cramped space. Thus, the Pythagorean "seasoning" is even more pleasant than the Socratic one. For Socrates used to say that "hunger" was the seasoning <note>original: "opson"—a side dish or relish used to make plain food savory</note> for food, but Pythagoras said that the best seasoning was "to do no injustice to anyone" and <margin>10</margin> to sweeten the meal with justice. For the avoidance of animal food <note>original: "empsychou trophes"—literally "food with a soul"</note> was truly an avoidance of the injustices associated with such food. For surely God did not make our own preservation impossible without the harming of another; for if that were the case, He would have grafted a fundamental principle of injustice onto our very nature. <margin>15</margin> Furthermore, those people who thought they could introduce justice only through a kinship restricted to humans seem to be entirely ignorant of the specific character of justice itself. For such a restricted bond would merely be a form of "human-friendliness" <term>philanthropia: literally a love of humanity, here contrasted with a more universal justice</term>. But true justice consists <margin>20</margin> in restraint and harmlessness toward anything whatsoever that is not itself harmful. And this is how the "just person" is truly understood—not in that other narrow way—since justice extends even to all living beings and is rooted in being harmless. Because of this, the very essence of justice lies in the rational part <term>logistikon: the calculating, reasoning part of the soul</term> ruling over the irrational part, with the irrational <margin>25</margin> following its lead. For when the rational rules and the irrational follows, it is an absolute necessity that one be harmless toward everything whatsoever, including other humans. For when the passions are contracted, and the desires and angers have withered away, and when reason holds its proper <margin>30</margin> rule, there immediately follows an assimilation <term>homoiōsis: the Platonic ideal of "becoming like God" by imitating divine virtues</term> toward the Higher Power. And the Higher Power in the universe is entirely harmless; through its own power, it is the preserver of all things, the benefactor of all things, and stands in need of nothing...

<summary>Porphyry argues that true justice is a universal principle of harmlessness rooted in the rational soul's control over passions, rather than a social contract limited to humans. He contrasts the Pythagorean ideal of "just eating" with the Socratic focus on appetite, suggesting that a vegetarian diet is an imitation of the divine nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the bottom of page 153, where Porphyry was discussing the scope of justice. He is now refuting the idea that humans must be "unjust" to nature to survive, arguing instead for a hierarchy of harmlessness that aligns the soul with the divine.</meta>

-># ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK III<-

...of things. We, on the one hand, are harmless toward all things because of justice; on the other hand, because of our mortal nature, we are in need of necessities. But the taking of necessities does not harm plants when we take what they cast off, nor fruits when <margin>5</margin> we use the fruits of those that have died, nor sheep when we actually benefit them through shearing and share in their milk while providing them with our care. Therefore, the just man appears as one who diminishes himself <note>The "just man" is described as *elattōtikos*, meaning he is willing to take less for himself than he might be entitled to, for the sake of a higher principle.</note> in things regarding the body, yet he does not treat himself with injustice; <margin>10</margin> for by this discipline and self-control, the internal good increases—that is, the **likeness to God** <note>original: *homoiōsis theō*—a central goal in Platonic philosophy, meaning to become as much like the divine as a human can.</note>. 

<margin>27</margin> Neither, then, if pleasure is the goal <note>A reference to Epicureanism, which Porphyry rejects here.</note> is true justice preserved, nor if justice consists in those things which complete happiness according to nature—at least not if all those things are set out as the goal. <margin>15</margin> For in many cases, the impulses of the irrational nature and its needs take the lead in injustice. For instance, they <note>Referring to those who eat meat.</note> found it necessary to eat meat <note>original: *zōophagia*—the eating of living things.</note> so that they might keep their nature, as they say, free from pain and lacking nothing that it craves. 

But since the goal is to become like God as much as possible, <margin>20</margin> **harmlessness** <note>original: *to ablabes*—the state of doing no harm, often linked to the concept of *ahimsa* in other traditions.</note> toward all is preserved. Therefore, just as the person driven by passions is harmless only toward his children and wife, but contemptuous and greedy toward everyone else—since the irrational part rules within him—he is roused toward mortal things and is awestruck by them; <margin>25</margin> but the person led by reason maintains harmlessness toward fellow citizens, and even more so toward strangers and all human beings—having brought his irrationality into subjection—and he himself is more rational than those others, and for this reason, more divine. 

Thus, the one who has not only established harmlessness among humans, <margin>30</margin> but has also extended it to other living beings, is more like God; and if it were possible to extend it even to plants, he would preserve the divine **image** <note>original: *eikōn*</note> even more. And if not, at least from here the characteristic of nature...

<summary>Porphyry argues that true justice is "harmlessness" toward all living things, which allows the human soul to achieve its ultimate goal: becoming like God. He distinguishes between the harmful taking of life and the harmless use of natural byproducts like fallen fruit or wool.</summary>

He now explains that our dependency on the physical world is a form of metaphysical "poverty" resulting from the soul's fall.</meta>

-># ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK III<-

...defect of our nature; from this comes the lament of the ancients, that
> "from such strifes and such contentions have we been born," <note>original: *toion ek t' eridōn ek te neikeōn genomenostha*—a quote from the Pre-Socratic philosopher Empedocles, referring to the cosmic forces of Love and Strife that govern the cycle of souls.</note>
<margin>5</margin> because we are unable to preserve the divine within us as undefiled and harmless toward all things. For we were not self-sufficient in all things; the cause is our birth <note>original: *genesis*—the process of coming into physical existence, which Neoplatonists viewed as a descent from the perfect divine realm into the changing material world.</note> and the fact that we were born into poverty, as the source of plenty <note>original: *poros*—Porphyry is alluding to the myth in Plato’s *Symposium* where Plenty (Poros) and Poverty (Penia) conceive Love (Eros). Here, the soul’s "plenty" flows away during its descent into matter.</note> flowed away. Poverty sought its preservation and its order—through which it received its existence—from things outside itself. Whoever, then, requires more external things <margin>10</margin> is all the more "nailed" to poverty; and to the degree that one lacks more, by that much is one without a share in God and a housemate to poverty. 

For that which is like God possesses true wealth immediately by that very likeness. No one who is truly wealthy and in need of nothing acts unjustly; for as long as one acts unjustly—even if he possesses all the money <margin>15</margin> and all the acres <note>original: *plethra*—a Greek unit of land measurement, roughly 100 feet or a quarter of an acre.</note> of the earth—he is poor, living as a companion to poverty. For these reasons, such a person is unjust, godless, impious, and guilty of every vice; these vices find their substance in the soul's fall toward matter <note>original: *hylē*—physical substance, which Porphyry views as the lowest level of reality and a source of limitation for the soul.</note>, produced by the loss of the Good. 

Therefore, everything is mere trifles so long as one <margin>20</margin> has slipped away from the first principle; such a person is in want of everything as long as he does not look toward the Source, and he yields to his mortal nature until he recognizes his true self. 

Injustice has a terrible power to persuade itself and to bribe those held in its grip, because it keeps company with its foster-children by means of pleasure. <margin>25</margin> Just as in the choice of lifestyles, the person who has experienced both is a more accurate judge than the person who has tried only one, so too in the choices and avoidances of our duties: the safer judge is the one who judges from a higher perspective <note>original: *epanabebēkotos*—literally "one who has ascended," referring to the philosopher who has elevated his mind above physical desires to view things from the level of Intellect.</note> and looks down upon the lower, rather than the one who judges these matters from a lowly position. <margin>30</margin> Consequently, the person living according to the Intel <note>original: *nous*—the highest rational faculty of the soul, capable of perceiving divine truth.</note> is a more accurate judge of what should be chosen and what should not than the person living according to irrationality; for the rational man has also passed through the state of irrationality...

<summary>Porphyry argues that human dependency on external things is a metaphysical "poverty" caused by the soul's fall into matter. He asserts that the philosopher, living by the "Intellect," is the only one qualified to judge what is truly necessary because he has experienced both the rational and irrational states of being.</summary>

...since he has associated with this <note>external wealth or bodily needs</note> from the beginning. But the man who is inexperienced in the things of the mind <term>mind: *nous*—the higher intellect which Neoplatonists believed could perceive divine reality directly</term> persuades those like himself, like a child talking nonsense among children. But if everyone, they say, were persuaded by these arguments, what would become of us? Is it not clear that we would be happy? <margin>5</margin> Injustice would be exiled from among men, and Justice would govern us, just as she does in heaven. 

But as it stands, it is as if the Danaids <note>original: *Danaïdes*—In Greek mythology, these were fifty sisters punished in the underworld by being forced to eternally fill a leaky jar using sieves; Porphyry uses them as a metaphor for the futility of trying to satisfy endless physical desires.</note> wondered what kind of life they would lead if they were freed from the labor of serving that leaky jar with a sieve. <margin>10</margin> For they wonder what will happen if we cease providing for our passions and desires—through which everything "leaks away" because of our inexperience with truly beautiful things—we who love a life centered on mere necessities or even things beyond what is necessary. 

What then shall we do, you ask, O man? <margin>15</margin> Let us imitate the Golden Race <note>The first and most perfect race of humans described by the poet Hesiod; they lived in harmony with nature and the gods.</note>; let us imitate those who have been set free. For with them, Reverence <note>original: *Aidōs*</note>, Indignation <note>original: *Nemesis*</note>, and Justice <note>original: *Dikē*</note> associate, because they were content with the fruit of the earth; for 
> the life-giving soil bore them fruit
<margin>20</margin> > of its own accord, many and abundant. <note>original: *epheren zeidōros aroura automatē pollon te kai aphthonon*—a quote from Hesiod’s *Works and Days* (line 117-118).</note>

Those who have been set free provide for themselves the very things they once used to provide while serving their masters. In no other way, then, once you are freed from the slavery of the body <margin>25</margin> and from serving the passions caused by the body—just as you used to feed those passions in every way with things from the outside—so you will nourish yourself in every way with things from within. You will be justly reclaiming what is your own, and no longer forcibly taking away what belongs to others.

<summary>Porphyry argues that a life of abstinence and justice is not a state of deprivation, but a return to the "Golden Age" where the soul is nourished by internal virtues rather than external passions.</summary>

## BOOK FOUR

<margin>1</margin> We have already addressed, O Castricius, almost all the excuses of those who—while in reality adopting the eating of flesh for the sake of their own lack of self-control and indulgence—have provided themselves with shameless defenses based on "necessity." This is a need they attribute to nature much more than is proper, and we have countered these claims through what we have already stated. <margin>5</margin> However, some specific questions still remain. Among these, the claim of "utility" <term>utility: *to sympheron*—the argument that eating meat is advantageous or necessary for human health and social survival</term> especially deceives those who are ruled by their pleasures. Furthermore, there is the testimony—often repeated by those ignorant of true history—that no wise men and no nation have ever refused to eat meat. This claim leads listeners to a great sense of injustice. <margin>10</margin> Since we intend to conduct an examination of these points, we will attempt to set forth the solutions to these questions regarding utility and other matters.

<margin>15</margin> Let us begin then with the abstinence practiced by certain nations. The Greeks shall lead our account, as they are the most familiar witnesses. <margin>2</表达> Among those who have collected Greek history both concisely and accurately is the Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: a student or follower of Aristotle’s philosophy</term> Dicaearchus. In his description of the ancient life of Greece, <margin>20</margin> he says that the ancients—who lived close to the gods—were the best by nature and lived the most excellent life. As a result, they were considered a "Golden Race" <note>original: *chrysoun genos*—the first and most perfect age of humanity described by the poet Hesiod</note> when compared to the people of today, who are counterfeit and made of the basest materials. He states that they killed no living creature. <margin>25</margin> This is what the poets also mean when they refer to the "Golden Race," saying that "all good things" <note>A reference to Hesiod's *Works and Days*, line 116, describing the abundance and peace of the first humans.</note> were theirs...

<margin>5</margin> In explaining these verses, Dicaearchus says that the life in the time of Cronus <term>Cronus: in Greek mythology, the Titan who ruled during the "Golden Age" before Zeus</term> was truly like this. He argues that we should accept this account as historical fact rather than a baseless rumor; however, we should set aside the overly mythical elements and reduce the story to a natural, rational explanation. Everything grew "spontaneously" <margin>10</margin> for a logical reason: the people themselves did not yet practice any labor, as they did not yet possess the art of agriculture nor, quite simply, any other craft. This very lack of industry was also the cause of their leisure <term>leisure: *schole*—not mere idleness, but freedom from the labor required for survival</term> and of their passing their lives without toil or worry. Furthermore, if we are to follow the reasoning of the most refined physicians, <margin>15</margin> this was also the reason they did not suffer from disease. Indeed, one could find no greater prescription for health than the avoidance of "residues" <term>residues: *perittomata*—in ancient medicine, the undigested excess of food believed to cause disease</term>, and those early people kept their bodies entirely pure. They did not consume food that was "stronger" than their own nature—meaning food difficult to digest—but rather food which their nature could easily master. <margin>20</margin> Nor did they eat more than was moderate simply because it was available; rather, for the most part, they ate less than was sufficient because of its scarcity. Moreover, they had neither wars nor civil strife among themselves. <margin>25</margin> There was no prize of any value set before them for which someone might have started such a great conflict. Thus, the defining characteristics of their life were leisure, ease from the burdens of necessity, health, peace, and friendship. To those of later generations, however, who desired great things and fell into many evils, <margin>30</margin> that earlier life naturally became something for which they yearned. The simplicity and improvised nature of the first people's food is revealed by the later proverb, "enough of the oak" <note>original: "ἅλις δρυός" (*halis dryos*). Those who possessed much gained no advantage, for there was no <margin>5</margin> path for their wealth to reach the public; instead, it remained shut up within the house and idle. For this reason, even the most common and necessary items of furniture—couches, chairs, and tables—were crafted by them to the highest standard. The Laconian cup <note>original: "kothon," a famous Spartan drinking vessel known for its utility</note>, as Critias says, was <margin>10</margin> particularly esteemed for military service. For the water that had to be drunk out of necessity, though it might be unpleasant to look at, was hidden by the color of the vessel; moreover, as the sediment was blocked and caught by the curved rim <note>The "ambon" or projecting lip of the cup</note>, the liquid that reached the mouth was cleaner. <margin>15</margin> The lawgiver <note>Lycurgus, the semi-legendary founder of the Spartan constitution</note> was the cause of these developments, according to Plutarch. By freeing the craftsmen from useless tasks, they displayed their artistry in the things that were truly necessary. Furthermore, intending to strike an even greater blow against luxury and to strip away the envy of wealth, he <margin>20</margin> introduced a third and most excellent reform: the institution of the <term>syssitia</term> <note>The "common messes" or public dining clubs required for all Spartan citizens</note>. This required them to dine with one another, coming together for shared and regulated dishes and food, and not to live at home reclining on costly bedding <margin>25</margin> and tables. He wished to prevent them from being in the hands of artisans and cooks in the dark, like gluttonous animals, fattening themselves and ruining their characters alongside their bodies, which were surrendered to every desire and excess. Such a life required long periods of sleep, hot baths, <margin>30</margin> and much rest—a state that was, in a sense, a daily illness. While this reform was a great thing, an even greater achievement was making wealth "unenviable," as Theophrastus says, and "unwealthy" by means of the common...

# DE ABSTINENCE IV.

...the simplicity concerning their lifestyle, although it was legislated for the masses. For this reason, those who emerge from this form of government are handed down as being more courageous, more self-controlled, and more concerned with what is right <margin>5</margin> than those from other states, who are corrupted in both their souls and their bodies. It is clear, then, that total abstinence <note>original: "apochē," the act of refraining from eating animal flesh</note> is suited to such a constitution, while eating meat is suited to corrupted ones.

Moving on to other nations <margin>10</margin> that have turned toward good laws, gentleness, and piety <note>original: "eusebeia," meaning proper respect and duty toward the divine</note> toward the divine, it will be clear that abstinence was commanded for the salvation and benefit of cities—if not for all citizens, then at least for some. For those who sacrifice to the gods on behalf of the city <margin>15</margin> and serve them used to propitiate the sins of the many. For just as in the Mysteries, the boy called "from the hearth" <note>The "pais aph' hestias" was a child chosen by lot to be initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries at public expense, serving as a symbolic mediator to win the gods' favor for the entire city</note> propitiates the divine on behalf of all those being initiated by performing exactly what is commanded, so too throughout nations and cities, the priests <margin>20</margin> are able to do this on behalf of everyone, drawing the divine toward their protection through their piety. Therefore, it is strictly commanded for priests to abstain from eating either all animals or at least certain ones, whether you examine Greek customs or those of the <margin>25</margin> "barbarians" <note>The Greek term for non-Greek speakers, used here to include civilizations like the Egyptians or Persians</note>; indeed, these rules vary among different peoples. The result is that when all these traditions are taken together, it appears that priests everywhere abstain from all animals, if one were to consider them all as a single group. If, then, those who preside over the salvation of cities and <margin>30</margin> are entrusted with the city's piety toward the gods abstain from animals, how could anyone dare to claim that abstinence is disadvantageous to cities? At any rate, the customs of the Egyptian priests, as described by Chaeremon... <margin>6</margin>

-># ON ABSTINENCE IV.<-

...Chaeremon the Stoic <note>Chaeremon of Alexandria was a 1st-century Stoic philosopher and an Egyptian priest (hierogrammateus), making him a primary source for Porphyry on Egyptian customs.</note>, in his account of those who are understood to be philosophers among the Egyptians, explains that they chose the temples as the place to practice their philosophy. For living near the sanctuaries of the gods was consistent with their entire yearning for contemplation <term>theoria: the meditative observation or mental vision of the divine</term>. 
<margin>5</margin>This environment provided them with security born from the reverence for the divine, as everyone honored these philosophers as if they were certain sacred animals. It also allowed them to remain at peace, since social interaction occurred only during public assemblies and festivals; 
<margin>10</margin>for the rest of the time, the temples were almost inaccessible to anyone else. Indeed, it was required that those who approached be purified <term>hagneia: ritual purity involving specific washings and dietary restrictions</term> and abstain from many things. This is a common law, as it were, of the temples throughout Egypt. Having renounced 
<margin>15</margin>all other occupations and human labors, they dedicated their entire lives to the contemplation and vision of divine matters. Through this vision, they secured for themselves what is honorable, safe, and pious; through contemplation, they gained knowledge; and through both, they developed a certain hidden 
<margin>20</margin>and ancient discipline of character. For to be always in the presence of divine knowledge and inspiration places one far beyond all greed, suppresses the passions, and awakens the life toward true understanding. They practiced simplicity, restraint, self-control, and endurance, as well as 
<margin>25</margin>justice and a lack of grasping in all things. Their solitary nature also rendered them venerable; during the times of the so-called "purifications," they did not even associate with their closest relatives or kinsmen, and were hardly seen by anyone else, except when performing necessary 
<margin>30</margin>duties alongside those also undergoing purification. They reserved the inner sanctums <term>adyta: literally "not to be entered"; the most sacred restricted areas of a temple</term> as inaccessible to those not purified, keeping them holy for sacred rites. At other times, they associated more simply with their peers, but from outsiders...

...of other forms of worship; they were always seen near the gods or their statues, either carrying sacred objects or leading processions and arranging them with order and solemnity. <margin>5</margin>Their solemnity was also visible from their physical bearing. For their gait was orderly, and they practiced a steady gaze, even to the point of not blinking when they so desired. Laughter was rare, and if it ever occurred, it went no further than a smile. Their hands were always kept within their robes <note>original: "schema," referring to the specific cut and drape of their priestly vestments</note>. 
<margin>10</margin>And each priest bore a symbol that clearly indicated the rank <note>original: "taxis," referring to the hierarchical order of the priesthood</note> he had been assigned in the temples, for there were several such ranks.

Their diet was simple and plain. As for wine, some did not touch it at all, while others tasted very little, claiming it caused damage to the nerves, a heaviness in the head that hindered discovery <note>meaning intellectual or spiritual insight</note>, 
<margin>15</margin>and they said it provoked sexual desires. For this reason, they were also cautious about other things, never using bread at all during periods of purification <term>hagneia: ritual purity involving specific washings and dietary restrictions</term>. If they ever ate bread when they were not undergoing purification, they ate it crushed with hyssop; for they said the hyssop neutralized much of the bread's [nutritive] power. 
<margin>20</margin>They abstained from oil for the most part, and most of them entirely. If they did use it with vegetables, they used a very small amount, just enough to soothe the sense of taste. 

<margin>7</margin>Furthermore, it was not lawful for them to touch foods or drinks produced outside of Egypt. 
<margin>25</margin>In this way, many avenues of luxury were shut off. Of the things produced within Egypt itself, they abstained from all fish and from all quadrupeds that were solid-hoofed, multi-cloven, or lacked horns. They also avoided all carnivorous birds. <margin>30</margin>and during periods of purification, all of them did so, at which times they would not even eat an egg. Furthermore, they rejected other items as well, not without careful consideration, such as the [flesh] of cows...

<margin>10</margin>not eat the turtle-dove. To ensure they did not accidentally encounter a bird that had been spared in such a manner, they avoided the entire species. <margin>15</margin>were specific to each god. However, the rites of purification <term>hagneiai: specific periods of ritual cleanliness and separation from the mundane</term> were strictly observed by everyone.

During the period when they were about to perform any part of the sacred worship, they set aside a specific number of days in advance. For some, this was forty-two days; for others, more; for others, fewer;
<margin>20</margin>however, it was never less than seven. During this time, they abstained from all animal food, all vegetables and legumes, and above all, from the company of women. As for sexual relations with men, they did not partake of this at any other time either.

They washed themselves three times a day in cold water: after rising from
<margin>25</margin>bed, before the midday meal, and before sleep. If it ever happened that they had a nocturnal emission, they immediately purified the body with a bath. Indeed, they used cold water throughout the rest of their lives as well, though not as excessively as during these times.

-># ON ABSTINENCE IV.<-

...lifestyle. Evidence of their self-control <note>original: "egkrateia"</note> is found in the fact that they lived their lives free from disease, using neither amulets nor incantations <margin>8</margin>, and remained vigorous with a moderate level of strength. Indeed, during their sacred rites, they undertook many heavy burdens and services that exceeded the strength of common men. They divided the night for the observation of the heavenly bodies, and sometimes also for ritual service <term>agisteia: a period of sacred performance or purification</term>, <margin>5</margin> while the day was dedicated to the worship of the gods. During the day, they would sing hymns to the gods three or four times: at dawn and at evening, when the sun reached its zenith, and when it was sinking toward its setting. <margin>10</margin>

The rest of their time they spent on mathematical and geometrical theorems, always working to perfect or discover something new; in general, they were constantly occupied with the pursuit of empirical knowledge. They practiced these same habits even during the long winter nights, staying awake for the love of learning <margin>15</margin>, as they had no concern for making money and were liberated from that "evil master," extravagance. 

Their tireless and continuous labor testifies to the men's endurance, while their lack of desire testifies to their self-control. They even considered it <margin>20</margin> among the most unholy of acts to sail away from Egypt, being deeply cautious of foreign luxuries and ways of life; for such travel seemed holy only to those who were compelled by royal duties. There was a great concern among them to remain faithful to their ancestral customs; if they were found to have transgressed even in small ways <margin>25</margin>, they were expelled. 

The truly philosophical element of the priesthood was found among the "Prophets" <term>prophetai: the highest rank of Egyptian priests, who managed the temple's resources and interpreted sacred law</term>, the Robe-Keepers <term>hierostolistai: priests responsible for dressing the divine statues and managing the sacred wardrobe</term>, the Sacred Scribes, and also the Time-Keepers <term>horologoi: priests who studied the stars to keep the calendar and determine the hours for rituals</term>. The rest of the <margin>30</margin> multitude of priests—the shrine-bearers <term>pastophoroi: lower-ranking priests who carried the sacred images in processions</term>, the temple-wardens, and the assistants—remained pure in a similar fashion, but certainly not with such exacting rigor and self-control.

Such were the customs of the Egyptians as described by the man... <note>The text likely refers to Chaeremon of Alexandria, a Stoic philosopher and priest of the 1st century AD, who is Porphyry's primary source here.</note>

<margin>9</margin> Starting from this ascetic discipline <note>original: "askēseōs"</note> and this intimacy with the divine, they recognized that the divine did not pass through man alone, and that <margin>5</margin> the soul did not take up its dwelling on earth in man alone, but rather almost the same soul passed through all living creatures. For this reason, they included every animal in their deification <note>original: "theopoiian"</note> and, in a way, mixed together wild beasts and humans, and again the bodies of <margin>10</margin> birds and humans. For among them, some figures are depicted as human-shaped up to the neck, but possessing the face of a bird or a lion or some other animal. And again, conversely, they display a human head with the parts of other animals, sometimes placed below and sometimes <margin>15</margin> above. Through these symbols, they show that, by the will of the gods, these creatures also share a fellowship with one another, and that even the wild beasts are our companions and are tamed, not without some divine purpose. 

Hence even the lion is worshipped as a god, and a certain part of Egypt, which they call a <term>nome: a provincial administrative district</term>, <margin>20</margin> is named "Leontopolite" <note>original: "Leontopolitēn," meaning City of Lions</note>, another "Busirite," and another "Lycopolite" <note>original: "Lykopolitēn," meaning City of Wolves</note>. For they worshipped the power of God that extends over all things through the associated animals which each of the gods provided. 

Of the elements, they especially revere water <margin>25</margin> and fire, as these are the primary causes of our preservation; they display these in their temples, as even now, for instance, during the opening of the temple of the holy Sarapis <note>A major Graeco-Egyptian deity representing both abundance and the afterlife</note>, the service is performed using fire and water: the singer of hymns pours the water as a libation and displays the fire, <margin>30</margin> at the moment when, standing upon the threshold, he awakens the god in the ancestral tongue of the Egyptians. Therefore, they revere these shared elements, and they worship even more those things which are more fully involved in the sacred...
