-># ON ABSTINENCE IV.<-

...having [these qualities]. After all these things, they respect all animals; they even worship a human being in the village of Anabis, where sacrifices are offered to him and the sacrificial victims are burned upon the altars. <margin>5</margin> Shortly afterward, he would eat the items specifically prepared for him as a human. Therefore, just as one must abstain from eating humans, so too should one abstain from other animals. 

Furthermore, out of their exceptional wisdom and their intimacy with the divine, they understood that certain animals are more dear to some of the gods than humans are. For example, the hawk is sacred to the Sun <note>The Greek text uses "Helios," whom the Egyptians identified with Ra.</note>. <margin>10</margin> They observed that its entire nature consists of blood and breath <note>original: "pneumatos," referring to the vital spirit or life-force</note>, and that it shows pity even to humans, wailing over a corpse lying on the ground and heaping earth upon its eyes—the place where they believe the solar light dwells. They also understood that the hawk lives for many years, and that after its life ends, it possesses <margin>15</margin> prophetic <note>original: "mantikēn"</note> power. They believed that, once released from the body, it becomes most rational and capable of foreknowledge, and that it can consecrate statues and even cause temples to be moved. 

An ignorant person, unacquainted with divine matters, might be disgusted by a beetle <note>The scarab beetle (*Scarabaeus sacer*).</note>, but the Egyptians <margin>20</margin> worshipped it as a living image of the sun. For every beetle is believed to be male; it discharges its seed into a ball of mud, and having made it spherical, it pushes it backward with its hind legs—just as the sun appears to move across the sky in a direction opposite to the heavens—and it waits for a lunar period of days for its offspring to emerge. They <margin>25</margin> philosophize in a similar way about the ram, and they have other reasons regarding the crocodile, the vulture, and the ibis. In general, they came to worship animals as a result of their wisdom and their profound divine knowledge <note>original: "theosophia"</note>. 

An ignorant man would never have even suspected this. He might assume that they were led astray by some common, unthinking impulse, <margin>30</margin> walking the path of ignorance themselves. On the contrary, having transcended the ignorance of the masses—which is the first state everyone encounters—the Egyptians elevated those things which the masses consider worthless into objects of worship...

->## DE ABSTINENTIA IV.<-

...considered them worthy. In addition to what has already been stated, the animals themselves contributed no less to their faith and reverence. For they understood that the soul of every animal, once released from the body, is rational <note>original: "logikēn"</note>, capable of foreknowledge regarding the future, oracular <note>original: "chrēmatistikēn," referring to receiving divine messages or warnings</note>, <margin>5</margin> and effective in all the same ways as a human soul is when released. For this reason, they quite reasonably honored them and, as far as possible, abstained from eating them. However, since the explanation of why the Egyptians worshiped the gods through animals is a lengthy discourse and <margin>10</margin> exceeds the scope of the present study, the details already provided concerning them will suffice.

Nevertheless, one thing must not be passed over: when the Egyptians embalm those of high birth who have died, they remove the intestines <note>original: "koilian," literally "belly" or "gut"</note> separately and place them in a chest. Among the other rites they perform <margin>15</margin> on behalf of the deceased, they hold the chest toward the sun and call him to witness, while one of the embalmers delivers a speech on behalf of the dead. This speech—which Ecphantus <note>A philosopher who translated Egyptian texts into Greek</note> translated from the ancestral dialect—is as follows:

> “O Lord Sun and <margin>20</margin> all you gods who gave life to humans, receive me and deliver me to dwell with the eternal gods. For I continued piously worshiping the gods whom my parents pointed out to me for as long as I lived my life in that age. I always honored those who <margin>25</margin> begat my body. Of other humans, I neither killed any nor deprived anyone of a deposit <note>original: "parakatathēkēn," a legal trust or item left in one's care</note>, nor committed any other irremediable deed. But if I happened to sin at all during my own life by eating or drinking <margin>30</margin> things that were not permitted, I did not sin because of myself, but because of these,”

pointing to the chest in which the belly was kept. Having said this, he casts the chest into the river, and then embalms the rest of the body as if it were pure.

Neither shouting nor clamor ever defiles the house; instead, they take turns speaking <margin>10</margin> in an orderly fashion, and to those on the outside, the silence of those within appears like some solemn mystery <note>original: "μυστήριόν τι φρικτὸν" — Porphyry uses "frightful" or "awesome" to describe the profound, almost religious silence that outsiders observed when passing an Essene house</note>. The reason for this is their constant sobriety and the fact that their food and drink are measured out only until they are satisfied.

To someone who desires to join the sect <note>original: "αἵρεσιν" (hairesin) — often translated as "heresy" today, but in the ancient world, it simply referred to a chosen school of thought or "philosophy"</note>, entry is not granted immediately. <margin>15</margin> Instead, they prescribe the same way of life <note>original: "δίαιταν" (diaitan) — the source of our word "diet," meaning a complete regimen of living</note> for him while he remains outside for a full year. They give him a small hatchet <note>used for hygiene and burying waste</note>, a loincloth, and a white garment. When he has given proof of his self-control during this time, he approaches closer to their way of life and shares in the purer waters for sanctification <note>ritual immersion or baptismal washings</note>, <margin>20</margin> but he is not yet admitted into their communal living. For after this demonstration of endurance, his character is tested for two more years, and if he appears worthy, he is then <margin>13</margin> admitted into the group. But before he may touch the communal food, he must swear solemn oaths to them: first, <margin>25</margin> that he will be pious toward the divine; next, that he will observe justice toward men and neither harm anyone by his own choice nor by command; that he will always hate the unjust and strive alongside the just; that he will show good faith to all, but especially to those in power, <margin>30</margin> for no one gains the right to rule without God’s will. And if he should rule himself, he must never abuse his authority, nor outshine those subject to him with his clothing or any excessive finery...

->## ON ABSTINENCE IV.<-

...[they swear] to keep their minds shining with clarity, to always love the truth and to expose those who lie; to keep their hands pure from theft and their soul from unholy gain; and neither to hide anything from their fellow members <term>sectarians</term> <note>original: "αἱρετιστὰς" (hairetistas) — here referring to fellow members of the Essene order</note> nor to reveal any of their secrets to outsiders, even if one is tortured unto death. <margin>5</margin> In addition to these things, the initiate swears to transmit the doctrines to no one in any way other than he himself received them, to refrain from robbery, and likewise to preserve the books of their sect and the names of the angels <note>The Essenes were known for a secretive form of Jewish mysticism that included specific names and hierarchies of angelic beings</note>. Such are their oaths. <margin>10</margin>

Those who are caught in serious faults and are expelled from the order often perish by a wretched fate. Because they are bound by their oaths and customs, they are not able to partake of food from other people; instead, they are forced to eat nothing but grass, and with their bodies wasted by hunger, they pass away. <margin>15</margin> For this reason, the community has often taken pity on many in their final extremities and readmitted them, considering that the agony they suffered—reaching even to the gates of death—was a sufficient punishment for their sins. 

They also give a small spade <note>This "small spade" (skalis) was one of the three items given to a new initiate, alongside a loincloth and a white robe</note> to those about to join the sect, for they never <margin>20</margin> relieve themselves without first digging a pit a foot deep; they then cover themselves with their cloak so as not to insult the rays of God <note>Porphyry and Josephus suggest the Essenes viewed the sun’s light as a direct manifestation of the divine, requiring them to cover themselves even when performing natural functions</note>. So great is the simplicity and frugality of their diet that on the seventh day they do not even need to relieve themselves <note>original: "κενώσεως" (kenōseōs) — literally "evacuation." The text implies their moderate eating and discipline were so extreme they could avoid physical needs on the Sabbath</note>, which day they are accustomed to keep strictly for hymns to God and for rest. <margin>25</margin> 

From this rigorous training, they have achieved such a degree of endurance that when they were racked, twisted, burned, and passed through every possible instrument of torture—in order to force them either to blaspheme their lawgiver <note>Moses, the traditional author of the Jewish Law</note> or to eat some unaccustomed food <note>likely meaning food that was not kosher or was prepared by non-Essenes, which would violate their sacred vows</note>—they could be forced to do neither. <margin>30</margin> They clearly demonstrated this during the war against the Romans, when...

# DE ABSTINENTIA IV.

...nor did they stoop to flatter their tormentors or to weep. Instead, smiling during their agonies and scoffing at those inflicting the tortures, they cheerfully released their souls, as if they were certain to receive them back again. For this belief is firmly held among them: that bodies are perishable and their matter is not permanent, but that souls remain immortal forever. They believe that souls, descending from the thinnest ether, are entangled in bodies—as if drawn down by a natural spell—but once they are released from the bonds of the flesh, as if freed from a long slavery, they then rejoice and are carried upward. 

Because of this way of life and their dedication to truth and piety, it is only natural that many among them also foresee the future, being thoroughly educated in the sacred books, various purifications, and the sayings of the prophets. It is rare if they ever miss the mark in their predictions. Such is the order of the <margin>14</margin> Essenes among the Jews. <note>original: "ὅτι ἐκ τῆς ἀρίστης διαγωγῆς τὸ προφητεύειν" — a marginal observation noting that the power of prophecy arises from a superior way of life</note> 

To all Jews, however, it was forbidden to eat the meat of pigs, or of fish without scales (which the Greeks call <term>selachia</term> <note>original: "σελάχια" — cartilaginous fish such as sharks or rays, which lack standard scales</note>), or any of the <term>solid-hoofed</term> animals <note>original: "μωνύχων" (monychōn) — animals like horses or donkeys which have a single, undivided hoof</note>. It was also forbidden to kill even those animals that act like suppliants and, as it were, take refuge in their houses—much less to eat them. Nor did their lawgiver <note>A reference to Moses and the laws found in the Torah</note> permit taking the parents along with the young from a nest; he commands mercy even in a hostile land toward those animals that work alongside us, and forbids their slaughter. 

And he <note>The lawgiver</note> was not afraid that if the species of animals not used for sacrifice increased in number, it would cause a famine for humanity. For he knew, first, that those animals which produce many offspring are generally short-lived; second, that many perish when they do not receive care from humans; and furthermore, that there are other animals which, through their increase...

# DE ABSTINENTIA IV.

...attacks the person sacrificing. The evidence for this is that we abstain from many creatures—such as lizards, worms, mice, snakes, and dogs—and yet there is no fear that we might die of hunger while they overpopulate because of our abstinence. <margin>5</margin> Furthermore, eating is not the same as killing; for even when we destroy many of these creatures <note>Porphyry refers here to "pests" or "vermin" that might be killed for safety but are not eaten</note>, we do not taste any of them.

Moreover, historians report that the Syrians anciently abstained from animals and for this reason did not even sacrifice them to the gods; later, they did sacrifice them to avert certain evils, but they themselves did not admit meat-eating <note>original: "σαρκοφαγίαν" (sarkophagian) — the consumption of flesh</note> at all. <margin>10</margin> As time went on, as Neanthes of Cyzicus and Asclepiades of Cyprus say, meat-eating was introduced during the time of Pygmalion—a Phoenician by birth who ruled the Cypriots—as a result of the following transgression. <margin>15</margin> Asclepiades says the following in his work *On Cyprus and Phoenicia*:

"At first, no living creature <note>original: "ἔμψυχον" (empsychon) — literally 'something with a soul'</note> was sacrificed to the gods, nor was there even a law about this because it was forbidden by natural law. But they tell a story that on certain occasions a victim was first sacrificed, as people were asking for a soul in exchange for a soul <note>original: "ψυχὴν ἀντὶ ψυχῆς" (psychēn anti psychēs) — the concept of substitutionary sacrifice, offering an animal life to save a human one</note>. <margin>20</margin> Then, once this happened, they would burn the whole sacrifice <note>This refers to a 'holocaust' sacrifice, where the entire animal is consumed by fire rather than shared as a meal</note>.

Later, while a victim was burning, a piece of flesh fell to the ground. The priest picked it up, and because he was being burned, he involuntarily brought his fingers to his mouth to soothe the burn. <margin>25</margin> Having tasted the savory steam <note>original: "κνίσσης" (knissēs) — the specific aroma of roasting fat which ancient Greeks believed was the portion of the sacrifice that nourished the gods</note>, he was filled with desire and did not abstain, but even gave some to his wife. 

When Pygmalion discovered this, he threw both the man and his wife off a cliff and handed the priesthood over to another. <margin>30</margin> Not much time passed before this man happened to perform the same sacrifice, and because he also ate of the same meat, he fell into the same misfortunes as the first. As the practice proceeded further..."

# DE ABSTINENTIA IV.

...superstition <note>The text continues a thought from the previous page regarding those who view religious abstinence with suspicion</note>. But those who have made progress in their own wickedness are ready not only to speak impiously against those who advise and demonstrate these things, but even to slander what is holy as mere sorcery and vanity <note>original: "τῦφον" (typhon) — refers to smoke, conceit, or empty delusion</note>. <margin>5</margin> But these people, by paying the penalty for their sins before both gods and men, receive sufficient punishment first from this very disposition of theirs. 

We, however, having mentioned one more famous and just nation among the foreigners—one believed to be pious and devout in divine matters—will then move on to other topics. <margin>10</margin> For while the social order of the **Indians** is divided into many parts, there is among them a certain class of "divine-wise" men <term>theosophists: literally "those wise in the things of God"</term>, whom the Greeks are accustomed to call **Gymnosophists** <term>Gymnosophists: "naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks for Indian ascetics who often practiced extreme poverty and minimal clothing</term>. The lifestyle of these groups is as follows, as *Bardesanes*—a *Babylonian* man <note>A famous scholar and poet from Edessa (154–222 AD), often called "the Babylonian" in late antiquity</note> who lived in the time of our fathers—recorded in his writings after meeting with the Indian ambassadors sent with *Dandamis* <margin>20</margin> to the *Emperor* <note>Likely Emperor Elagabalus or Severus Alexander; Bardesanes met these Indian envoys in Syria</note>. For all *Brahmins* are of one race; they all descend from one father and one mother. The *Samanaeans*, however, are not of the same race, but are gathered, as we said, from the entire nation of the **Indians**. <margin>25</margin> A *Brahmin* is not subject to a king, nor do they pay any tribute to others. 

Among these philosophers, some live on the mountains, and others near the *Ganges* river. The mountain-dwellers feed on seasonal fruits and cow's milk thickened with herbs; <margin>30</margin> while those near the *Ganges* live on the fruits which grow in abundance near the river. The **Samanaeans** <note>Likely referring to Buddhist or Jain monks, derived from the Sanskrit "Sramana," meaning "one who strives"</note> are, as we said, a selected group. Whenever someone intends to be enrolled into the order, he approaches the <margin>15</margin> rulers of the city or wherever the town or village happens to be, and renounces his possessions and all other property. After shaving off the superfluities of the body <note>a reference to the ritual shaving of the head and beard common in monastic initiation</note>, he receives a robe and departs to join the Samanaeans. He has no further concern or <margin>20</margin> regard for his wife or children, if he happens to have them, nor does he think of them as belonging to him at all. Indeed, the King takes care of the children to ensure they have the necessities, and the relatives look after the wife. 

Such is the life of the Samanaeans: they spend their days outside the city, passing the time in <margin>25</margin> discussions about the divine. They have houses and sacred precincts <term>temene: areas of land dedicated to a god or used for religious purposes</term> built by the King, in which there are stewards who receive a fixed allowance from the King for the nourishment of those who gather there. This preparation consists of rice, bread, fruit, and vegetables. <margin>30</margin> When they enter the house at the sounding of a bell, those who are not Samanaeans depart, while the monks pray. After they have prayed, the bell rings again, and the attendants [serve] each man...

# DE ABSTINENTIA IV.

Once they have been fed, they quickly return to their usual occupations. They are all without wives <margin>5</margin> and possess no property. The others hold both them and the **Brahmins** <term>Brahmins: the hereditary priestly class of ancient India, known for their strict religious observances</term> in such high regard that even the King visits them, entreating them to offer prayers and asking for advice on behalf of the country's affairs regarding what should be done.

<margin>10</margin> They themselves are so disposed toward death <margin>18</margin> that they unwillingly endure their time of living as if it were a kind of necessary public service <note>original: "λειτουργίαν" (leitourgian) — a duty performed for the state, here used metaphorically for the burden of physical life</note> to nature, while they hasten to release their souls from their bodies. Often, when they decide the time is right, they depart from life even though no misfortune <margin>15</margin> presses upon them or drives them out; they first announce this to others. No one attempts to stop them; instead, everyone considers them blessed and gives them messages to deliver to their own deceased relatives. So firm and true is the belief—held by them <margin>20</margin> and the common people alike—that souls enjoy a shared life with one another after death.

Once they have heard the requests entrusted to them, they commit their bodies to the fire so that they might separate the soul in its purest state from the body; they die amid songs of praise. For their loved ones send them off to death <margin>25</margin> more readily than other people send off fellow citizens on the longest journeys. They weep for themselves, who must remain in this life, but they celebrate the departed as they receive their immortal inheritance <note>original: "λῆξιν" (lēxin) — a lot or portion assigned by fate</note>. Neither among these people nor among any of the others mentioned has any **sophist** <note>sophist: here used disparagingly by Porphyry to refer to a clever but shallow professional debater</note> <margin>30</margin> come forward—of the kind of "mortals as they are now" <note>A Homeric reference used to contrast the perceived decline of contemporary Greek philosophy with the ancient wisdom of India</note> among the **Greeks**—to raise a difficulty by asking: "If everyone follows your example, what will become of us?" # DE ABSTINENTIA IV.

...human affairs were not thrown into confusion; for not everyone imitated them, and those who did imitate them have been the cause of good order <note>original: "εὐνομίας" (eunomia) — a state of well-ordered laws or civil harmony</note> rather than chaos for the nations. Furthermore, the law did not compel these men; rather, while permitting others to feed on meat, it allowed these men to be autonomous <margin>5</margin> <note>original: "αὐτονόμους" (autonomous) — self-governing or living by their own rules</note> and held them in reverence as being superior to the law itself. It did not subject them to its own legal penalties as if they were the initiators of injustice, but rather it subjected the others. However, to those who ask, "What would happen if everyone imitated such men?" one must state the saying of **Pythagoras**: <margin>10</margin> for if everyone became kings, he says, life would be hard to manage, yet surely one should not avoid kingship on that account. And if everyone were earnest and excellent men, one could not find a way for political systems to maintain a status worthy of that excellence, yet surely no one would be so mad <margin>15</margin> as to think that everyone should not strive to be excellent. Indeed, the law concedes many other things to the common person <note>original: "χυδαίῳ" (chydaio) — the ordinary or 'vulgar' populace</note> which it does not permit to a philosopher, nor even to one who conducts himself well as a citizen. For the law would not admit people from every craft into the government— <margin>20</margin> even though it does not forbid people from pursuing those crafts—nor would it admit those from every occupation. Nevertheless, it bars those from the mechanical trades <term>mechanical trades: 'banausoi', or manual labors that were often viewed by Greek elites as degrading to the soul and unfit for political leadership</term> from holding office; in general, it forbids them from positions where there is a need for justice and other virtues. For the law does not forbid the masses from consorting with courtesans, <margin>25</margin> and it even collects a tax on the earnings of such women, yet it considers association with them to be a reproach for moderate men and a shameful thing. The law has not forbidden living in taverns, and yet this is a reproach to the <margin>30</margin> moderate man. Something of this kind also appears to be the case regarding diet; one would not concede to the best of men that which has been conceded to the masses. A man who practices philosophy should, above all, prescribe these sacred laws for himself...

<summary>Porphyry defends asceticism against the argument that it would be impractical if adopted by everyone, using analogies of kingship, political office, and social decency to show that philosophers must follow higher standards than the general populace.</summary>

# DE ABSTINENTIA IV.

...laws <note>The text begins mid-word: "μους" (mous), likely the conclusion of "νόμους" (nomous), meaning laws.</note>, which both gods and men established by following the divine. <meta>This page concludes the poetic fragment from Euripides' *Cretans* regarding the initiates of Zeus and begins a philosophical investigation into the nature of purity (hagneia) and pollution (miasma). It links dietary habits to a broader metaphysical preference for the "unmixed" and "pure," positioning vegetarianism as a necessary practice for maintaining the soul's integrity.</meta>

# DE ABSTINENTIA IV.

...not drawing near [to births], and I have guarded myself against the eating of food made from living creatures <note>original: "ἐμψύχων" (empsychon) — literally "beings with a soul," referring to animals.</note>.

<margin>20</margin> For the holy ones <note>The priests or initiates mentioned previously.</note> defined purity <note>original: "ἁγνεία" (hagneia)</note> as the state of being unmixed with what is opposite, and pollution as the act of mixing. Therefore, they believed that by consuming a diet of fruits—which are not taken from dead things nor are they <margin>5</margin> living creatures <note>literally "ensouled"</note> by nature—they would not defile the bodily functions governed by nature. But regarding animals, since they are sentient beings, they considered their slaughter and the taking of their souls to be pollutions <note>original: "μιασμούς" (miasmos) — ritual defilement or "miasma."</note> against the living. And <margin>10</margin> even more so, they thought it a pollution to mix a sensory body that has been made dead and deprived of sensation with the sensation of a living person. For this reason, purity in all things consists in the setting aside and holding back from the many and the opposite, and in the <margin>15</margin> isolation and acceptance of things that are proper and fitting.

This is why sexual acts also pollute; for they are a "coming together" <note>original: "σύνοδος" (synodos) — a meeting or conjunction.</note> of female and male. If the seed is retained, it causes a pollution of the soul through its association with the body; if it is not retained, it pollutes through the death of what was discharged. Sexual acts between <margin>20</margin> males are also polluting because they involve a "dead thing" <note>Likely referring to the non-procreative or "unproductive" nature of the act in this philosophical context.</note> and are contrary to nature. Indeed, all sexual acts and nocturnal emissions are pollutions because the soul is mixed with the body and dragged down toward pleasure. The passions <term>passions</term> <note>In ancient philosophy, "passions" (pathe) refer to irrational emotions or impulses that act upon the soul, making it passive rather than active.</note> of the soul also pollute through the entanglement with the irrational part, as the inner male element <margin>25</margin> is "feminized" <note>A common Platonic metaphor where the rational soul is described as masculine and the irrational/appetitive part as feminine.</note>.

Furthermore, both "defilement" and "pollution" signify the mixing of one kind with another, especially when it becomes difficult to wash away. Hence, in the case of dyes, which are created through mixtures where one form is entangled with another, they are said to "pollute" <note>Porphyry is noting that the Greek word for "dyeing" or "staining" (*miainein*) is the same word used for "polluting."</note>:

<margin>30</margin> > As when some woman stains <note>original: "μιήνῃ" (miēnē) — from the same root as pollution/miasma.</note> ivory with crimson dye.

And conversely, painters call these mixtures "corruptions," whereas common usage calls that which is unmixed and pure "incorruptible," "sincere," and "untainted." For indeed, when water is mixed with earth...

<summary>Porphyry defines purity as the avoidance of "mixing" opposite natures, arguing that eating meat pollutes the living with the dead. He extends this logic to sexuality and the passions, using the linguistics of dyeing and painting to show that mixing is inherently a form of corruption.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument from the previous page, further defining "purity" as the absence of mixing and "pollution" as the combination of opposites. # DE ABSTINENTIA IV.

...once mixed, it is corrupted and is not pure; but that which flows through and escapes strikes away the earth that is brought near to it, when—as Hesiod says—it flows from an ever-flowing and trickling source that is unclouded <note>original: "ἀθόλωτος" (atholotos) — clear or free from mud.</note>. Indeed, such a drink is healthy precisely because it is uncorrupted and unmixed. Even a female who has not received into herself the exhalation <note>original: "ἀναθυμίασιν" (anathumiasin) — a term often used for vapors or medicinal "effluvia."</note> of seed <margin>5</margin> is called "uncorrupted." Thus, both corruption and pollution are the mixing of opposites. If, then, the introduction of dead things and the introduction of those who once lived with sensation into the living—that is, of dead flesh into living bodies—rightly brings defilement and pollution to our natural state, so too is <margin>10</margin> the soul defiled whenever it becomes embodied. For this reason, the one who is born is polluted by the mixing of the soul with the body; and the one who has died, when they leave behind a dead body, leaves behind something of a different race <note>original: "ἀλλόφυλον" (allophylon)</note> and foreign to the living. The soul is also polluted <margin>15</margin> by rages, desires, and a multitude of passions, for which diet is also in some way a contributing cause.

Just as water flowing over a rock remains uncorrupted compared to water passing through marshes, because it does not drag along much silt, so too a soul that manages its own affairs through a "dry" body <note>Ancient philosophers, following Heraclitus, believed a "dry" soul was the wisest and most pure.</note>—one not <margin>20</margin> irrigated by the juices of foreign flesh—is better, uncorrupted, and readier for understanding. Indeed, they say that for bees, the finest honey is produced from the driest and most pungent thyme. Therefore, the intellect—or rather, the thinking subject—is polluted <margin>25</margin> when it is mixed with the faculties of imagination or opinion <note>In Porphyry's philosophy, "opinion" (doxa) and "imagination" (phantasia) are lower, less reliable levels of the mind.</note> and blends its own activities with theirs. Purification <note>original: "καθαρμός" (katharmos)</note> is the separation from all these things, and purity <note>original: "ἁγνεία" (hagneia)</note> is isolation. Nourishment, then, is that which preserves each thing in its own state of being. For in this way, you might say that the "nourishment" of a stone <margin>30</margin> is the cause of its staying together and remaining in its state of cohesion; for a plant, it is that which preserves it in growth and fruit-bearing; and for an animal body, it is that which maintains its constitution.

<summary>Porphyry argues that purity consists in remaining "unmixed," comparing the soul's need for a meat-free "dry body" to clear spring water and the best honey. He defines the soul's purification as its separation from physical sensations and lower mental faculties like imagination.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument concerning purity and the soul's detachment from the physical. # DE ABSTINENTIA IV.

...it is one thing to nourish, another to fatten, and yet another to provide only what is necessary, just as it is one thing to provide for luxuries. Diets, therefore, are diverse according to the diversity of the beings being nourished. And while it is necessary to nourish every part of ourselves, we must strive especially to fatten <margin>5</margin> the most sovereign parts within us. Now, the nourishment of the **rational soul** <note>original: "ψυχῆς λογικῆς" (psyches logikes)</note> is that which preserves its rationality. This nourishment is **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — in Neoplatonic thought, the highest part of the soul that perceives divine truths</note>; therefore, we must nourish the soul with Intellect and strive to fatten it from this source, rather than fattening the flesh from the things we eat. For the one [Intellect] holds together our eternal life, but the body, when it is fattened, causes the soul <margin>10</margin> to starve of the blessed life. It increases the mortal part, taking away from and hindering the way toward the immortal life; it defiles the soul by binding it to the body and dragging it down toward that which is foreign to its nature.

The magnetic stone <note>original: "μάγνης λίθος" (magnes lithos)</note> gives a kind of "soul" to iron when it comes near it, and even the heaviest iron is lightened, running up toward the "breath" <note>original: "πνεύματι" (pneumati)</note> of the stone. <margin>15</margin> Who then, having been suspended toward God—who is incorporeal and purely intellectual—would busy themselves with the food that fattens the body, which is the very obstacle to the Intellect? Would he not rather, having contracted the necessities of the flesh into a small and easily obtained <margin>20</margin> amount, nourish himself by clinging to God more closely than iron clings to the magnet? 

Indeed, it would be ideal if we could even abstain from the nourishment of fruits, if only this were not required by the corruptible part of our nature. For if, as **Homer** says, we needed neither food nor drink, then we would truly be immortal. <margin>25</margin> The poet beautifully showed that food was a provision <note>original: "ἐφόδιον" (ephodion) — literally travel-money or supplies for a journey</note> not only for living, but also for dying. If, then, we did not need even this [fruit], we would be as much more blessed as we were more immortal. But as it is, being in a mortal state, we make ourselves even more <margin>30</margin> mortal—if one may say so—by ignoring our true selves in the pursuit of food. For the soul pays no small "rent" <note>original: "ἐνοίκιοv" (enoikion)</note>, as **Theophrastus** <note>A student of Aristotle who wrote extensively on botany and ethics</note> says somewhere, to the body...

<summary>Porphyry argues that we should prioritize nourishing the "Intellect" (Nous) over the body. He uses the analogy of a magnet and iron to describe the soul's attraction to God and warns that heavy consumption of food binds the soul to mortality.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE IV.

...of dwelling in the body, but rather attaching its whole self to it. Would that we could possess the legendary **hunger-less and thirst-less state** <note>original: "ἄλιμον καὶ ἄδιψον" (alimon kai adipson) — referring to mythical herbs or states of being mentioned by writers like Hesiod where bodily needs are suspended</note>, so that by restraining the constant flux of the body, one might briefly remain focused on the highest things—at which point, being in that presence, a god is a god. 

But why should one lament these things to men who are so darkened <margin>5</margin> that they cherish their own evil, and hate first themselves and the one who truly fathered them, and then also those who remind them and exhort them to sober up from their **intoxication** <note>original: "μέθης" (methes) — a common Platonic metaphor for the soul being dazed or confused by its descent into a physical body</note>? Therefore, dismissing such people, we must move <margin>10</margin> on to the remaining parts of our inquiry.

For those who bring up the customs of foreign nations to counter our arguments—mentioning **Nomads**, or **Cave-dwellers**, or **Fish-eaters** <term>Ichthyophages: tribes described by ancient geographers who lived primarily on fish</term>—are unaware that these people turned to this diet out of necessity. <margin>15</margin> Their land is so barren that it does not even produce grass, but only dunes and sand; thus, they were forced into this necessary way of feeding. Evidence of this necessity is the fact that they cannot even use fire for lack of fuel, but instead dry their fish <margin>20</margin> upon the rocks or in the sand. 

These people do so from necessity. But some nations have become savage and are brutal by nature; it is not right for reasonable people to misrepresent human nature based on these. For if we did, then not only the eating of animals but also **cannibalism** <note>original: "ἀνθρωποφαγίας" (anthropophagias)</note> and every other form <margin>25</margin> of refinement would be a matter of dispute. It is recorded, for instance, that the **Massagetae** and **Derbices** consider those among their kin who die naturally to be most wretched. For this reason, they anticipate death by sacrificing and feasting upon those of their loved ones who have grown old. The **Tibareni** <margin>30</margin> cast their oldest relatives down from cliffs while they are still alive. The **Hyrcanians** and **Caspians** behave similarly: some throw the living to birds of prey and dogs, others the dead. The **Scythians**...

<summary>Porphyry argues that the soul must transcend bodily needs and defends his vegetarian stance by explaining that meat-eating tribes do so out of environmental necessity or inherent savagery, rather than natural law.</summary>

# DE ABSTINENTIA IV.

...and they bury them alive and slaughter upon the pyres those whom the deceased loved most. The Bactrians, indeed, throw the elderly while they are still living to the dogs. When Stasanor <note>Stasanor was a general of Alexander the Great who became the governor (satrap) of the regions of Aria and Drangiana; he famously tried to civilize the local customs.</note>, <margin>5</margin> Alexander’s governor, attempted to abolish this custom, he very nearly lost his command. 

But just as we do not abandon our human gentleness because of such people, neither should we imitate those nations who eat flesh out of necessity. Instead, we should imitate those who are pious and more dedicated to the gods. For as Democrates <note>Likely the Pythagorean philosopher, though sometimes confused with the more famous Democritus. He emphasizes that a life without virtue is a slow death.</note> <margin>10</margin> used to say, to live poorly—without wisdom, temperance, or holiness—is not merely to live badly, but to be "dying for a long time." 

<margin>22</margin> Next, let us also bring forward a few testimonies from specific men concerning **abstinence**; for this was one of the charges brought against us. Among the Athenian <margin>15</margin> legislators, we have received Triptolemus <note>A legendary figure in Greek myth who was taught the art of agriculture by the goddess Demeter and was said to have spread the knowledge of grain throughout the world.</note> as the most ancient. Concerning him, Hermippus writes the following in his second book *On the Legislators*: 

"They say that Triptolemus gave laws to the Athenians, and the philosopher Xenocrates <note>Xenocrates (c. 396–314 BCE) was the third head of Plato’s Academy; he was known for his strict moral character and interest in Pythagoreanism.</note> says that three of his laws still remain at Eleusis <note>The site of the famous Eleusinian Mysteries, the most sacred religious rites of ancient Greece.</note> to this day: <margin>20</margin> **to honor one's parents, to glorify the gods with the fruits of the earth, and not to harm animals.**" 

The first two, Xenocrates says, were well-handed down. For it is right that we should repay our parents, who were our benefactors, as far as possible; and to the gods, we should offer the first-fruits of the things they gave us that are useful for our lives. <margin>25</margin> But regarding the third, he wonders what Triptolemus was thinking when he commanded people to abstain from animals. 

"Was it," he asks, "because he thought it altogether terrible to kill one’s own kind <note>original: "τὸ ὁμογενὲς κτείνειν" (to homogenes kteinein) — Xenocrates is questioning if Triptolemus recognized a kinship between humans and animals.</note>, or because he saw that humans were slaughtering the most useful animals for food?" <margin>30</margin> Wishing, therefore, to make life more civilized and gentle, he attempted to preserve those animals that live alongside humans—especially those that are tame. Unless, perhaps, it was because...

<summary>Porphyry argues that civilized people should not imitate the "barbaric" customs of meat-eating tribes and cites the ancient Athenian laws of Triptolemus, which forbade harming animals.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV

# ON ABSTINENCE, BOOK IV

I chose you, Marcella—a mother of five daughters and two sons, some still infants and others already approaching the age of marriage—to be my <unclear>wife, neither because</unclear> <unclear>of</unclear>

# TO MARCELLA

<margin>5</margin> any necessary help I might receive from them, nor for the sake of having children from your body. For I have decided that my children are those who love true wisdom <note>original: "τῆς ἀληθινῆς σοφίας" (tēs alēthinēs sophias) — A core Platonic concept where spiritual or intellectual offspring are valued above biological ones.</note>, and your own children might also become so, if they should ever take hold of right philosophy while being raised by us. Do not imagine that this irrational turmoil of <term>passion</term> <note>original: πάθους (pathous) — in Neoplatonism, this refers to irrational emotions or "passions" like grief or fear that disturb the soul's peace.</note> concerns trivial matters—you, who have been initiated into true philosophy through divine teachings. One who has come to believe must <margin>5</margin> live in such a way that they themselves become a faithful witness to the things they say to their listeners. Was it not that, to you, I am not this tangible man, subject to the <margin>10</margin> senses, but rather that which is most distant from the body—the colorless and formless part, which can never be touched by hands but is grasped by the mind alone? We do not receive from external sources the truths that have been placed within us; rather, those outside only provide the "starting note," as in a chorus, leading us toward <margin>15</margin> the <term>recollection</term> <note>original: ἀνάμνησιν (anamnēsin) — the Platonic concept that the soul already possesses all truth and only needs to "remember" it.</note> of those things we once possessed from the Giver, but from which we have wandered. 

<margin>9</margin> Furthermore, did we not learn that every passion of the soul is the greatest enemy to its salvation? Did we not learn that lack of discipline is the mother of all passions, and that true education consists not in the accumulation of vast knowledge, <margin>20</margin> but in being set free from the soul's passions? Passions are the origins of diseases; the disease of the soul is vice; and all vice is a thing of shame. Since shame is the opposite of the <term>Beautiful</term> <note>original: καλῷ (kalō) — in Greek thought, beauty and moral goodness are often the same concept.</note>, and since the Divine is Beautiful, it is impossible for one to draw near to the Divine while steeped in vice. For as <margin>25</margin> Plato says, it is not permitted for the impure to touch the pure. For this reason, even now, one must remain pure from passions and the errors that arise from them. Were these not the very principles you most agreed with—reading them within yourself like divine scriptures, brought to light by the <margin>30</margin> explanation of words? How, then, is it not absurd for you—who are convinced that within yourself resides both the Savior and the saved, as well as the destroyer and the destroyed...

# EPISTLE TO MARCELLA.

...the divine is wisdom. And one must adorn the temple for Him within the mind through wisdom, rejoicing in the mind as a **living statue** <note>original: ἐμψύχῳ ἀγάλματι (empsychō agalmati) — In Neoplatonism, the soul is seen as a "statue" or "shrine" that must be sculpted and purified to reflect the divine.</note> modeled after Him... For while God needs nothing, the wise person needs only God. Indeed, no one could become 
<margin>5</margin> **noble and good** <note>original: καλὸς κἀγαθὸς (kalos kagathos) — a classical Greek phrase describing a person of ideal moral and social virtue.</note> unless he understands that which is Good and Beautiful, which emanates from the Divine. Nor, on the other hand, is any man more wretched than he who has fashioned his soul to be a dwelling place for evil spirits. But to a wise man, God
<margin>10</margin> grants the authority of a god. A person is purified by the thought of God, and, starting from God, pursues **righteous action**.

<margin>12</margin> Let God be present as an observer and overseer of every deed, work, and word. Let us consider God the cause of all the good things we do; but of evils, we who choose them are the cause, while **God is blameless**. <note>original: θεὸς δὲ ἀναίτιος (theos de anaitios) — This is a direct reference to Plato’s *Republic* (617e), a foundational concept in Greek philosophy meaning that humans have free will and are responsible for their own moral failings.</note>
<margin>15</margin> Therefore, one must pray for things worthy of God. We should ask for things we could not receive from anyone else; and for those things where the labor accompanying virtue leads the way, let us pray for these to come to pass after the labor; for the prayer of the lazy is empty talk.
<margin>20</margin> Whatever you cannot hold onto once you have acquired it, do not ask from God; for every gift of God is **irrevocable**; <note>original: ἀναφαίρετον (anaphaireton) — literally "not to be taken away." Porphyry argues that God only gives eternal, spiritual gifts, not temporary material ones.</note> thus, He will not give what you cannot keep. Despise those things you will not need once you are released from the body; and those things you will still need after that release, pray to God to be your helper as you practice to attain them.
<margin>25</margin> You will then have no need for anything that Fortune often gives and takes away again. One should not make a request before the proper time, but only when God reveals to you the **correct request**,
<margin>13</margin> which exists in you by nature. Through such requests, God is most naturally reflected, since He is
<margin>30</margin> neither visible through the body nor through a soul that is ugly and darkened by vice. For His beauty is pure, and His light is the life-giving radiance of truth...

# EPISTLE TO MARCELLA.

...but every <insert>expectation</insert> is deceived by ignorance and distorted by shame. Therefore, desire and ask of God those things that He Himself desires and that He is, knowing well that 
<margin>5</margin> to the extent that one desires the body and the things that belong to the body, to that same extent they are ignorant of God and have darkened their own vision of Him, even if they are glorified as a god by all other people. But a **wise person** <note>original: σοφὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος (sophos de anthrōpos) — In this context, the 'wise person' is the philosopher who lives according to reason rather than impulse.</note>, though known by only a few—or, if you prefer, even if ignored by everyone—is known by God. Therefore, let the 
<margin>10</margin> **Mind** follow God, reflecting the likeness of God; and let the **Soul** follow the Mind; and in turn let the **Body** serve the Soul, as far as possible, as a pure servant to a pure mistress. For when the body is defiled by the passions of the soul, the pollutions return back upon the soul itself.
<margin>14</margin> In the God-loving soul and the 
<margin>15</margin> God-loving Mind within a pure body, let there be consistent action and speech. It is better for you to cast a stone at random than a word, and better to be defeated while speaking the truth than to conquer through deceit. For that which conquers by deceit is defeated in **character**. <note>original: ἐν τῷ ἤθει (en tō ēthei) — referring to one's moral disposition or "ethics."</note> False words are witnesses of 
<margin>20</margin> evil things. It is impossible for the same person to be a **lover of God** and a lover of pleasure or a lover of the body. For the lover of pleasure is also a lover of the body; and the lover of the body is surely also a **lover of money**; and the lover of money is, of necessity, unjust. The unjust person is unholy toward God and his parents, and lawless 
<margin>25</margin> toward everyone else. Therefore, even if he sacrifices **hecatombs** <note>original: ἑκατόμβας (hekatombas) — traditionally a sacrifice of one hundred oxen, here used to mean any lavish, expensive religious ritual.</note> and adorns the temples with ten thousand offerings, he is impious and godless and, in his underlying intent, a temple-robber. <margin>15</margin> Do not share your life or your discourse about God with anyone whose opinions you would not respect. 
<margin>30</margin> For it is not safe to speak of God to those corrupted by false opinion; for even to speak the truth among such people concerning...

<margin>5</margin> But one should listen to and speak the word about God as if in the presence of God. <margin>10</margin> God. Choosing to neither say, nor do, nor even know anything at all unworthy of God will make you worthy of Him. 
<margin>16</margin> Now, the person who is worthy of God would be a **god** <note>original: θεός (theos) — This refers to the Neoplatonic concept of "deification" (theosis), where a human soul reaches a divine state by purifying its intellect and living virtuously.</note>. <margin>15</margin> **virtue** <note>original: ἀρετή (aretē) — Moral excellence or the internal "fitness" of the soul.</note> alone. For virtue alone draws the soul upward and toward its kin. God is greater than virtue, but God strengthens the person doing good; whereas an **evil spirit** <note>original: κακὸς δαίμων (kakos daimōn) — Not necessarily a "demon" in the modern sense, but a malevolent spiritual influence or a lower impulse that leads the soul away from reason.</note> is the leader of evil deeds. 
<margin>20</margin> Therefore, an evil soul flees from God and does not wish for there to be a divine providence; such a soul completely falls away from the divine law which punishes everything base. But the soul of a **wise person** <note>original: σοφός (sophos) — The philosopher who lives according to reason and divine principles.</note> is harmonized with God, always sees God, and is always with God. And if the ruler rejoices in the subject, God also cares for and provides for the wise person; and 
<margin>25</margin> for this reason, the wise person is blessed, because they are overseen by God. It is not the tongue of the wise person that is precious before God, but their deeds. For a wise man honors God even while silent; but an ignorant person defiles the divine even while praying and sacrificing. Therefore, only the wise person is a priest, only the 
<margin>17</margin> <margin>30</margin> wise person is beloved of God, and only the wise person knows how to pray. And whoever practices wisdom practices the knowledge of God—not by constantly petitioning and sacrificing, but by showing [piety] toward God through their deeds...

<summary>Porphyry argues that true divinity is reached through virtue and silent wisdom rather than religious ritual or empty words. He identifies the "wise person" as the only true priest, whose deeds and harmonized soul make them worthy of God.</summary>

<margin>18</margin> For this is the greatest fruit of piety: to honor the divine according to ancestral customs, not as if He were in need of anything, 
<margin>15</margin> but because we are called toward His worship by His most revered and blessed majesty.

<margin>20</margin> superior to God. Therefore, the gods do not harm us because they have been angered, but because they have been ignored. For **anger** <note>original: ὀργή (orgē) — Porphyry explains that divine "anger" is a human metaphor; gods cannot feel anger because it is a reaction to something happening against one's will, and nothing happens against God's will.</note> is foreign to the gods, since anger is directed at things that happen against one's will, and for God, nothing is against His will. Therefore, do not defile the divine with human 
<margin>25</margin> false opinions; for you will not harm that which is forever blessed and from whose incorruptibility all harm has been driven out, but you will blind yourself to the discernment of the greatest and most sovereign things. 
<margin>19</margin> But consider that I say these things to you not as one commanding you to worship God—for he who commands this is 
<margin>30</margin> ridiculous, as if there were any doubt about it—but because it is not by merely doing or believing certain things well about God that we worship Him. Neither tears nor supplications turn God toward us, nor do sacrifices...

<summary>Porphyry argues that true piety consists in mental disposition rather than ritual, asserting that God is never harmed by human neglect nor moved by flattery, but that we harm ourselves by holding false beliefs about the divine.</summary>

...understood that everything is provided for by God, and that there are divine angels and **good spirits** <note>original: ἀγαθοὶ δαίμονες (agathoi daimones) — In Neoplatonic thought, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but benevolent intermediary beings between the human and divine realms.</note> who are observers of all that is done, whom it is impossible to escape. Thus, having cast themselves into unspeakable danger by irrational impulse and being prone to stumbling in their lives, they set themselves to every task and do all that is unlawful, attempting to destroy the common conception regarding the gods. And indeed, these people escape the notice of the gods because of their ignorance and unbelief; yet they themselves are unable to escape or hide from the gods or from **Justice** <note>original: Δίκην (Dikēn) — The personification of divine retribution and moral order.</note>, the attendant of the gods. Having chosen a wretched and wandering life, they are known by the gods and by the justice that comes from the gods, even while they remain ignorant of them.

<margin>23</margin> Even if they think they honor the gods and are convinced that gods exist, if they neglect **virtue** <note>original: ἀρετή (aretē)</note> and **wisdom** <note>original: σοφία (sophia)</note>, they have denied and dishonored the gods. For neither is **irrational faith** <note>original: ἄλογος πίστις (alogos pistis) — Belief without the foundation of reason or correct living.</note> successful in reaching God without living rightly, nor is honoring the gods an act of true piety without having learned in what way the Divine rejoices in being honored. For if the Divine is persuaded by libations or sacrifices, it would not be just, since it would be asking for an equal return from all when all have not received an equal fortune. But if it is none of these things, and it delights only in the mind being pure—which is indeed possible for anyone to possess by their own choice—how could this not be just? But if the Divine rejoices in being served by both, namely by sacrifices...

Therefore, you must first understand the **law of nature** <margin>27</margin>, and from this you must ascend to the divine law, which also ordained the law of nature; starting from these, you will in no way fear the **written law** <note>original: ἔγγραφον (eggraphon) — referring to human civil or criminal law.</note>. -># EPISTLE TO MARCELLA.<-

Any possession that is sufficient is wealth, but in relation to unlimited desires, even the greatest wealth is <note>The Greek text here says "wealth," but Porphyry is quoting a philosophical maxim where the sense is often "even the greatest wealth is poverty" (penia) when measured against infinite greed.</note>. For none of the foolish are satisfied with what they have, but rather they suffer for what they do not have. Just as those suffering from a fever, due to the malignancy of the disease, are always thirsty and desire the most contrary things, so too those whose souls are in a bad state are always in want of everything and fall into manifold <margin>28</margin> desires through greediness. Therefore, the gods also commanded purification through **abstinence** <note>original: ἀποχῆς (apochēs) — a central concept in Porphyry’s philosophy, especially regarding his vegetarianism and asceticism.</note> from foods and sexual pleasures, leading those pursuing piety toward the **will of nature** <note>original: βούλημα τῆς φύσεως (boulēma tēs physeōs)</note>, which they themselves established, since everything that exceeds that will is defiled and deadly. For the common man, fearing a simple way of life, proceeds because of this fear toward actions that especially provide wealth. And many, having obtained wealth, found not a release from evils, but a change to greater ones. Therefore philosophers say nothing is as necessary as knowing well what is *not* necessary; they take the view that **self-sufficiency** <term>self-sufficiency: (original: αὐτάρκεια / autarkeia) the state of needing nothing external for one's happiness or virtue.</term> is the richest of all things and that needing nothing is a holy thing. Wherefore they also advise us to practice not how we might provide ourselves with something necessary, but rather how we might be confident <margin>29</margin> even if it is not provided. Let us neither blame the **flesh** <note>original: σάρκα (sarka) — Porphyry argues that the body itself is not the source of sin, but rather the soul's misplaced focus on the body.</note> as the cause of great evils, nor turn our distress toward external things; rather, let us seek the causes of these things in the soul, and having broken off every vain desire for ephemeral things and every hope, let us become entirely our own masters. For a person is miserable either through fear or through unlimited and empty desire; by bridling these, one can provide for oneself the **blessed reasoning** <note>original: μακάριον λογισμόν (makarion logismon) — the state of a mind that is at peace and aligned with divine truth.</note>.

It is better for you to be confident while lying on a straw pallet than to be troubled while possessing a golden couch and a luxurious table. From a savage way of working, a mass of property is heaped up, but a wretched life is constructed. <margin>30</margin> Consider nothing to be inconsistent with the study of nature when the soul cries out along with the crying flesh. The voice of the flesh is: not to be hungry, not to be thirsty, not to be cold. While it is difficult for the soul to prevent these sensations, it is dangerous to ignore the nature that has commanded her through the self-sufficiency natural to her every day. Do not think that the affairs of the soul are of lesser importance; you should recognize that those who are successful in the world's eyes are actually unfortunate, while those who are unfortunate should not think much of the things that constitute "success." For through the love of true **philosophy** <note>original: φιλοσοφία (philosophia)</note>, every turbulent and painful desire is dissolved. Empty is the word of that philosopher by whom no human **passion** <note>original: πάθος (pathos) — referring here to an emotional disturbance or a disease of the soul</note> is healed; for just as there is no benefit in medicine if it does not treat the diseases of the body, so there is no benefit in philosophy if it does not cast out the passion of the soul. These things, and others like them, <margin>32</margin> are what the law of **nature** <note>original: φύσις (physis)</note> commands. But the divine law cries out in the pure volume of the intellect: "Unless you keep the body attached to you only as the afterbirth is to the developing embryo, or as the stalk is to the sprouting grain, you will not know yourself." <meta>This page continues Porphyry’s philosophical letter to his wife, Marcella. Having previously discussed the necessity of mastering physical needs like hunger and thirst, Porphyry now moves into a deeper Neoplatonic argument: the body is merely a temporary attachment or "afterbirth" of the soul. He urges Marcella to transcend her physical gender and focus on the "virgin soul," which alone can produce immortal offspring.</meta>

# EPISTLE TO MARCELLA.

He who thinks this way has truly known himself. For just as the placenta <note>original: χορίον (chorion). Porphyry uses the biological term for the afterbirth or fetal membrane to emphasize the body's temporary, disposable nature.</note> is formed along with the child, or the stalk along with the grain—yet both are cast away once they are worn out—so too the body that is attached to the soul is not a part of the human being. Rather, <margin>5</margin> just as the placenta was woven around the child so it could exist in the womb, the body was joined to the soul so it could exist upon the earth. To the degree that a person turns toward the mortal, they make their own mind <note>original: γνώμην (gnōmēn) - here meaning the seat of judgment or will.</note> unsuitable for the greatness of immortality. And to the extent that one distances themselves from attachment to the body, <margin>10</margin> by that same measure they draw near to the divine. An intelligent man who is dear to God will strive to labor for the sake of his soul just as much as others toil for the sake of the body. He does not think it is enough simply to remember what he has heard, but rather he practices returning to the things he must reach by means of what <margin>15</margin> <margin>33</margin> he has heard. When he is sent away naked and lives unburdened, he will call upon the One who sent him. For God listens only to the one who is not weighed down by foreign things <note>Porphyry refers to physical possessions and bodily desires as "foreign" to the soul's true nature.</note>, and He stands above all that is pure from corruption. Consider it a great provision for a blessed life to "bind the binder" that is bound by nature. <margin>20</margin> For we have been bound by nature’s bonds which she wrapped around us—the belly, the genitals, the throat, and the other parts of the body—and by the uses, pleasures, and fears that arise through them. If we rise above their enchantment and guard against the trap of their plot, <margin>25</margin> we have "bound the binder." Therefore, do not concern yourself with whether your body is male or female, nor look at yourself as a woman, for I did not attend to you as such. Flee from everything feminine in the soul, even as if you had a male body wrapped around you. <margin>30</margin> For the most blessed offspring are born from a virgin soul and a god-filled mind; for incorruptible things come from the incorruptible. But the things the body births are considered defiled by all...

<summary>Porphyry argues that the body is a temporary vessel to be discarded like a placenta, and he encourages Marcella to transcend her physical gender to achieve a "virgin soul" capable of divine union.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Neoplatonism, soul and body, asceticism, gender transcendence, immortality, divinity, Marcella</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s ethical instructions to his wife, Marcella. On the previous page, he described the body as a "foreign" shell or a placenta that the soul must eventually discard. This page begins by concluding that the person who masters the physical realm is recognized by the divine, then moves into practical advice on self-discipline, the treatment of domestic servants, and the essential link between human kindness and religious piety.</meta>

# EPISTLE TO MARCELLA.

[Such a person] is recognized by the gods. It is therefore a great education to rule over the <margin>34</margin> body. People often amputate certain parts of themselves for the sake of the salvation of the body; but you, for the sake of the salvation of the soul, must be ready to cut away the whole body <note>Porphyry uses a striking medical metaphor: just as a surgeon might remove a gangrenous limb to save a patient's life, the philosopher must be willing to "sever" their attachment to the entire physical body to save the eternal soul.</note>. For those things for which you wish to live, do not hesitate to die for them as well. <margin>5</margin> Therefore, let Reason <note>original: λόγος (logos)</note> lead every impulse, banishing those terrible and godless masters from us—for it is even more difficult to be a slave to the passions than to be a slave to tyrants. It is impossible for one who is conquered by the passions to be free; <margin>10</margin> for as many passions as there are in the soul, so many are its cruel masters. <margin>35</margin> Try not to wrong your servants, and do not punish them while you are angry. When you are about to punish them, first persuade them that you are doing so for their own benefit, and give them a chance to speak in their own defense. Avoid <margin>15</margin> acquiring servants who are arrogant. Practice doing most things for yourself <note>original: αὐτουργεῖν (autourgein) - literally "self-working" or manual labor. Porphyry advocates for the philosophical ideal of self-sufficiency (autarkeia).</note>; for self-sufficiency is simple and easy to provide for, and humans ought to use each part of themselves for the purpose nature intended, since nature requires nothing else. For those who do not use their own limbs, but instead misuse the labor of others, the burden <margin>20</margin> is doubled, and they are ungrateful toward the nature given to those parts. Never use your limbs for the sake of mere pleasure; for it is much better to die than to darken the soul through a lack of self-control . . . . correcting the vice of nature . . . . as one who shares honor <margin>25</margin> with servants, grant a portion of that honor to those who are better. For there is no way for a person who wrongs a human being to truly revere God; rather, let philanthropy <note>original: φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpia) - here meaning a general love or kindness toward fellow human beings, regardless of status.</note> be considered by you as the foundation of piety and . . . .

<sig>14*</sig>

<summary>Porphyry advises Marcella on the necessity of self-mastery over the body and passions, arguing that true freedom is internal. He also provides practical ethical guidance on treating servants with reason and fairness, concluding that one cannot truly worship God while mistreating other human beings.</summary>

<keywords>Porphyry, Marcella, self-mastery, asceticism, treatment of slaves, Reason (Logos), passions, philanthropy, piety, Neoplatonism</keywords>
